  • A single-ended profile also sets the class's pair width.
  • Profiled nets get no neck-down, because the profile's width is also KiCad's minimum.

The reader now also drops the profiles of schema-4 settings, with a warning, as KiCad does. After the fixes, plane_smd routes 48/49 with no added error. RoyalBlue drops from 125/147 to 102/147 with the single-ended profile (every Default net now keeps 0.25 mm on the outer layers and 0.2 mm inside, with no neck-down at fine-pitch pads) and to 104/147 with both profiles. Neither has a track_width error. The pair profile leaves 5 diff_pair_gap_out_of_range errors, which §59 explains. "Narrowing is free" no longer holds: the earlier 125 came from the judge that read no profile.

docs.title: 59. Time-domain matching: delays as KiCad 10.0.6 measures them (doc 18 B2, 2026-10-28, D147)
docs.text:
KiCad 10 measures a net's length and propagation delay in LENGTH_DELAY_CALCULATION (pcbnew/length_delay_calculation). A length or skew constraint given in ps or fs is compared with the delay. The engine read the units but measured lengths its own way, ignored time rules, and had no tuner aiming at a delay.

Measurement (drc/length.hpp, drc::net_length). This is a port of 10.0.6's calculation, with its quirks:

  • Pieces. A net's tracks and arcs, in file order, are chained where ends meet. In 10.0.6 a chain grows at an end only where exactly one other line end remains, on the same layer, and the first line of each chain is taken out of the search first. On a branched net the result therefore depends on the order KiCad visits the lines, which is the order of their addresses (a std::set of pointers). KiCad master merges only at simple two-end joints.
  • Vias. A via counts when its span is used: a line ends at its centre or strictly inside its disc, or a pad it touches is on the net (an SMD pad on its copper layer, a through-hole pad on its footprint's side). Its height is the stackup distance between the outermost layers used (doc 05 §38's via_heights, moved to drc). A via joining one layer only is a stub: counted, with no height. Without "use height for length calculations", vias count for nothing.
  • Clipping. A chain end inside a via's disc is replaced by a straight line from the via's centre to where the chain crosses the disc's edge. A chain end exactly on a pad's position is clipped at the pad's outline.
  • Rounding. Segment lengths are rounded to the nanometre and arc lengths are truncated. A layer's delay is its delay per mm times the length in mm, truncated to the attosecond. A via's delay is the profile's override for its signal and via layers (upper layer first), else its delay per mm times its height, and only with time-domain tuning on. A pad's die delay counts only when the net has a profile.

Check (drc.cpp, check_lengths). This is KiCad's matched-length test:

  • Every pad, track, arc and via is grouped by the last rule giving it a length or skew constraint at its layer, then by net. Each group is sorted by net name.
  • A length outside the window is reported on its minimum first. A rule in ps compares the delay.
  • Skew is measured against the net with the most length or delay. In 10.0.6 that net is measured against itself too, so a minimum skew always fails on it (KiCad's QA board shows exactly that one violation). within_diff_pairs pairs each net with its partner.
  • A rule at severity ignore is skipped.

Net classes, as 10.0.6 resolves them (DesignRules::classes_of). A net's effective class is built from every class that matches it. Default joins when the matched classes leave any of ten fields unset (clearance, track width, via and microvia sizes, pair width and gap, wire and bus width), or when none of them has a tuning profile and Default has one. Such a composite is named "A,Default", so hasExactNetclass('A') misses it. hasNetclass('A') is true when any constituent is named exactly A; it is now evaluated, and was taken as false before. A class with an empty profile takes Default's. Net settings older than schema 5 lose every profile when KiCad migrates them, and the reader does the same and warns. A missing schema version means no migration.

Coupling check (drc/coupling.hpp, check_diff_pairs). This is a port of KiCad's diff-pair coupling test, which the engine did not have, so diff_pair_gap rules were not checked at all:

  • A P track and an N track on one layer are coupled where their lines are exactly parallel (a zero integer cross product) and not collinear, and their projections overlap. The pair is skipped when anything else on the layer crosses the line between their nearest points, apart from tracks and vias touching the coupled ends and pads that either track leaves.
  • The gap is the centreline distance minus the half widths, with KiCad's rounding. It must lie within the rule, with the DRC epsilon.
  • Items are grouped by pair and rule names under KiCad's key comparator. Its quirk keys an item twice when both a gap and an uncoupled rule apply, so the gap errors are reported even then. diff_pair_uncoupled compares the longer half's track length minus the coupled length.
  • Arc pairs are not coupled (the router writes no arcs).

A tuning profile's pair gap is a rule with min = max = gap and no uncoupled limit. Every parallel stretch of the two halves that can see the other must therefore be at exactly the gap, which includes stretches far apart with nothing between them.

Routing (Router::tune_delays, after tune_lengths and tune_skew). Each net with a length rule in ps is tuned into its window. A meander raises the delay by the delay per mm of the layer it is on, so only tracks on layers with a delay are candidates. The tuner measures with the same calculation as the check, and its last meander is cut to fit. Then each skew rule in ps: the nets it groups, or each pair with within_diff_pairs, are brought to within a quarter of the limit below the net with the most delay. Nets of a profiled class are not necked down (§58). When the meanders do not fit, the tuner rips the routed connections in their way and routes them again (§61, D152).

Pair names (drc::match_dp_suffix, D149). Nets are paired as KiCad 10.0.6's MatchDpSuffix pairs them: - From the end of the name, digits and underscores are skipped. The next character must be P or + (positive) or N or − (negative). - The partner's name swaps that character, so LVDS_N0_1 pairs with LVDS_P0_1. - inDiffPair('x') matches the base, which is the name before that character. If the base ends in an underscore, it also matches the base without it. So D_P1 is in inDiffPair('D') and in inDiffPair('D_').

Before, the engine looked only at the last character and matched the whole name minus that character, or the whole name. Among the 4,143 fixture boards, only vme-wren (its DDR4 DQS_P0..3/DQS_N0..3) and one freerouting fixture pair differently. Pair routing, the relaxed gap between pair halves and the DRC's pair polarity all use the same pairing.

Routing around coupling errors (Obstacles::coupling_state, D148). This applies when a pair net has a diff_pair_gap rule, not ignored, with a minimum or a maximum on a layer. A new track of that net is then tested against each track of its partner on that layer with the same coupling test as the check, the same epsilon included. A coupling out of range blocks the track if the partner track is fixed copper. If the partner track was routed, it can be ripped up. The test is part of segment_state, so the exact check at commit applies it to merged segments. The search also applies it to each lattice step of such a net, because otherwise a path that the exact check rejects at the end is found again and again. When looking for something between the two tracks, the router does not consider pad holes on layers that have none of the pad's copper. It is therefore stricter than KiCad there, never looser. Boards without such a rule do not run the test.

Results (bench/records/m21-b2, KiCad 10.0.6 as the judge):

  • KiCad's QA board time_calculations (copied into tests/boards): the six classes' delays match KiCad's to 0.01 ps, and the DRC reports the same single CLASS7 skew violation.
  • Length parity on four demo boards (StickHub, RoyalBlue, interf_u, CM5_MINIMA_3), with a rule no net can meet so that both DRCs print every length: 329 nets were measured by both. 313 agree to 0.0001 mm and 12 more to under 1 µm. Four power or mesh nets differ by 0.04 to 1.58 mm (StickHub GND and +5V, RoyalBlue GND and /Debugger/D-), all branched inside vias, where 10.0.6's result depends on pointer order. A simulation of the merge in file order gave the engine's value on /Debugger/D-.
  • ddr8 (bench/make_delay_boards.py): a byte lane from a front controller to a back memory, with a 205–215 ps window, at most 3 ps of skew and 0.5 ps within the strobe pair. Before: 11 window and 9 skew errors. After: 17/17 routed and KiCad finds none.
  • interf_u (four memory-data lanes, 2 layers, a 245–260 ps window and 3 ps skew) and RoyalBlue (the debugger USB pair, 0.5 ps within the pair), both 3 M work. The build before B2 left 4 window and 3 skew errors on interf_u and 1 pair-skew error on RoyalBlue. B2 leaves none, at the same routed counts (145/164 and 119/147). The engine's DRC gives the same verdicts as KiCad on all four boards (timing-verdicts.json). RoyalBlue's 119, against 125 without the rule file, is the exact-check mode that any custom rule other than a disallow turns on in this branch. D139, on its own branch, fixes that.
  • B1 rejudged (§58): the five diff_pair_gap_out_of_range errors on RoyalBlue with the USB pair profile are found by the engine's DRC as well, at the same places with the same gaps. They are where the USB-C connector's interleaved D+/D− pads, 0.5 mm apart, are joined pad to pad and leave in parallel before the pair forms.
  • Routing around coupling errors (runs/couple-b1, runs/couple-b2, same settings): RoyalBlue with the pair profile still routes 104/147, with 353 tracks against 349. KiCad's five gap errors are gone. The other four B1 boards and the three B2 boards are identical to the runs before the change (routed counts, tracks, vias, added errors).

Not done.

  • fromTo() is not evaluated, so length rules written with it (vme-wren) are unchecked.
  • The bus tuner (§38) ignores ps skew rules.
  • A net in two classes takes its parameters from the first.

Tests:

  • [length], four cases: the QA board's delays and its one skew violation; clipping, via span, a stub, and height off; layer, via and override delays with time-domain tuning on and off; ps parsing.
  • [coupling], four cases: pair names as MatchDpSuffix reads them; coupled stretch and gap, direction, diagonals; lines that meet, collinear, end to end, about 1 nm; and a routed pair whose pads are 2 mm apart under a 0.15–0.25 mm gap rule. With the rule ignored, the straight tracks break the rule; with the rule in force, the routed pair has no gap errors.
  • rule_parity: static_has_class_* (four), tuning_profile_inherited, tuning_profile_schema4, and diff_pair_gap, diff_pair_gap_ignored and diff_pair_uncoupled (cross-stretch couplings, a shielded pair, and the doubled key). Two more with D149: diff_pair_suffix and diff_pair_suffix_base. All 231 cases match; the build before D149 fails diff_pair_suffix.
  • delay_tuning (integration): ddr8 routed with the rules is clean by the engine's DRC and by KiCad; routed without them, it misses.

docs.title: 60. Vias and pads that remove unconnected copper (2026-10-28, D150)
docs.text:
KiCad lets a via or a through-hole pad drop its copper on the layers where nothing connects to it (the padstack's "remove unconnected layers"). The engine read such a via as copper on every layer of its span. On boards that use the option it reported clearance and shorting errors against copper KiCad does not have, filled zones around rings that are not there, and on vme-wren judged diff pairs as hidden from each other by rings KiCad had removed.

Reading (io/kicad/board_reader.cpp). The mode is set token by token in file order, as KiCad's parser sets it: a via's (remove_unused_layers) switches removal on, its (keep_end_layers) keeps the outer layers, its (start_end_only) keeps only them; a pad's (remove_unused_layers) and (keep_end_layers) set the mode either way. (zone_layer_connections ...) lists the layers a zone joins it on.

Flashing (drc/copper.cpp, drc::flash_layers). A layer of a via or pad that may lose its copper keeps it when the file says a zone joins it there, or when a same-net track, arc, via or pad reaches it on that layer. As in KiCad's connectivity (CN_VISITOR), the item is looked at as its hole on such layers: a track that touches the ring but not the hole does not keep the ring. A pad reaches F.Cu to B.Cu if it is plated through and only its first layer otherwise; the items of the pad's own footprint, and two pads whose layers are both conditional, do not count.

Copper model. A via or pad with bare layers is two items: its copper on the flashed layers, and a hole-shaped bare part on the others, which KiCad's clearance test checks at copper clearance. The bare part has no connectivity of its own (its root and net are the main item's) and is left out of the checks that look at copper (rings, widths, edges, keepouts, lengths, pairs, dangling); a rule's existsOnLayer and area tests use the whole span.

Zones (drc/refill.cpp). Before filling, KiCad's filler works out again which layers a zone joins each via and pad on (the highest-priority zone of the net that contains the hole there, with its accuracy and keepout quirks); the refill does the same on a copy of the board. A same-net via that no zone joins on a layer is knocked out of the fill there like another net's.

Router (route/obstacles.cpp). A new track or via of the net does not flash a bare layer it did not plan to reach, so the router keeps its own net clear of bare parts (and new vias clear of same-net rings that may be removed). This is stricter than KiCad, which would flash the layer and connect them.

Nearly parallel pairs. KiCad couples two tracks whose lines do not meet (!SEG::Intersect(..., lines)). In line mode SEG reports no crossing when the crossing point does not fit in 32 bits, so tracks a few nanometres off parallel are coupled (vme-wren's DQS0 has two 45° stubs 10 nm off). drc::couple computes the crossing as SEG does and couples them too; the router uses the same function.

Tuning patterns. KiCad's diff-pair coupling test (isInTuningPattern) leaves out tracks and arcs that are members of a tuning pattern (a (generated (type tuning_pattern) (members ...)) group): they are neither coupled nor counted in the uncoupled length. The reader marks them, and the DRC and the router's coupling test skip them. vme-wren's DDR4 pairs have 89 tuning patterns.

Results. Four fixture boards use the option: vme-wren and jetson (KiCad demos) and two srj24 samples. None is in a bench tier.

On vme-wren (bench/records/d150-padstacks) the engine's DRC went from 22,362 clearance and 21 shorting reports, where KiCad reports none, to 425 and 20. Those left have other causes: pad-to-track pairs judged at 0.125 mm where KiCad resolves 0.1 mm, and shorts against copper graphics. With flashing, tuning patterns and nearly parallel pairs, its 28 coupling-gap errors and 6 uncoupled-length errors are KiCad's, values included. jetson still matches KiCad on the routing-relevant types. The eight B1/B2 boards with pair rules route byte for byte as before.

Tests:

  • [flash], two cases: modes read in file order and the layers flashed for a via with an inner track, a zone connection, no end layers, start-end only and none; the refill joining a GND via to its plane and filling up to a bare S hole, with no DRC errors.
  • [coupling], two cases: tracks in a tuning pattern are not coupled, members of a plain group are; DQS0's stubs 10 nm off parallel are coupled at KiCad's 1.8573 mm.
  • rule_parity: via_unused_layers (four vias, each passed by tracks inside the ring's clearance and outside the hole's) and diff_pair_tuning_pattern and diff_pair_near_parallel. All 234 cases match; the build before D150 fails these three.

docs.title: 61. Delay tuning that makes room (2026-10-28, D152)
docs.text:
The delay tuner (§59) puts a meander only where nothing else is. When it runs, after negotiation and clean-up, the board's other connections are all in place. On RoyalBlue54L-Feather-delay with D139, the extra connections took the room beside the USB pair. D+ stayed 2.7 ps short of D- against a 0.5 ps rule, and KiCad reported skew_out_of_range.

Router::tune_with_room. It applies to every delay window and every delay skew group or pair.

  1. Plain tuning first. If the net ends in range, the step stops there.
  2. Start over from the untuned net. The board goes back to the net with no meanders, because the small meanders of the plain attempt fill the free room.
  3. Try ripping at each height. After both free sides of a meander, the tuner tries each side that only routed copper of other nets blocks. The rippable owners are those segment_state reports when routed copper is ignored. Those connections are ripped and the meander is placed.
  4. Who may be ripped. A connection may be ripped if it is:
  5. routed, and not implicit;
  6. not coupled, and not a bus or bundle lane;
  7. not of the net or of its pair partner;
  8. of a net with no length or skew rule of its own.

At most 16 connections are ripped. 5. Route them again. The ripped connections, and those of their nets that lose an implicit route, are routed again strictly, in connection order. Each gets the transaction cap. Together they get 400,000 work units beyond the spent budget (2 % of the time limit with --time). 6. Keep or roll back. The board is kept if the net is in range and all of them route again. Otherwise it goes back to the plain attempt's result.

Result (bench/records/d152-room, 3 M work, --refill --soft-zones). RoyalBlue54L-Feather-delay routes 125/147 with no added KiCad errors. One connection is ripped and routed again, and D+ ends at 79.43 ps against D-'s 79.49 ps. The other B2 boards never reach the step. Test: delay_room (it skips without build/demos).

Open. mm length windows, mm pair skew and the bus tuner do not make room yet.

docs.title: 62. Search speed: late reachability proofs and output-preserving speed-ups (2026-10-29, D154)
docs.text:
Where the time went. gprof on five hard PCBench boards (logicbone, sbc, Teensy_test_layout, LeeChee, kitspace_d20), one variant, 20 M work, CPU fields: the A* loop 27–57 % of CPU, cost-to-go fields on the CPU 14–33 %, legality checks most of the rest. Every board spent the whole budget in the strict first pass. A few failed searches took most of it: 15 failures 77 % of logicbone's budget, 108 failures 84 % of sbc's, 60 failures 91 % of kitspace_d20's. Successful searches expanded a median of 30–230 states. A per-search log showed that most failures exhaust their region (no path exists) rather than hit the 3 M cap. On LeeChee 28 % of the run was point_in_polygon on its 572-edge outline, called by the inside-board test in boundary cells. Records in bench/records/d154-speed.

What changed.

Change Output Effect Late reachability proof (--reach-after 100000, --reach-after-cap 10000) changes (exact; more budget left for the rest) see below CPU field: the six sweeps that change row, and the via step, run a row at a time without branches and vectorise (field_cpu.cpp gets -ftree-vectorize -fvect-cost-model=dynamic under GCC); the line-by-line version is field_cpu_reference identical (fields and round counts; test) field time about halved (logicbone 9.5 → 5.3 s at 20 M) Inside-board test: the outline's and cut-outs' edges indexed by raster row; a point in a boundary cell is tested against its row's edges only (Obstacles::inside_exact, reference inside_exact_linear) identical (test on a toothed outline with a round cut-out, points on edges and row boundaries) LeeChee 27.6 → 18.2 s CPU; a --global run there 158 → 7.5 s (§19) Per-class obstacle caches (LazyCodes) allocated in chunks of 4,096 codes on first write; unwritten chunks read as not computed identical memory per router 1.6 GB → 0.56 GB (Teensy), 1.65 GB → 0.44 GB (logicbone) Target marks of a search in a reused buffer instead of a fresh array per search identical small

Late reachability proof. The pre-check of §13 floods before a strict search; run on every search (--reach-check 2) it pays a flood on searches that would have succeeded at once. The late proof instead runs only inside a strict search that has expanded reach_after states without reaching its target. Two floods, forward from the sources and backward from the targets, take a cell in turn, over the pre-check's moves (no bends, turn limits or costs; any via landing the A* allows, including on target cells of layers without tracks). The backward flood enters a cell's neighbours when a planar move may enter the cell (it is a target or legal), and the cell's other layers when a via may land on it. Both admit every path the A* can find, so when one runs out before they meet there is no path. The search stops as an enclosure (the region did not touch the window edge; when it is the target's, "boxed in (target)", which spares the reverse probe) or a window miss. When they meet, or reach_after_cap cells are visited, the A* goes on as before: the floods only filled the legality caches it reads. Flood cells count against --work at --flood-work-pct, as the pre-check's do. --reach-verify runs the A* on after every proof and counts paths it finds: 0 on the five boards (the proof at 20,000 expansions, no cap: 389 proofs, 64 of them "no path"). Breakout boards keep the pre-check on every strict search (D98), so the late proof does not run there.

One variant, 20 M work, routed connections:

Board before trigger 100 k, no cap 30 k, no cap 100 k, cap 10 k (default) 50 k, cap 10 k kitspace_d20_r0.1 228 256 256 259 259 oskirby_logicbone 804 873 858 883 883 sbc_sbc 310 334 334 341 345 KiCad-Library_Teensy_test_layout 1,090 1,080 1,056 1,093 1,093 LeeChee_1800 1,010 991 895 1,010 1,010

Without a cap, floods on long searches that do succeed (they meet late) cost more than the proofs save on Teensy and LeeChee. With the cap no board loses. The same result in less time: the old router needs 40 M work on logicbone (41.8 s CPU) for the 883 the new one routes at 20 M (30.0 s); on kitspace_d20 80 M (56.9 s) for 259 (22.1 s); on sbc 40 M gives 329 (29.1 s) against 341 at 20 M (20.8 s). At 10 M the new router routes more than the old one at 20 M on all three (250, 858, 327 against 228, 804, 310).

Tiers (KiCad 10.0.6 judge):

Set Budget Before → after Output Route CPU quick (30) 1 M work, 8 variants 26 → 26 clean, 99.3 % → 99.3 % 30/30 byte-identical 385 → 299 s (−22 %) mid (11) 20 M work, 8 variants 7 identical; decelerator 620 → 630, LimeSDR 810 → 813, EEZ 549 → 570, logicbone 1,036 → 1,036 7/11 identical 6,157 → 4,357 s (−29 %) mid (11) 60 s, 8 variants 9,349 → 9,401 routed (6 boards up, 4 down, 1 equal) – – B (40) 120 s, 8 variants 29 → 29 clean, 5,197 → 5,198 routed 12/40 identical 16,935 → 16,036 s (−5 %) C (30) 120 s, 8 variants 16 → 17 clean, 9,529 → 9,537 routed 7/30 identical 19,254 → 18,476 s (−4 %)

At 120 s, the boards that finish early mostly finish sooner (tier B APM-RPi-Shield 370 → 147 CPU s, avr_ledprojector 862 → 464; tier C Apple-M0110 529 → 196, PocketBone 794 → 572), some later (Horticulture 363 → 444, PSLab 575 → 668): the portfolio stops when one variant completes, and which one does first changes. Boards that use the whole 120 s route as many or more within noise. The mid comparison prints Gates: FAIL for both runs alike: KiCad's DRC list is capped on LeeChee, LimeSDR and logicbone (bench/records/m16/README.md).

Tried and left off.

  • Field only for long searches (--field-after N): the A* starts with the octile bound and builds the field after N expansions, re-keying its open list. On logicbone 78 % of field work went to searches that ended in under 2,000 expansions, and at N = 2,000 field time fell (logicbone 5.0 → 3.6 s), but total CPU rose (LeeChee 18.3 → 25.6 s, logicbone 21.3 → 25.8 s): without the field the A* spreads over more cells, and first visits to cells (legality checks) cost more than the field saved. Routed counts were equal.
  • Ties to the deeper state (--tie-deep): on equal f, the larger g first. With the late proof, 20 M work: Teensy 1,093 → 1,095, sbc 341 → 333, others ±1. Not kept.
  • Compiler flags: -O3 with link-time optimisation instead of -O2 (RelWithDebInfo) changed CPU time by about 1 % on four boards (output identical).
  • Open list as a vector with a heap of structs (needed to re-key it): 4–8 % slower on sbc and logicbone than std::priority_queue of pairs; the open list stays a priority_queue whose container is reached for the re-key.

docs.title: 06 — Failure memory: learning from every failed attempt
docs.text: Part of the TraceMaker plan. Start at ../PLAN.md.

docs.title: 1. Requirement
docs.text:
"Try an optimal algorithm, but any time something doesn't work, store that information and use it to improve the next attempt." TraceMaker implements this as a failure memory with four tiers. Each tier borrows a mechanism with a published track record:

Tier Scope Mechanism Prior art T0 One search Explain the failure: which objects bounded the explored region, where the closest approach was Conflict analysis in CDCL SAT solvers T1 One run, all connections History cost maps, targeted penalties, conflict graph, activity scores PathFinder / VPR history cost; FGR; TritonRoute-WXL marker cost; VSIDS T2 One run, strategy level Nogoods (do not retry what failed in the same configuration), escalation state, bandit over strategies, restarts that keep what was learned Nogood learning; tabu search; ALNS operator weights; UCB/Thompson bandits; Luby restarts T3 Across runs and boards Persistent knowledge base: escape templates, strategy priors per board type, warm-start maps, trained models Experience replay; algorithm configuration (SMAC/irace); learned net ordering (DreamerV3+FR, PCBWorld)

docs.title: 2. T0 — explaining a failed search
docs.text:
When an A* search exhausts its window or budget, the router builds a FailureRecord:

struct FailureRecord {
  ConnId conn; NetId net; Stage stage; Rung rung; StrategyId strategy; uint32_t attempt;
  Cause cause;            // BLOCKED, CUT_OVERFULL, PIN_INACCESSIBLE, NO_VIA_SITE, WINDOW_INFEASIBLE,
                          // BUDGET, DRC_ON_INSERT, LENGTH_RULE, ECO_REJECTED
  Rect region; LayerMask layers;
  uint64_t region_sig;    // Zobrist signature of the window (§3.3)
  SmallVec<ObjRef, 16> blockers;      // objects on the boundary of the closed set, ranked by contact
  SmallVec<NetId, 8>   blocker_nets;
  Point closest_a, closest_b;         // nearest approach of the two search trees (bidirectional)
  Segment cut; int32_t cut_demand, cut_capacity;   // when a Maley cut was evaluated
  WorkUnits spent; Score score_before;
};
  • Blockers come for free from bidirectional A*: the boundary of each closed set is a closed curve of obstacles. The two curves around the source and target are the "boxed-in" explanation (Contour).
  • Boundary owners are ranked by how much of the boundary they form; the top ones are the conflict explanation, analogous to a learned clause in a SAT solver.
  • The record is appended to an append-only failure log (also streamed to the viewer, where failed attempts show as red ghost paths with their blockers highlighted).

docs.title: 3. T1/T2 — using failures within a run
3.1 History cost (PathFinder) — global and detailed
docs.text:
c(e)  = b(e) + α · h(e) · p(e)
p(e)  = 1 + pres_fac · max(0, use(e) + w − cap(e)) / cap(e),   pres_fac = 0.5 · 1.3^k (capped)
h(e) ← 0.9 · h(e) + overflow(e)   each iteration; α keeps present overflow dominant (BoxRouter)

As in the clean-sheet doc §5.3. Shared by global routing, detailed routing and repair.

For DRC markers in detailed repair, use the TritonRoute-WXL scheme as implemented in OpenROAD drt: each marker adds +10 to a saturating per-cell byte counter, the counter decays ×0.95 per repair pass, and a cell with a non-zero counter adds marker_cost × step_length (default marker_cost = 32, shape cost 8). The repair schedule varies window size (7/5 tiles), offset, marker cost (0 → 1× → 2×) and rip-up mode (all / DRC / near-DRC), and portfolio arms run marker cost ×½ and ×2.

docs.title: 3.2 Targeted penalties from failure records
docs.text: Plain history only marks over-used resources. A failure record also says where a connection got stuck. - Along the boundary of the closed set near the closest approach, add a penalty to cells owned by the ranked blocker nets: learned(cell) += κ · rank_weight. Next time, those blockers see a higher cost for staying there, so they move aside (like history, but aimed at the cause). - Along an over-full cut, raise the cost of every net crossing the cut that could route elsewhere. - Decay: learned ← 0.85 · learned per repair iteration, so stale lessons fade.

docs.title: 3.3 Region signatures and nogoods
docs.text:
• The window around a failure is described by a 64-bit Zobrist hash: one random key per (cell-block, layer, owner-class) where cell-blocks are 4×4 lattice cells and owner-class ∈ {free, own net, fixed, rippable-foreign}. XOR-updating the hash when copper changes is O(changed blocks), so every window's signature is maintained incrementally.
  • A nogood is (conn, rung, strategy, params_hash, region_sig) → FAILED. Before trying a rung, the router checks the nogood store (an ankerl::unordered_dense set, ~16 B/entry). A hit skips the rung: the exact same attempt in the exact same situation is never repeated.
  • Any copper change in the window changes the signature, so the attempt is allowed again once something relevant changed (no stale tabu).
  • Aspiration: a nogood is ignored if the global score improved by more than a threshold since it was recorded (from tabu search).

docs.title: 3.4 Conflict graph and ordering
docs.text:
• Weighted directed graph blocked_net → blocker_net, weight bumped per failure, decayed per iteration.
  • Victim selection in rip-up prefers blockers with high in-weight from many failing nets.
  • Net ordering: an activity score per net (VSIDS-like): act(n) += bump on each failure of n, bump *= 1/0.95 per iteration (equivalent to decaying all). Nets are routed in descending activity, so hard nets get first pick of resources on the next pass.
  • Precedence learning: if A failed because of B, and B rerouted cheaply after a rip-up, add a soft precedence "A before B" for the rest of the run.

docs.title: 3.5 Strategy selection (bandit)
docs.text:
• Arms: rung variants and parameters (cost schedules, window sizes, pitch, via cost, bend cost, order heuristic) and placement-ECO move types.
  • Reward = score improvement per work unit. Discounted Thompson sampling (or discounted UCB) per (stage, failure cause), so the router learns, on this board, which strategy fixes which kind of failure.
  • Priors come from T3.

docs.title: 3.6 Restarts that keep the lessons
docs.text: When the repair stage stalls (failure predictor says zero markers is unreachable in budget), the scheduler may restart detailed routing from the global solution on a Luby schedule, keeping history, learned penalties, activity, precedence and nogoods — the routing analogue of a SAT restart that keeps learned clauses. Portfolio branches share T1 lessons only at deterministic synchronisation points.

docs.title: 3.7 Infeasibility cores → placement
docs.text: An R4 exact window solve that returns infeasible yields a minimal conflicting set of boundary terminals. That core plus the R6 cut proof is the ECO placement request (doc 04 §4). A rejected ECO move is itself a failure record (ECO_REJECTED) keyed by the cut signature, so the same move is not proposed again.

docs.title: 4. T3 — the persistent knowledge base
docs.text:
SQLite file (WAL mode) at ~/.local/share/tracemaker/kb.sqlite, also exportable to share between machines.

Table Key Content Used for boards board content hash features (layers, part count, pin density, BGA count, net count), outcome similarity search runs run id settings, seed, version, metrics regression tracking strategy_stats (feature cluster, stage, cause, arm) Beta(α, β) or mean/var of reward bandit priors escape_templates (footprint geometry hash, rule class, layer count) escape stubs, via sites, layer per pin first candidate in escape planning warm_start board hash (+ ECO diff) final history map, activity, net order, corridors rerouting the same board after edits failure_hotspots footprint-pair geometry hash typical failure causes and fixes ECO move ranking models name, version trained weights (ONNX) learned net ordering / congestion prediction

Learned models (later phase) — trained offline with PyTorch from benchmark runs: - Congestion predictor: a small CNN over RUDY/pin-density/blockage maps that predicts global-routing overflow; used in placement step (B) as a faster routability term. - Net-order policy: a GNN over the netlist/placement scoring "route this connection next"; used as one ordering arm in the bandit, never as the only one. (Prior art: DreamerV3+FR and PCBWorld show RL over ordering decisions can lift completion; TraceMaker keeps it optional and benchmark-gated.)

docs.title: 5. Visibility
docs.text: Every lesson is visible: failure ghosts, blocker highlights, history heatmaps, the conflict graph, bandit arm probabilities and the nogood count are panels in the viewer (doc 09). The report lists every unrouted connection with its full failure history.

docs.title: 6. Novelty note
docs.text: No published VLSI or PCB detailed router uses CDCL-style nogood learning (closest: conflict-driven ASP for optical routing, 2015). The nogood store and infeasibility cores (§3.3, §3.7) are therefore TraceMaker's own contribution, and their benefit must be shown by ablation in the benchmark (roadmap M5 gate).

docs.title: 7. Guarantees
docs.text:
• Learning changes costs, order and which attempts are made, never the legality check. Nothing learned can create a DRC error.
  • All learning updates are deterministic functions of (seed, events in deterministic order).
  • Memory bounds: failure log capped (oldest summarised), nogood store capped with LRU on aspiration.

docs.title: 8. Implementation status (2026-10-02)
docs.text: Tier Mechanism Status Where T0 Failure explanation: boxed-in source (open list exhausted without touching the window edge), window, search budget, exact-check rejection, protected victims Done; reasons appear in every unrouted line of the report route/router.cpp (Miss, why) T0 Learned blocked lattice points after exact-check failures Done learn_block T1 PathFinder history on contested lattice points (recorded before rip-up), added to every later search Done (sparse map) bump_history, hist_cost T1 Negotiated rip-up: soft crossing of other connections' copper, victims ripped and requeued, rip cap per connection, best legal state kept Done commit, rip, run T1 Activity ordering: failed connections retried hardest (most failures) first Done run T2 Nogoods: (connection, mode, signature of routed copper in the window) attempts that failed are not repeated until the surroundings change Done search_and_commit T2 Strategy selection: portfolio of 8 router variants in parallel threads, best kept Done route_portfolio T3 Persistent SQLite knowledge base: Thompson-sampling bandit over variants per board-feature bucket; per-board failed connections routed first on re-runs Done learn/knowledge_base.cpp, tracemaker route --kb T3 Learned models (congestion predictor, ordering policy) Not started — Conflict graph between nets, precedence learning, Luby restarts Not started — Failure record for outside readers (2026-10-14, D112): structured unrouted list (reason code, rips, fails, pad positions, blocker nets), failure event region and blocker_nets, the stuck report; advice (typed hints) fed back through --advice. Advice changes costs, order and which attempts are made, never the legality check, exactly as the learned state does. The closed-set boundary blockers of §2 are not built Done route/router.cpp, advice/, doc 17

docs.title: 07 — GPU acceleration
docs.text: Part of the TraceMaker plan. Start at ../PLAN.md.

docs.title: 1. Hardware facts that shape the design
docs.text:
Device Arch Memory Implications Tesla P100 PCIe 12 GB Pascal, sm_60 HBM2 ~550 GB/s fp32/fp64 strong; no tensor cores; good for FFT and stencil sweeps Tesla V100 PCIe 16 GB Volta, sm_70 HBM2 ~900 GB/s Independent thread scheduling; tensor cores (fp16) not needed here
  • Build for sm_60;sm_70 with CUDA 12.x. CUDA 13 removed offline compilation for Maxwell, Pascal and Volta, so the project stays on CUDA 12.x while these GPUs are in use.
  • No bf16, no sm_80+ features (async copy, cuda::pipeline hardware path). Integer atomics and warp intrinsics (__shfl_sync, __ballot_sync) are the main tools.
  • The GPU path must never be required for correctness (CPU fallback, cpu-only preset).
  • Verified on 2026-10-02: nvcc 12.4 rejects GCC 15 (gcc versions later than 13 are not supported) and builds for sm_60 + sm_70 with -ccbin g++-12; the test kernel ran correctly on the P100 (the V100 was full). The build uses CMAKE_CUDA_HOST_COMPILER=g++-12; host C++ code may still use GCC 15, so CUDA-facing headers must compile under both.
  • The GPUs are shared. On 2026-10-02 a llama-server process held 11.4 of 12 GB on the P100 and 16.1 of 16 GB on the V100, and a 128-byte cudaMalloc failed on the V100. TraceMaker must treat GPU memory as scarce and variable (see §4).
  • CUDA's default device order is fastest-first (V100 = device 0) while nvidia-smi lists the P100 first. Select devices by name/UUID, never by index.

docs.title: 2. What runs on the GPU
docs.text: Workload Kernel design CPU reference Expected gain Placement density (doc 04 B) Bin charge scatter (atomic int fixed-point), DCT/DST via cuFFT, field gather FFTW-style CPU DCT (pocketfft) Large for batched multi-start (B = 32–256 starts at once) Placement SA (doc 04 E) Parallel tempering: one block per replica; per-move incremental HPWL by warp over net pins; conflict-free move subsets Same algorithm, sequential Many replicas per second instead of one Global pattern routing One thread per (connection, pattern, layer pair): L/Z-shape costs from prefix sums of edge cost along rows/columns CPU loop Thousands of connections per launch Global maze routing (GAMER-style) Alternating horizontal/vertical sweeps with parallel prefix-min (scan) per row/column per layer, plus via relaxation between layers, iterated to convergence. Batches formed by fine-grained 3-D overlap of routed tiles rather than bounding boxes (InstantGR), so more connections share a launch CPU A* GAMER: 19.85× coarse / 2.59× fine maze vs CUGR, no quality loss Cost-to-go fields (doc 05 §5.2) Same sweep kernels on a detailed window, multi-layer, from the target CPU Dijkstra Turns A* into near-linear expansion along the optimal path Free-space BFS (last gasp, strict mode) Bit-parallel wavefront: 32/64 cells per thread word, dilate-and-mask per step CPU bit-parallel BFS Whole-board reachability in milliseconds Conservative rasterisation of obstacles One thread per primitive × covered tiles; atomic OR into bit-planes CPU rasteriser Board-scale planes rebuilt fast after placement moves DRC broad-phase LBVH (Karras 2012) built per stage; parallel traversal emits candidate pairs; exact narrow phase on CPU or GPU with the same integer predicates Uniform spatial hash Full-board sign-off in well under a second RUDY / pin-density / crossing maps Scatter kernels CPU Cheap; keeps placement loop interactive

docs.title: 3. Correctness and determinism rules
docs.text:
1. Every kernel has a CPU reference with the same integer arithmetic; a test runs both on random and fixture inputs and requires identical output.
  2. Costs and charges are int64/int32 fixed-point, so atomic accumulation is order-independent.
  3. Batch selection (which connections/moves run together) is computed on the CPU in a deterministic order.
  4. Floating-point stages (placement Nesterov steps) snap positions to a 1 µm grid each iteration and use deterministic reductions (fixed-order tree reductions, no float atomics).

docs.title: 4. Service design
docs.text:
• GpuService owns per-device context, streams, cudaMallocAsync memory pools, and pinned staging buffers.
  • Jobs are pure functions on device buffers: FieldJob, SweepRouteJob, DensityJob, AnnealJob, BroadphaseJob. The scheduler queues them; results return through futures.
  • Device roles default to V100 = routing/DRC, P100 = placement; a job may run on either.
  • Graceful degradation: if a device is busy or absent, the CPU reference runs.
  • Memory admission control: at start and before each large job, query cudaMemGetInfo; size batches to the free memory minus a safety margin; on cudaErrorMemoryAllocation shrink the batch and retry, then fall back to CPU for that job. Results are identical either way (rule §3.1), so this never changes output.
  • Back-off after a refusal (2026-10-26, src/gpu/backoff.hpp): a CUDA device that refused a job is not asked again for 30 s, the delay doubling while it keeps refusing (up to 15 min) and resetting when it accepts. With both GPUs full of other jobs, asking before every field queued the router's threads on the driver lock for seconds per field: the soak of 2026-10-25 measured interf_u at 2,900 s against 20 s with --no-gpu, byte-identical boards.
  • Settings: --gpu auto|off|<uuid,...> and --gpu-mem-limit per device; the report records which jobs ran where.

docs.title: 5. Libraries
docs.text:
• CUB/Thrust from the CCCL 2.x bundled with CUDA 12.4. CCCL 3.x builds with CTK 12 but is untested below sm_75.
  • cuFFT for placement density.
  • In-house linear-probing device hash table. cuCollections supports Pascal only partially (no blocking structures).
  • No PyTorch or DREAMPlace runtime dependency. Current PyTorch wheels dropped Volta (only cu12.6 wheels cover Pascal/Volta). The placement kernels are written directly in CUDA following the ePlace maths; PyTorch is used only offline for training learned models (doc 06 T3), with a cu12.6 wheel.
  • Code to study or port (BSD-3): Xplace cpp_to_py/gpugr (GGR + GAMER sweep maze routing, pattern routing), InstantGR (batching, node-level parallelism), DREAMPlace/Xplace density kernels. OpenDRC (MIT) for GPU DRC structure; PDRC (DAC 2024) for non-Manhattan GPU DRC ideas.

docs.title: 6. Prior art
docs.text:
No published work implements a full GPU detailed router; GPU maze routers use sweeps/BFS/Bellman-Ford rather than priority-queue A, because A parallelises poorly. This confirms decision D5: the GPU builds fields and batches, the CPU runs the octilinear A* searches.

GAMER (GPU-accelerated maze routing, sweep with parallel scan), FastGR and GGR (GPU global routing with pattern routing and batch scheduling), DREAMPlace and Xplace (GPU analytic placement with FFT density), Karras 2012 (LBVH), Lee/Moore wavefront with bit-parallel BFS. OrthoRoute (MIT) shows GPU PathFinder in a KiCad plugin, and its weak results on mixed boards are why TraceMaker keeps octilinear CPU detailed routing as the quality path.

docs.title: 7. Implementation status (2026-10-02)
docs.text: Workload Status Notes Cost-to-go fields (router A* heuristic) Done: src/gpu/field_cuda.cu + CPU reference field_cpu.cpp GAMER-style line sweeps (rows, columns, both diagonals, both directions) + via relaxation to a fixpoint; one thread per line; cudaStreamPerThread so the 8 portfolio routers share the two GPUs. Exact equality with the CPU reference tested on random grids on the P100 and V100; routed boards byte-identical with --no-gpu. Used for windows ≥ 60k lattice points; GPU ~2x faster than the CPU field was. Since D154 the CPU field runs the sweeps that change row a row at a time, without branches and vectorised, and the via step likewise; each sweep leaves what the line-by-line sweep leaves (kept as field_cpu_reference, compared in a test), so fields and round counts are unchanged and the CPU field is about 2x faster on routed boards (logicbone 7.8 s → 3.7 s of field time at 5 M work). Gain on routing is modest today because routed copper and soft costs (not in the field) dominate the remaining search effort Philox RNG fill Done (toolchain test) Placement density / annealing Not started DRC broad-phase Not built (D55) The broad-phase (uniform grid) takes 14 ms on the largest board; the DRC's time was in exact tests against zone fills, fixed on the CPU with an edge index: vme-wren 730 s → 7 s (doc 05 §19) Global pattern and maze routing (GAMER / GGR port) Not built (D56) The CPU global router routes the tile graph in 0.02–0.5 s per board, and its plan does not improve routing (doc 05 §19)

docs.title: 8. Native macOS / Metal (2026-10-06, D70)
docs.text:
What was built

Part What Build macos-metal and macos-cpu presets use Apple Clang; Metal uses Objective-C++20. CUDA and Metal are mutually exclusive; non-Apple builds retain the CUDA default Device API compiled_backend, DeviceInfo::index, and field_gpu select the compiled backend. CPU references are always built; unavailable devices and failed jobs fall back to CPU device_metal.mm Registry-ID-ordered discovery with METAL-<registry-id> identifiers. Memory admission uses recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize - currentAllocatedSize with a 256 MiB margin: process working-set headroom, not free system RAM field_metal.mm Embedded MSL, cached per-device pipelines, and per-thread shared buffers and command queues. Ordered integer line sweeps and via relaxation return only converged fields; buffer barriers order dispatches, and the CPU reads results after completion Scope Cost-to-go fields only. Philox remains CUDA-only; placement, A*, and exact legality checks stay on the CPU

Results. On Apple M4 Pro, a private 4-layer sensor board (218 connections), seed 7, one variant, and 5,000,000 work units produced byte-identical CPU/Metal boards: 118/154 connections routed, 342 added tracks, 47 added vias, 73 Metal fields, zero fallbacks. The first kernel took 1.53 s for fields versus 0.88 s on CPU; §8.1 replaces it.

KiCad 10.0.3 sign-off was not clean: 36 unconnected items and three added vias inside J5's footprint-local keepout, on top of 17 input errors. Both backends reproduced this router/rule-coverage limitation. The input board and project were unchanged.

There was no executable quick manifest. Regression used a seeded 30-board tier-A sample (bench/run.py --tier A --limit 30 --seed 1), one variant, seed 7, no knowledge base, and 1,000,000 work units per board. All 30 CPU/Metal outputs were byte-identical, with no added judged routing errors. Each backend completed 13/30 cleanly; mean completion was 89.33%. These runs are not comparable to the README's longer portfolio runs. Results: bench/results/macos-{cpu,metal}-quick/. The generated table's RC12 zero means missing baseline data; the summary records null.

CTest (first kernel): Metal 117 passed / 14 skipped; CPU 114 passed / 17 skipped; zero failures in each 131-test suite. Skips covered unavailable fixtures, Docker-dependent KiCad parity, YAML tooling, and unsupported GPU workloads. Native KiCad judged the private board and regression sample separately. The migrated CUDA sources could not be compiled or run on macOS.

docs.title: 8.1 Parallel line scans (2026-10-06, D71)
docs.text:
Before. Fields used 50% of busy CPU time on the cleared private board (20M work, 8 variants): 2,311 fields, mean 262k lattice points × layers, 4 layers, median 8 rounds, maximum 15, about 21 ms each. One thread per line left the first Metal kernel slower than CPU with concurrent callers.

What was built. GAMER's line recurrence is a segmented prefix-min: d'[i] = c·i + min_{j≤i}(d[j] − c·j) within each open run. One 32-lane SIMD-group scans a line in 32-cell blocks, carrying the minimum between blocks. The backward scan mirrors the forward scan; each lane rereads only cells it wrote. Disjoint lines and layers share dispatches without changing field_cpu's per-round state. A round uses four line dispatches and one via dispatch. Command buffers batch 16 rounds initially, then 8; rounds after convergence do no work. GPU field time is about 0.4–1.5 ms.

Results. Apple M4 Pro, macOS 26.4; CPU/Metal outputs were byte-identical.

Measurement CPU Metal (first kernel) Metal (scan kernel) 2,311 captured fields, one caller 47.7 s 41.7 s 10.3 s, 0 mismatches 8 concurrent callers × 2,311 fields 54.1 s 107.9 s 18.2 s Field time per rip-up variant 8.3–12.0 s 8.5–11.4 s 1.0–1.5 s Cleared private board, 20M work, 8 variants 16.2 s (21.4 s wall) 15.2 s 9.2 s (11.8 s wall), 208/218 tracemaker-place --mode routable, 17 routes 336.0 s — 228.5 s

Rules caveat. The table used a renamed board without its project, hence default rules and a 0.075 mm lattice. With project rules (0.050 mm lattice), the route took about 121 s on either backend; field time per variant was 1.6 s on Metal or 6.4 s on CPU. A* dominated. The default 120 s --time limit stopped the run before 20M work, so non-best variants differed between runs; the output boards remained identical. Placement's 600 s router safety limit gave 55–147 s per route, 987 s for 7 routes.

The same 30-board sample gave 30/30 byte-identical CPU/Metal boards, 43.3% clean pass, 89.3% completion, and no added errors (bench/results/macos-metal-scan-quick/). The [gpu][field] tests cover thin grids, blocked targets, buffer reuse, concurrent callers, and a 300-cell winding corridor requiring more than 32 rounds.

docs.title: 8.2 macOS 15 (2026-10-17, D135; contributed by Chris Hemingway, PR #46)
docs.text:
The port in §8 was built on macOS 26.4. On macOS 15 it did not compile: Apple's libc++ makes floating-point std::from_chars available only from macOS 26. tmk::parse_double (core/parse_double.hpp) uses from_chars elsewhere and strtod_l in the "C" locale on Apple platforms, held to from_chars' grammar. The test scripts also needed changes for macOS's bash 3.2 (no mapfile; an empty array is unbound under set -u), and clang rejected an unused constant that GCC accepts.

Results. Apple M2, macOS 15.7.9, Apple clang 17, native kicad-cli 10.0.6 (Homebrew cask), KiCad demo and Freerouting fixtures fetched. Records: bench/records/macos15/.

Check Result CTest, macos-metal and macos-cpu all pass, including DRC parity against kicad-cli (14/14 boards) and broken-board parity CTest under ASan + UBSan (macos-cpu flags plus the asan preset's) no sanitizer report; 368/368, crules_two_stage run alone: at -j4 it went over its 3,600 s limit (records) parse_double on macOS against libstdc++'s from_chars 2,000,000 strings, 0 mismatches Quick tier, 1M work, CPU against Metal 30/30 byte-identical, 25/30 clean, 99.0 % completion Quick tier against Linux (bench/records/m17, --no-gpu) 30/30 boards with the same routed count, tracks, vias, completion and style metric

The Linux comparison uses what boards.jsonl keeps, not the routed files, which stay on the machine that made them (compare_boards.py in the records).

docs.title: 08 — KiCad integration
docs.text: Part of the TraceMaker plan. Start at ../PLAN.md. Facts below were verified on 2026-10-02; sources in ../research/kicad-and-benchmarks-2026-10.md.

docs.title: 1. Target versions
docs.text: Item Target KiCad 10.0.x (10.0.6 stable as of 2026-08-29); read 9.0 files too; track KiCad 11 (master) changes Board file version 20260206 (10.0). Accept older versions KiCad 10 accepts; write the same version that was read Schematic file version 20260306 (10.0) IPC client kicad-python (kipy) 0.8.x kicad-cli 10.0.x, natively or in Docker kicad/kicad:10.0.6 (no GUI needed)

docs.title: 2. Three integration paths
docs.text: Path Used for How Files (primary) CLI, batch, benchmarks, schematic-to-board Native C++ s-expression readers/writers for .kicad_pcb, .kicad_sch, .kicad_pro (JSON), .kicad_dru, .kicad_mod, fp-lib-table/sym-lib-table kicad-cli (judge and cross-check) DRC sign-off, netlist cross-check, zone refill Subprocess; pcb drc --format json --severity-all --exit-code-violations --all-track-errors [--schematic-parity] [--refill-zones] IPC API (live in pcbnew) Plugin: route the open board, show results immediately, one undo step Python plugin with kipy; out-of-process engine

docs.title: 3. File I/O (src/io/kicad)
docs.text:
• One generic s-expression lexer/parser producing a lossless tree (tokens, original formatting of untouched nodes, unknown nodes preserved). Typed views (board, footprint, pad, track…) read from the tree; writes patch the tree.
  • Round-trip guarantee: parse → write without changes is byte-identical (gate of M1). Changes touch only the nodes TraceMaker owns: footprint at/layer/flipped pads, new segment/arc/via nodes, removed tracks it ripped.
  • Legacy zone fills: KiCad 5 filled_polygon nodes without a layer inherit the zone's copper layer only when its copper mask contains exactly one bit. Explicit fill layers take precedence (even an unknown explicit layer); missing, unknown or multi-copper-layer zones never guess a fill layer. This affects the typed copper/connectivity view only; the original text stays untouched (D105).
  • Project rules: .kicad_pro (JSON) holds net classes, net-class patterns/assignments, board design settings (min track width, clearances, via sizes, hole clearances), and severity settings. .kicad_dru holds custom rules (constraint keywords in the research note §A). The rule compiler (doc 03) consumes both. The reader seeds supported KiCad 10 defaults and applies legacy board rules. Project values overlay defaults only where KiCad's legacy migration permits loading them; missing keys preserve current values and explicit zeros remain zero (D108).
  • Schematic: netlist from the hierarchical .kicad_sch set (symbols, pins, labels, power symbols, net class directives, DNP / exclude-from-board flags). Cross-checked in tests against kicad-cli sch export netlist --format kicadsexpr.
  • Footprints: from the board if present; otherwise resolved through fp-lib-table to .kicad_mod files (schematic-to-board mode builds the footprints itself, like "Update PCB from Schematic").
  • Specctra DSN reader / SES writer for the Freerouting fixture set, plus a DSN writer so Freerouting can be run as a baseline on our own .kicad_pcb fixtures (KiCad 10 has no kicad-cli DSN export, and the SWIG exporter disappears in KiCad 11).

docs.title: 3.1 Supported native rule defaults (D108)
docs.text:
Defaults are taken from KiCad 10.0.3's include/board_design_settings.h, BOARD_DESIGN_SETTINGS constructor and common/netclass.cpp. The constructor sets m_resetParamsIfMissing = false: absent project keys keep constructor values or values read from the legacy board. In particular, use the constructor's 0.1 mm annular width, not the different reset default in the JSON parameter declaration.

Supported board constraint Default (mm) Overall clearance / minimum connection width 0 / 0 Minimum track width 0.2 Minimum via diameter / annular width 0.5 / 0.1 Minimum through-hole drill 0.3 Minimum microvia diameter / drill 0.2 / 0.1 Hole-to-copper / hole-to-hole clearance 0.25 / 0.25 Copper-to-edge clearance 0.5 Silk clearance / mask-to-copper clearance / mask web width 0 / 0 / 0

The native Default class has clearance/track width 0.2/0.2 mm, via diameter/drill 0.6/0.3 mm, microvia diameter/drill 0.3/0.1 mm and differential-pair width/gap/via-gap 0.2/0.25/0.25 mm. Class dimensions are routing preferences, not permission to violate a board or custom minimum. Project classes inherit missing/null fields from Default. Native legacy net-class migration takes precedence over project class definitions and assignments. Board-local fields retain their existing precedence. Missing or malformed projects remain warned about; they do not turn supported minimums into zero.

Legacy migration precedence: the reader follows KiCad 10.0.6's BOARD::SetProject and parseSetup / parseNETCLASS: tokens that set m_LegacyDesignSettingsLoaded (for example trace_min, via_min_size, user_trace_width or defaults) suppress loading the project's board settings as a whole, including minimums and severities. The reader detects those exact legacy tokens, not merely setup. Local pad_to_mask_clearance, solder_mask_min_width, origins, stackup and plot settings do not set that flag and do not suppress project rules. Present project keys, including zero, remain authoritative on boards without a legacy design-settings trigger.

Net classes migrate independently: any root net_class transfers legacy classes and assignments over project classes/patterns, but does not itself suppress project board minimums. Conversely, legacy design-setting tokens alone do not suppress project net classes.

tests/integration/no_project_defaults.py generates isolated native DRC probes for absent, empty, partial and zero-valued projects, project overrides and legacy preservation/migration, then routes a legacy 0.15 mm class under the built-in 0.2 mm minimum and checks preservation of a wider legacy class despite a conflicting project class. Assertions use violation types and actual written copper widths, not rendered diagnostics or echoed options. Unit tests cover default boundaries, cross-property legacy suppression, nontriggering local fields and independent class migration.

docs.title: 3.2 The order a clearance is resolved in (D151)
docs.text:
The engine resolves a copper clearance in the order of KiCad 10.0.6's DRC_ENGINE::EvalRules (drc/rule_engine.cpp, RuleEngine::clearance):

  1. Net tie: 0.
  2. Local override of either item (a pad's clearance, else its footprint's; the larger of the two items'): wins over everything but the board minimum, which floors it.
  3. Custom rule (the last matching .kicad_dru rule with a clearance minimum): final, even below the board minimum. vme-wren allows 0.1 mm under its FPGA and DDR with a 0.125 mm board minimum.
  4. Net class: the larger of the two items' classes, with the coupled-pair relaxation and a zone's own clearance; floored at the board minimum.

hole_clearance and hole_to_hole work alike: a matching custom rule replaces the board's value instead of being raised to it. Rule parity checks each step against KiCad: clearance_custom_below_minimum, clearance_local_over_custom, hole_rules_custom_below_minimum and hole_rules_minimum.

The router's exact check, which decides what is committed, uses the same function. Its class-level shortcuts (grid costs, escape planning, the ramp) still take the class clearance floored at the board minimum; they only steer the search.

docs.title: 4. Rule coverage policy
docs.text:
• Every rule TraceMaker cannot interpret is reported as a warning with its location, and the router uses the most conservative interpretation (for example, the largest clearance that could apply).
  • Phase 1 custom-rule conditions: A.NetClass, A.NetName, A.Type, A.Layer, A.insideArea(...), A.intersectsArea(...), A.isPlated(), A.Pad_Type, A.Reference, boolean && || !. Others later.
  • The router also enforces disallow track/via by net and layer, and physical_hole_clearance between holes and copper of any net (doc 05 §27). Positional disallow rules are warned and left to the DRC.

docs.title: 5. IPC plugin (kicad_plugin/)
docs.text:
Facts that shape it: - KiCad 10 IPC runs only with a running pcbnew GUI (headless server is a KiCad 11 feature). - 10.0 has no IPC call to read design rules and no IPC call to run DRC. The plugin therefore reads the rules from the project files on disk (the plugin knows the project path) and runs kicad-cli pcb drc on a saved copy when the user asks for sign-off. On KiCad 11 it switches to GetBoardDesignRules / GetCustomDesignRules.

Flow: 1. Plugin (plugin.json, Python, own venv with kicad-python) starts or connects to tracemakerd. 2. Reads the board via SaveDocumentToString (exact file content) — simplest lossless transfer — plus project files from disk. 3. Engine routes (and places, if the user chose a placement mode); the viewer URL opens in a browser for the live view. 4. Results are applied in one commit (begin_commit → CreateItems/UpdateItems/DeleteItems/ FlipItems → push_commit), so a single Ctrl-Z undoes the whole run. RefillZones afterwards. 5. Packaged for KiCad's Plugin and Content Manager (PCM).

# sketch (kipy 0.8; exact class names to be checked against the installed version during M11)
from kipy import KiCad
kicad = KiCad()                               # uses KICAD_API_SOCKET / KICAD_API_TOKEN
board = kicad.get_board()
text = board.save_to_string()                 # SaveDocumentToString
result = engine.route(text, project_dir, mode="eco")
commit = board.begin_commit()
board.update_items(result.moved_footprints)   # position/orientation
board.create_items(result.new_tracks + result.new_vias)
board.remove_items(result.ripped_items)
board.push_commit(commit, "TraceMaker route")
board.refill_zones()

docs.title: 6. DRC judge (bench and sign-off)
docs.text:
kicad-cli pcb drc --format json --severity-all --all-track-errors --exit-code-violations \
                  --refill-zones --output out.json routed.kicad_pcb
  • Run on the input board and on the output board; the score is the multiset difference by violation type and location ("added errors"), so pre-existing problems are not blamed on the router.
  • Unconnected items are counted separately (they measure completion, not legality).
  • Exit code 5 means violations exist; parse the JSON for the details.

docs.title: 7. Pitfalls to design around
docs.text:
• Footprint flips mirror pad layers and change rotation conventions; test flips against KiCad's output.
  • KiCad rotation is counter-clockwise in a y-down coordinate system (see pcbgolf/placer.py rot_pt).
  • Zones must be refilled after routing; never write stale fills (use --refill-zones for the judge).
  • Net-class assignment can come from the schematic (directives), pattern rules in .kicad_pro, or the board; resolve in KiCad's priority order.
  • Locked items (locked flag) and user groups must never move or be ripped.

docs.title: 8. Implementation status (M11)
docs.text:
• IPC action plugin (kicad_plugin/): saves a copy of the open board with its project (save_as(..., include_project=True); the rules come from the copied project files), routes it, and adds the new tracks and vias with begin_commit → create_items → push_commit (one undo step). Since 2026-10-06 also, each by an environment variable (README): TRACEMAKER_REROUTE=1 removes the unlocked tracks and vias and routes the board again (route --reroute; locked copper, arcs and zones stay); TRACEMAKER_PLACE=<mode> runs tracemaker-place first and moves the footprints with update_items (side changes are not applied; when parts move, the old copper is routed again and the zones are refilled); TRACEMAKER_REFILL=1 refills the zones. Removal, moves and new copper are one commit. KiCad records a zone refill as a step of its own, so with a refill the result takes two undos; that is why refill is off unless footprints moved. Not built: a long-running tracemakerd (each run starts the engine afresh). The plugin is tested offline against kicad-python 0.8 (test_offline.py).
  • Round trip in a running KiCad GUI (scripts/kicad_gui_roundtrip.py, KiCad 10.0.6): pcbnew from the Docker image runs on an Xvfb display with the API server enabled (kicad_common.json), the first-run wizard is clicked away through XTEST, and the plugin talks to the live board over the API socket. On multichannel_mixer-unrouted: tracks 140 → 316 and vias 19 → 21 in the open board (80 connections in 30 s); one Ctrl+Z gives back 140 / 19, Ctrl+Y the result; KiCad's DRC of the board saved from the GUI: unconnected 148 → 65, no new errors. With --place refine: 65 footprints moved, old copper routed again, zones refilled, two undos restore tracks, vias and footprint positions, no new DRC errors. The script is not a ctest (it needs Docker, Xvfb and about three minutes); screenshots in report/m11-gui/.
  • Engine access: the plugin imports the Python module tracemaker when it can and otherwise runs the tracemaker binary (route --emit-items). TRACEMAKER_ARGS uses CLI spelling for both (decision D17).
  • Python bindings (bindings/, pybind11, CMake option TM_BUILD_PYTHON, on when pybind11 is found and the build is not a sanitizer build): read_board, route, emit_items, drc. route calls tmk::app::run_route_job (src/app/route_job.hpp), the function behind the CLI's route subcommand, so both give byte-identical boards (ctest python_bindings checks this on a PCBench board). The GIL is released while routing and checking. The module is built into build/<preset>/python/ (D18).
  • PCM package: scripts/make_pcm_package.py writes build/pcm/tracemaker-<version>.zip (metadata schema v2 as shipped with KiCad 10, type: plugin, runtime: ipc, kicad_version: 10.0, the plugin under plugins/, the brand icon as resources/icon.png (64×64) and as the action's toolbar icons (icons-light/icons-dark, 24 and 48 px, D123); reproducible archive). scripts/validate_pcm.py checks the layout and metadata and also runs kicad-python's official validator when it is installed; ctest pcm_package builds and validates the archive. The engine is not bundled by default (D19); --binary/--module bundle the Linux builds for use on the same machine. Installed through the Plugin and Content Manager of a running KiCad 10.0.6 (headless, as above; Install from File…): the manager lists TraceMaker 0.1.0 as installed and compatible, and the files are in 3rdparty/plugins/org_tracemaker_autoroute/ (report/m11-gui/pcm-installed.png). Not checked: that KiCad then builds the plugin's virtual environment and shows the toolbar button (the container had no network for pip).
  • Release package (M17, D121): scripts/make_release.py builds the dist preset (CPU only, libstdc++, libgcc, SQLite and zstd linked statically; the binary needs glibc 2.38) and writes a tarball and tracemaker-<version>-pcm-linux-x86_64.zip, the same package with plugins/bin/tracemaker, plugins/bin/tracemaker-place and the built viewer (plugins/share/tracemaker/viewer, found because the binaries look in ../share/tracemaker/viewer and TM_VIEW_DIR) inside. scripts/test_release_install.py installs the tarball in a clean container with no compiler and no Python (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13 and Fedora pass; Debian 12 fails on glibc, as expected), serves the viewer page, routes the example board (49 of 49 connections; tracemaker drc --refill-zones finds no error and nothing unconnected) in 5 s, and validates the package. scripts/kicad_gui_roundtrip.py --package ZIP runs the plugin as unpacked from that zip (no executable bit kept, no TRACEMAKER variable) in the live KiCad 10.0.6 GUI: 498 tracks and 15 vias added, one undo removes them, redo restores them, no new DRC error. Not checked: KiCad's own Install from File on this archive, and its virtual environment for kicad-python.

docs.title: 9. Simple Route JSON (src/io/srj, D90)
docs.text:
tscircuit publishes autorouting problems as Simple Route JSON (SRJ): one JSON object with the layer count, the board bounds, rectangular or round obstacles, the connections to make and a few scalar rules; a solution adds traces. TraceMaker reads and writes it at the edge only. The model, the exact check and the judge stay KiCad's: a problem becomes a KiCad board with its project, the usual pipeline routes and judges it, and the routed board is written back as traces.

tracemaker srj-import problem.json -o board.kicad_pcb [--clearance-mm X] [--hole-to-hole-mm X] [--json summary.json]
tracemaker route board.kicad_pcb -o routed.kicad_pcb ...
tracemaker srj-export routed.kicad_pcb --problem problem.json -o solved.json [--json summary.json]

Field meanings are taken from lib/types/srj-types.ts and the code around it in github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter (MIT, read at 5bcf774) and from the page advanced/simple-route-json on docs.tscircuit.com, which is older and says less.

Geometry. SRJ is millimetres with y up; KiCad has y down. A point (x, y) becomes (x, −y) and back, with no offset, so the board looks the same on screen and ccwRotationDegrees is KiCad's pad angle unchanged. Layers are top, inner1 … innerN, bottom in stack order and map to F.Cu, In1.Cu …, B.Cu. A problem with one layer gets a B.Cu that a rule area closes to tracks and vias, since a KiCad board has two copper layers at least. The board edge is the outline polygon if there is one, else the bounds rectangle.

Nets. SRJ has no net table. An obstacle lists ids in connectedTo (connection names, port ids, net ids of the tool that made the file) and a connection point carries a pointId and a pcb_port_id. The reader forms the same groups as tscircuit's getConnectivityMapFromSimpleRouteJson: ids that appear together are one group, and an obstacle and a point with the same centre (to 0.01 mm) and layers are too. A group that holds a connection is a net, named after its first connection. An obstacle in a group without a connection gets no net: it is copper to keep clear of, and KiCad's ratsnest must not ask for a connection the problem does not ask for. An obstacle with an empty connectedTo is a keep-out and joins nothing.

Obstacles. One footprint per componentId at the origin; every obstacle is a pad at its absolute position.

Obstacle KiCad one layer SMD pad, rect (rotated by ccwRotationDegrees) or circle (shape: "circle", diameter = width) several layers, in a net plated through-hole pad. SRJ has no drill size: the drill is half the smaller side, at least 0.1 mm, as tscircuit's own conversion to Circuit JSON does. A through-hole pad spans the whole stack even if the obstacle lists fewer layers (warned) several layers, no net one SMD pad per layer: nothing has to join the layers, so no hole is invented isNonPlatedHole non-plated hole; a rectangular one is a slot plus a rule area over the rectangle, since the slot leaves the corners out isCopperPour zone of its net without a fill: tscircuit's pipelines leave pours out of their obstacle sets, so a pour is copper to be poured again around the routing (refill in KiCad)

A connection point that lies on no obstacle of its net gets a round pad of the track width, because KiCad's connectivity needs a pad to end on. The converter counts the point-to-point connections the problem asks for and the ratsnest the board implies (pads − 1 per net) and warns when they differ.

Rules. <board>.kicad_pro carries one net class and the board minimums, and nothing the problem does not state:

SRJ KiCad minTraceWidth minimum track width nominalTraceWidth (else minTraceWidth) track width of the Default class; a connection's own nominalTraceWidth puts its net in a class of that width min_via_pad_diameter / minViaPadDiameter / minViaDiameter, min_via_hole_diameter / minViaHoleDiameter via size and drill of the class, minimum via diameter, drill and annular width; resolved as tscircuit's getViaDimensions (pad 0.3 mm and hole half the pad when absent) defaultObstacleMargin copper clearance (class and board minimum). Absent: 0.15 mm, the fallback tscircuit's routers use, with a warning; --clearance-mm sets it minTraceToPadEdgeClearance, minViaEdgeToPadEdgeClearance custom rules in <board>.kicad_dru (track or via against pad) when they differ from the clearance minTraceToHoleEdgeClearance minimum hole clearance (KiCad applies it to plated holes too) minViaHoleEdgeToViaHoleEdgeClearance, minPlatedHoleDrillEdgeToDrillEdgeClearance minimum hole-to-hole distance (the larger); --hole-to-hole-mm sets it minBoardEdgeClearance minimum copper-to-edge clearance allowBlindAndBuriedVias the board setting; route --blind-vias then uses them allowViaInPad no KiCad setting: reported, and route --via-in-pad is the user's choice minPadEdgeToPadEdgeClearance not written: it concerns fixed pads only

Rules the problem leaves out are zero (no rule), not KiCad's defaults. Preloaded traces, differentialPairs, buses, jumpers, off-board connections and terminalVia hints are read and reported as not imported.

Determinism. The output depends only on the problem and the options: obstacles, footprints and nets keep the file's order, numbers are exact nanometres, and UUIDs are counted from a fixed Philox stream, not drawn. Two conversions give the same bytes (tested).

Export. srj-export writes the problem unchanged with traces set. Nets are matched by name and pads by position. A routed net is a graph (track pieces, vias, pads), joined wherever copper of the net touches, as KiCad 10's connectivity joins it: a track end or a via on another track, two tracks that cross, a track or a via over a pad; each connection gets the shortest path through its net's copper between the pads of its points, as wire points and via points (with via_diameter, via_hole_diameter, and the spanned layers when the problem allows blind vias). The trace starts and ends at the problem's own coordinates. A connection without a path is listed as unrouted and the exit code is 3. Copper that no connection path used (a stub, a partial route) follows as traces named <net>_extra_<n>, so a checker reading the file sees all the copper. Limits: arcs are exported as polylines; a path that changes layer through a through-hole pad has no via point there.

Tests: tests/test_srj.cpp on the hand-made tests/srj/mixed.json (rotated rectangle, circle, plated hole with a multi-layer point, keep-out, non-plated hole, pour, outline, merged connections, a point on bare board) and on inline problems (one layer, a slot, tracks that only touch); tests/integration/srj_roundtrip.py imports tests/srj/tiny.json, routes it, exports it and checks every trace point against the routed copper and, when kicad-cli is there, KiCad's ratsnest and DRC. The benchmark built on this is doc 10 §7.

docs.title: 9.1 Fan-out problems (M14, D96)
docs.text: tracemaker srj-import handles tscircuit's fan-out benchmark (fanout31) with these additions: plane terminations (buses[].termination of type plane) become zones of the net on that layer covering the bounds; a breakout point (pointId starting pcb_breakout_point) takes the layer its bus gives in connectionExitTargets; --unpointed-keepout turns the pads of a net that no connection point lies on into keep-outs; --outline-margin-mm grows the outline (breakout points lie on the bounds); the extension field tracemakerTrackLayers (layer names) closes the other layers to tracks with a rule area that lets vias through. bench/prepare_fanout31.py sets them for the 72 cases; bench/fanout31_run.py routes and scores them.

docs.title: 09 — Real-time visualisation
docs.text: Part of the TraceMaker plan. Start at ../PLAN.md.

docs.title: 1. Goals
docs.text:
• Watch placement and routing live, smoothly, on boards with up to millions of primitives.
  • Make the algorithms legible: what the search is exploring, why something failed, what was learned.
  • Look outstanding: a dark, glowing, layered PCB aesthetic that stays readable.
  • Work locally and remotely (the engine runs on a headless server).
  • Scrub back and forth through the whole run afterwards (replay).

docs.title: 2. Architecture
docs.text:
engine threads ─▶ per-thread SPSC rings ─▶ publisher thread ─┬─▶ replay log (JSON lines in zstd frames, keyframe; D45)
                                                               └─▶ WebSocket server ─▶ browser viewer
                                                                     (snapshot on connect, then deltas,
                                                                      coalesced to ≤ 60 Hz, LOD-filtered)
  • Protocol: binary WebSocket frames carrying FlatBuffers messages (zero-copy decode in the browser). On connect: a full scene snapshot (board, layers, footprints, current copper). Then deltas: added/removed objects by id, overlay updates (heatmaps as compressed tiles), transient events (frontiers, ghosts).
  • Back-pressure: the publisher keeps the latest value per overlay and merges deltas while the socket is busy; transient visual events are droppable, state deltas are not.
  • Replay: the same message stream is written to disk with a keyframe (full snapshot) every N seconds; the viewer opens a log file through the engine's replay mode and can seek anywhere. Built so far (D45): the JSON messages, one per line, in independent zstd frames with the snapshot as its own frame; replay plays from the start (seeking needs the control channel and periodic keyframes, not built yet).
  • Control channel (viewer → engine): pause/resume/step, change speed, pick an object, request detail (e.g., a failure record), adjust visual LOD. Changes to the routing itself stay in the CLI/plugin.
  • Security (issue #4, D116). The viewer streams a whole board, so who may connect matters.
  • It binds 127.0.0.1 by default. --view-host 0.0.0.0 (or a LAN address; TM_VIEW_HOST sets it once for every command) lets other machines connect, and then a token is required on the page and on /ws: random per run (or --view-token, 16+ characters), printed in the URL (http://host:8766/?token=...). The first request carries it in the URL; the server answers with an HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict cookie that the page sends back with every later request, the WebSocket included (the page also puts the token on the /ws URL, for a browser that refuses cookies). --view-insecure serves without a token, and the log says so.
  • Always: a WebSocket upgrade that names an Origin must come from the server's own origin. Browsers do not apply the same-origin rule to WebSockets, so without this a web page open in the user's browser could read the stream of a viewer on localhost. With a loopback bind and no token the Host header must also name this machine (a page on evil.example whose name resolves to 127.0.0.1 would otherwise pass the origin check: DNS rebinding). A reverse proxy or port-forwarding service that puts another name in Host is therefore refused by a loopback viewer: bind a non-loopback address and use the token instead.
  • At most 16 WebSocket viewers (counted from the upgrade, so a burst cannot overshoot; the next gets 503) and 128 open HTTP connections, at most 16 of them from one address (a host that opens idle sockets cannot use up the others' share before it has authenticated; many addresses together still can: this is not a defence against flooding). The cookie is named per port (tm_token_<port>: cookies ignore ports). A Host that is not a name or address with a numeric port is refused. Answers carry Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and X-Frame-Options: DENY (route --view-embed "<origins>" instead sends Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors <origins>, so a dashboard can frame the viewer, D133); the token is compared in constant time.
  • Not built: TLS (the token and the stream cross the network unencrypted: on an untrusted network keep the loopback bind and use an SSH tunnel), accounts, the control channel. The stream is read-only; nothing a client sends is acted on.

docs.title: 3. Renderer (browser, WebGL2 baseline, WebGPU when available)
docs.text:
Browser status (Oct 2026): WebGPU is on by default in Chrome/Edge on Windows/macOS/ChromeOS, depends on drivers in Chrome on Linux (≥ 144), is still behind a flag in Firefox on Linux, and ships in Safari 26. The server is Linux and users may view from Linux, so WebGL2 is the baseline renderer and WebGPU an automatic upgrade (compute-shader LOD and bloom are faster there). All shaders are written once against a thin backend interface; the WebGL2 path uses fragment-shader SDFs and render-to-texture for compute work.
