  • Instanced primitives: one draw per layer per primitive type. Tracks are instanced quads with round caps computed in the fragment shader (signed distance to the segment, KiCad GAL-style), arcs likewise; pads/vias are SDF circles, rounded rectangles and polygons (pre-triangulated in a worker).
  • Signed-distance anti-aliasing at every zoom; copper looks crisp from board view to 10 µm detail.
  • Layer compositing: each copper layer renders to its own target; a compositor blends layers with per-layer colour and opacity, the active layer on top, others dimmed (KiCad-like "high contrast" mode).
  • Bloom/glow pass (downsample–blur–upsample) applied only to active items: the trace being routed, the search frontier, the moving footprint. Static copper stays matte so glow carries meaning.
  • Heatmap overlays as float textures (congestion, history, learned penalties, RUDY, density) with perceptually uniform palettes (viridis/inferno/turbo selectable), blended under or over the copper.
  • Level of detail: below a zoom threshold, tracks become a density texture computed on the GPU (compute shader), so pan/zoom stays at 60 fps on very large boards.
  • Picking: an id buffer pass; hover shows net, class, rule, routing history of the object.

docs.title: 4. What the user sees
docs.text: View element Content Main canvas Board, copper per layer, pads, vias, zones, ratsnest (airwires fade as connections complete) Search frontier The current A* frontier as a fading, glowing wave per active thread (sampled, not every node) Rip-up Ripped tracks dissolve into particles; rerouted ones draw in along their path Failure ghosts Failed attempts shown as dashed red paths for a few seconds, blockers outlined in red, the over-full cut drawn as a red bar with "demand / capacity". On a stall the scene freezes on the stuck connection (§8, issue #8): the rejected paths stay, coloured by cause, with the numbers that rejected them and a verdict Placement motion Footprints glide (interpolated between frames) during global placement; the electrostatic density appears as a heat field; ECO moves pulse the moved part Overlays Congestion, history h, learned penalties, RUDY, pin density, escape plan Layer stack Toggle/solo layers; an exploded 2.5-D tilted view of the stack (each layer a translucent plane, vias as vertical glowing pillars) Timeline Score, unrouted count, DRC errors, overflow over time; stage bands; scrubber for replay Learning panel Bandit arm probabilities per stage, nogood count, top conflict-graph edges, per-net activity Stats HUD Stage, iteration, connections/s, GPU/CPU utilisation, work units, ETA Minimap Whole board with the viewport and hot spots Inspector Click a net/connection to see its escalation ladder history and failure records

docs.title: 5. Visual style
docs.text:
• Dark background (near-black navy), KiCad-familiar layer colours by default (F.Cu red, B.Cu blue, inner layers distinct hues) with an alternative "neon" palette; colour-blind safe option.
  • Motion is purposeful: 150–300 ms easing for state changes; transient effects fade out.
  • Typography: one monospace font for numbers, one sans for labels.

docs.title: 6. Technology
docs.text: Part Choice Viewer TypeScript, Vite, own renderer: WebGL2 baseline (GLSL ES 3.0) + WebGPU (WGSL) backend. deck.gl's WebGPU path is still "experimental" and PixiJS prefers WebGL, so neither is the core; PixiJS v8 is acceptable for UI overlays Debug viewer Rerun (MIT/Apache-2.0, C++ SDK) for kernel and algorithm debugging during M4–M6, before the product viewer has all panels; not a product dependency ("expect breaking changes") UI chrome Lightweight (Preact or Svelte) panels over the canvas; charts with a small canvas plotting library Engine server uWebSockets (Apache-2.0) or Boost.Beast; serves the built static viewer too Schema FlatBuffers, shared .fbs compiled for C++ and TypeScript, once the message set is stable; until then JSON (doc 13), compressed with zstd in recordings (D45)

docs.title: 7. Offline outputs
docs.text: • tracemaker render writes PNG/SVG snapshots and an MP4 time-lapse of a replay (headless WebGPU or a CPU raster path) for reports and the benchmark dashboard.

docs.title: 8. Implementation status (v1)
docs.text: v1 implements the JSON protocol of 13-viewer-protocol.md end to end, recording and replay (plain or zstd-compressed logs) and heatmap overlays. FlatBuffers is not built and no longer planned (D45, D61: the zstd-compressed JSON log is 12–13× smaller than plain JSON, recording leaves routing byte-identical, and the viewer parses JSON natively; a binary schema would add a second encoder and decoder for no measured need). Seeking in a replay, the control channel, the minimap and the WebGPU backend are not built yet.

docs.title: Heatmaps and replay log
docs.text:
• The router keeps two coarse grids (route/heat_grid.hpp, at most 128 cells on the long side, whole-µm cells over the routing lattice) while a sink is attached: expansions, A* expansions per cell (one sample per 64 expansions, cumulative over the run), and history, the largest PathFinder history cost per cell. Both are sent as heatmap messages (layer -1, square-root scaled bytes, "scale":"sqrt") every max(200k, budget / 40) expansions (2M without a work budget) and once at the end. They are counted by work, not wall time, so a recording is the same for the same input and seed; the router never reads them, so routing is unchanged (record_replay compares boards routed plainly, recorded and viewed byte for byte).
  • The server keeps the latest grid per name, so a viewer that connects late (or a replay) sees the current overlay. The viewer draws the selected one over the copper as an R8 texture with linear filtering and the inferno palette (zero cells transparent); M or the Overlay chips choose it, #heat=<name> in the URL preselects it, and the legend shows the raw maximum.
  • tracemaker route --record FILE writes one JSON message per line with a leading "t" (seconds). If FILE ends in .zst the log is a sequence of independent zstd frames (server/replay_log.hpp): the board snapshot is a frame of its own and later frames close every 1 MiB of text, so a killed run loses at most the open frame and any zstd tool reads the log (zstd -dc run.jsonl.zst | jq). On C-BISCUIT and CANadapter the compressed log is 12–13× smaller than the plain one (≈ 20 kB vs 260 kB). tracemaker-view --replay detects the format from the content.

docs.title: Engine side (src/server/)
docs.text:
Target Contents tm_viz_messages (tm::viz) server/messages.hpp: board_snapshot_json(board, name) plus builders for track_add/remove, via_add/remove, footprint_move, ratsnest, frontier, path_try, failure, stats, stage, log, heatmap, and message_type(). Depends only on model, drc and nlohmann_json, so the router can link it without Boost tm_server (tm::server) tmk::server::ViewerServer : events::Sink: Boost.Beast HTTP + WebSocket on one background I/O thread. Serves static files (MIME types, percent-decoding, .. and symlink escape rejected) from <repo>/viewer/dist or ServerOptions::web_root; WebSocket at /ws. Default bind 127.0.0.1:8766 (8765 is the dev progress site), a token when the bind is not loopback, Origin and Host checks, client caps (§2 Security) tracemaker-view tracemaker-view <board.kicad_pcb> [--port N] [--host H] [--token T] [--insecure] [--web DIR] [--demo] [--keep-tracks] [--replay LOG [--speed S] [--loop]] tm_replay (tm::replay) server/replay_log.hpp: ReplayWriter (plain, or zstd frames for .zst) and ReplayReader (format detected from the magic number; a truncated tail is ignored, corrupt frames throw). Links libzstd only tm_server_tests Catch2: message builders, snapshot of pic_programmer (skipped if the fixture is missing), HTTP serving and traversal rejection, snapshot-then-deltas delivery, late-client catch-up, back-pressure; replay log round-trips (plain, zstd, multi-frame, truncated, corrupt), HeatGrid sizing/scaling, and routing C-BISCUIT with a capturing sink: heatmaps sent, copper identical to routing without one. Registered with ctest

Server behaviour: - publish() only appends to a mutex-protected inbox and posts a drain to the I/O thread; it never touches sockets. wants_transient() is true only while a viewer is connected, so producers can skip frontier work. - The server keeps the latest board snapshot and the state since it (tracks/vias added or removed, footprint moves, the latest ratsnest, stats and heatmap per name/layer, and the last 300 stage/log/failure messages). A client that connects mid-run receives the snapshot, then that state, then the live stream. - Per-client back-pressure: beyond 2,000 queued messages or 8 MB, frontier/path_try are dropped and queued stats are coalesced to the latest; a new board supersedes queued scene deltas; a client more than 256 MB behind on state is disconnected (it reconnects and gets a fresh snapshot). - Additions to the protocol (all optional, ignored by older readers): pads carry fp (footprint index), num (pad number) and hole:{pts,r}; footprints carry value; the board outline is chained into closed loops where the pieces join. Arc tracks are sent as straight segments with negative ids (-1, -2, …), so producers can number new tracks from Board::tracks.size() upwards. Copper graphics (non-pad copper shapes) are not sent yet.

docs.title: Viewer (viewer/, TypeScript + Vite, no framework)
docs.text:
• WebGL2 renderer written against the raw API (GLSL ES 3.0, viewer/src/shaders.ts): instanced capsules with a signed-distance fragment shader (tracks, round/oval pads, polygon-pad edges with r > 0, outline, ratsnest, footprint boxes); vias as SDF rings with drill; polygon pads ear-clipped; zones and the board substrate filled with an even-odd stencil pass (robust to holes and fractured fills).
  • Layer compositing: each copper layer is drawn into a 4× MSAA offscreen target, resolved, and composited with its opacity, so overlapping copper on one layer never double-blends. "Active on top" draws the active layer last and dims the others; layers can be hidden individually. Through-hole pads, holes and vias draw above.
  • Effects use additive blending: new tracks glow and decay (two Gaussian halos, 1.4 s), frontier points are fading dots (0.6 s), path_try is a fading polyline, failures are pulsing red rings at both ends plus a moving red dashed line (4.5 s). Effects are suppressed while catching up after a snapshot or a stall.
  • HUD: stage, iteration, routed/total with progress bar, unrouted, rip-ups, failures, elapsed, messages/s, FPS, stats.extra; layer list (click = active, eye = visibility, keys 1–9); toggles for active-on-top (H), zones (Z), ratsnest (R), footprints, effects (E), follow activity (L); event log of log/stage/failure; cursor position in board millimetres; footprint reference labels; hover tooltip (net, layer, width/size, pad ref) from a CPU uniform-grid picker, with the hovered net highlighted.
  • WebSocket client reconnects with exponential backoff (0.4–5 s) and applies all queued messages once per animation frame; only the newest transient messages of a frame are kept after a stall.
  • Views can be linked as #view=<x mm>,<y mm>,<px per mm>&layer=<n>&hc=0|1&follow=1.

docs.title: Freeze on a routing stall (issue #8, D113)
docs.text:
• When. A stall is threshold (default 24, #stall=N in the URL) failed attempts without the routed count rising, the latest of them for a reason a rule or a placement could explain (boxed_in, no_legal_path, exact_check, rip_limit, layer_limit; not a budget that ran out, a skipped identical attempt, a rolled-back transaction). It is counted in the engine's own failures, not in seconds. Failures replayed while the viewer catches up after a snapshot, and a frame that carries the final done stats (a late client joining a finished run), never freeze. On by default for route --view; route --no-freeze (the board snapshot says "freeze": false) or #freeze=0 turns it off and nothing changes.
  • What freezes. A viewer latch (viewer/src/stall.ts), not the engine: the router keeps going. While latched, copper, ratsnest, heatmap and footprint messages are kept in order and applied when the user resumes (nothing is lost or reordered); the search frontier is dropped; the HUD (stats, stage, log) keeps counting. More than 400,000 held messages cannot be applied reliably, and Resume then reloads the page for a fresh snapshot.
  • What is shown. The stuck net stays highlighted; every rejected path of the selected connection (the last 16) stays drawn, coloured by cause (pin boxed in, blocked, exact check, rip limit), with rings at its two pads and a cross at the place the way is narrowest (or the closest approach). Beside it a label in board millimetres, need 0.25 mm track + 0.2 mm clearance; widest track that fits 0.12 mm on F.Cu, a verdict line (placement, rule, contested, unknown: doc 13 "The failure verdict") and the rule the numbers came from. The numbers are the engine's, measured with its own obstacle tests; the browser measures nothing. The side panel lists the stalled connections with their verdict chips; [ and ] (or a click on the list, or on copper of one of those nets) move between them. Space, Escape or the Resume button releases the scene and re-arms the latch.
  • Control channel. Still only this dismiss button, and it changes nothing in routing (§2).
  • Tested. viewer/src/stall.test.ts and stall_draw.test.ts (Node, no browser: the latch, the held messages, the label text, the drawing against a recording context); ctest viewer_stall; and by hand in headless Chromium against a live router (bench/records/issue8/).

docs.title: Return-path overlay (issue #7, D114)
docs.text:
The viewer draws the reference-return audit of doc 05 §42 from return_path messages: the signal in cyan, the return in red (shifted a few pixels, with arrows from the end of the trace back to its start), and for the selected net callouts (signal pad, assumed return pad, signal via, return via or capacitor or a missing stitch, the separation). Callout labels never overlap: one with no room is left out and its marker stays. P toggles the overlay; the Return paths panel lists the audited nets worst first (chips: +detour, split, stitch, ok) and a click selects one and zooms onto it. Served by route --return-paths ... --view and by tracemaker return-paths BOARD --nets ... --view.

The viewer draws the footprint check of doc 05 §43 from the footprint_check message: a ring on every footprint that differs from its datasheet (red) or has an untrusted reference (amber), and for the selected one a cross on each wrong pad with a short label (pad 3: 0.15 mm off, pad 1: 1.8x0.6 vs 1.55x0.6 mm, missing pad 4). The Footprint check panel lists the footprints with findings (errors first, the selected one scrolled into view); a click selects one, zooms onto it and prints the full sentences and the datasheet it was compared with (brand, part, document, revision, page). D toggles the overlay. Served by footprint-check ... --view, and by route --footprint-refs ... --footprint-warn-only --view.

The viewer lists the critical nets of doc 05 §44 from the critical_nets message after a route: a Critical nets panel with a tier chip (T1 clocks, crystals and RF; T2 high-speed links; T3 memory and fast buses), the vias the route added to each net and the voids of its reference plane it runs over; amber where a rule was missed (a split crossed, vias over --critical-via-max), with the reason in the row's tooltip and below the list when a net is selected. A click on a net whose return_path message was sent (every critical net on a board with a plane) shows its return path in the overlay of doc 09 above.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
cd viewer && npm install && npm run build            # -> viewer/dist (served by the engine)
cmake --build --preset release --target tracemaker-view
build/release/src/server/tracemaker-view bench/data/kicad/demos/video/video.kicad_pcb --demo
# open http://localhost:8766/ (from another machine: add --host 0.0.0.0 and open the URL it prints, token included); --demo clears the board's tracks and "routes" them again with synthetic events
cd viewer && npm run dev                              # hot-reload development, proxies /ws to :8766

Verified in headless Chromium (SwiftShader WebGL2) on the video (7,932 tracks, 4 layers) and RoyalBlue54L-Feather (8 layers, zone fills) demos. Firefox has not been tested on this machine; the renderer uses only core WebGL2 (instancing, MSAA renderbuffers, blitFramebuffer, stencil).

docs.title: Building unrouted fixtures
docs.text:
strip_routing in bench/prepare_dac2020.py removes every top-level segment/arc/via node and keeps everything else byte for byte, including zones. Both DAC2020 and bench/prepare_demos.py then prepare the unrouted derivative through bench/prepare_inputs.py: private native pcbnew.LoadBoard/SaveBoard conversion without refill, deterministic identity repair and item ordering, then native refill/DRC. Unique nonzero native source UUIDs are preserved; loader-generated, missing, zero and duplicate identities are repaired before the first authoritative refill. Stale fill caches are discarded, not zone geometry. This does not change the all-tracks/arcs/vias strip policy or add thermal-array retention.

Fixtures contain <out>/<name>/unrouted.kicad_pcb, byte-exact copies of the source .kicad_pro/.kicad_dru when present, and preparation.drc.json. DAC2020 also keeps its byte-exact human raw.kicad_pcb and Specctra fixture. Preparation never rewrites source/human boards. Work is private and the runnable board is published last; failure removes only generated unrouted board/rule/report artifacts, so an earlier successful board cannot masquerade as the requested input. Missing current rules do not reuse a previous fixture's rules. DRC findings are retained as evidence, not treated as a requirement that the unrouted input be clean.

Tools and reproducibility (D107). Host Python 3.8+ and its standard library suffice; conversion additionally needs KiCad 10's pcbnew Python bindings, with the exact major.minor.patch version of the selected CLI. KICAD_CLI and KICAD_PYTHON select executable paths (not shell command strings). Without overrides, preparation finds kicad-cli on PATH, falling back to scripts/kicad-cli; the repository ships an executable scripts/kicad-python companion using the same TRACEMAKER_KICAD_IMAGE (default kicad/kicad:10.0.6), home/current-directory mounts and caller UID/GID as the CLI wrapper. Native CLI installs use the host Python, or KiCad.app's bundled Python on macOS; set KICAD_PYTHON when pcbnew belongs to a different interpreter. A version mismatch fails before loading/refilling the board. For Docker, source, checkout and output must be under $HOME or the mounted current directory (the wrappers' mount contract); no personal paths or additional packages are required.

With the same source/rule bytes, fixture name and native tool versions, repeated preparations should yield byte-identical boards and rules. Native DRC report ordering/counts are not promised byte-identical (§4, judge noise); report hashes are not a determinism claim. Native conversion/refill intentionally changes the prepared input compared with the old strip-only scripts: rebuild inputs and measure fresh paired baselines against the same new fixtures, never compare old cached inputs with newly prepared ones.

Fixture-independent controls (own generated legacy board, no downloaded/redistributed PCB) are:

python3 tests/integration/fixture_preparation.py
python3 tests/integration/fixture_preparation_native.py

The native control first converts legacy zero-timestamp zones without refill and reports the missing/zero zone IDs, then invokes the actual demo entrypoint twice and compares board/project/custom-rule bytes, nonzero unique identities, preserved zone geometry, native fill presence and untouched source bytes. KiCad unavailability skips the native test; conversion/preparation failures do not. The place-and-route sets (unlocked footprints reset to a pile) remain built by bench/make_place_sets.py.

docs.title: 4. Harness (bench/)
docs.text:
bench/run.py routes each board of a set with a snapshot of the engine binary, judges input and output with kicad-cli pcb drc, and writes bench/results/<run-id>/{boards.jsonl, summary.json, report.md, boards/} (summary.json feeds the progress site). bench/compare_runs.py compares two runs board by board and checks the gates of §5.

Option Effect --set NAME the boards of bench/sets/NAME.txt (names the set in the summary) --work N deterministic work budget per board, no knowledge base; --time becomes a safety stop (3,600 s). Every portfolio variant gets the whole budget, so a board does up to eight times N --threads N router threads per board; with --work the default is the cores per job (at most 8), since the output does not depend on it (D47), but 1 with --halving in the route options, whose budget shares follow the thread count; without --work it is also the portfolio size (default 1) --refill KiCad refills zones before judging input and output; needed whenever fills may be stale (--soft-zones) --route-args=... extra tracemaker route options (also TM_ROUTE_ARGS) --fixtures DIR boards from DIR/<name>/unrouted.kicad_pcb instead of PCBench; a .kicad_pro/.kicad_dru beside it is copied next to the output so KiCad judges with the board's rules --tier, --limit, --seed sample PCBench boards by Freerouting tier instead of a set

Sets (bench/sets/):

Set Boards Command When quick the 30 PCBench tier-A boards of --limit 30 --seed 1 --set quick --work 1000000 --route-args "--variants 1" (≈ 30 s with --jobs 4) every routing change mid 11 large, hard PCBench boards --set mid --work 20000000 changes to search, plans or rip-up, which can move results at 20 M while quick stays identical planes 7 KiCad demos with zone fills plus tests/boards/plane_smd, routing stripped bench/prepare_demos.py --set planes, then --fixtures build/demos --set planes --work 3000000 --refill, once plain and once with --route-args=--soft-zones changes to zones, planes and plane targets

Comparing. bench/compare_runs.py BEFORE AFTER [--expect-identical] lists every board whose routed output differs or got worse, the clean-pass and completion totals and router seconds, and exits 1 if a gate fails. --expect-identical adds "every routed board byte-identical" for speed-ups and refactors. Build the "before" binary from the base commit (a clean origin/main worktree) and run both on the same machine. Route CPU time is printed per board and in total. When both runs used the same --work, boards whose output is byte-identical did the same work, so their CPU change is run-to-run noise or a change in speed that leaves the output alone; the report prints that band and lists the boards (and the total) that moved beyond it, and at least 10 %. When every identical board moved the same way by more than 10 % it says that too: one pair of runs cannot tell a faster binary from a quieter machine, a second run of one binary can. All of it is a pointer for gate 5, not a failure.

Other tools.

Tool Purpose Status speed_ab.py engine speed A/B at a fixed work budget: wall and CPU time, instructions, memory, byte-identical outputs (--demos for KiCad demos) maintained scripts/drc_parity.py, drc_broken_parity.py tracemaker drc against KiCad on demo and broken boards (ctest kicad_drc_parity, kicad_drc_broken_parity); counts are capped at KiCad's 199 per type maintained refill_parity.py tracemaker drc --refill-zones against kicad-cli pcb drc --refill-zones: unconnected items per net on boards with zones (--dir … --glob raw.kicad_pcb --sample N for PCBench; doc 05 §36) maintained quality.py, quality_bench.py, compare.py, human_baseline.py routing quality metrics; TraceMaker against Freerouting versions; the designers' own routing judged the same way maintained check_env.py, prepare_dac2020.py, prepare_demos.py, make_place_sets.py tool checks and fixture preparation maintained pair_eval.py, feasibility.py, crules_detect.py, crules_place.py, crules_tiers.py feature evaluations (diff pairs, escape feasibility, component rules) kept for re-measuring their features make_bus_boards.py, bus_eval.py generated bus boards and the bus evaluation (doc 05 §38): routes without and with the bus options at one budget, measures with tracemaker buses, judges with KiCad kept for re-measuring bus routing m6_bench.py, place_m8.py, place_auto.py, place_flip.py, place_intent.py, place_variants.py, compare_placed.py, rescore_placed.py, dsn_place.py milestone evaluations of the global router and placement historical; results are in the docs that cite them ses_import.py, record_fr.py import a Freerouting session; screen-record Freerouting utilities cpu_sample.py per-thread CPU sampling from /proc Linux only

Not built (planned in the first version of this document): manifest files, a standard (~300 boards) and full tier as named sets, bench/report.py with an HTML dashboard, and paired statistics (sign test, bootstrap interval). Seeds: best-of-1 is the headline; best-of-5 is reported separately where a comparison needs it (PCBWorld reports baselines as best of 5).

Judge noise. KiCad's solder_mask_bridge count can differ between runs on byte-identical boards when zones are refilled (StickHub: 17, 15 and 13); read a change in that type alone as noise.

Native error gates (D106). bench/drc_judge.py compares physical error instances, not totals by type: removing one clearance cannot cancel a new clearance somewhere else. Item ordering and regenerated UUIDs or footprint references do not change an identity when positions are available; kind, net, layer, geometry description and position do. Coordinates and dimensions are normalised to nanometres from report units; items without positions use UUIDs as a fallback. Duplicate findings retain their multiplicity. Violation-level layer context is also identity: multilayer zone/PTH pad labels may not identify the affected layer of a thermal defect. Changing its layer is a new instance; changing its minimum/actual spoke-count diagnostic on the same layer is not.

Routing gates include error-severity starved_thermal and isolated_copper even if KiCad names only pads or zones: routed copper can damage a refill without appearing in its report. Other pad/graphic-only changes remain diagnostic, including pad-only solder-mask refill noise and net-propagation clearance changes. Placement compares its existing placement-error types by instance, excluding internal errors of one rigid footprint; thermal/island findings are evaluated because they depend on surrounding zones, not only that footprint. Routing's existing immutable/type exclusions otherwise stay unchanged.

KiCad 10.0.x reports may truncate at 499 clearance findings and 199 findings of other types, across severities (constants and assumption isolated in the helper). Reaching a cap on either side makes that type's difference unknown; it is not reported as an exact added count. A capped evaluated type with errors on either side sets error_gate (or place_error_gate) to unknown, never clean or a passing comparison, even if the visible errors name only pads. Warning-only caps and routing-immutable types remain diagnostic, with evaluated and non-evaluated capped types recorded separately. added_errors, quality's router_errors, and the existing CLI options retain their meanings and type-count display, now backed by instance differences.

Connectivity limitation. Completion deliberately retains the existing ratio from KiCad's unconnected_items list. That list may truncate at 499; connectivity_capped discloses this independently of evaluated error caps. The ratio is not an exact connectivity measurement at saturation. No uncapped connectivity worker or new completion definition is included here.

docs.title: 5. Gates (used by the roadmap)
docs.text:
1. No board in quick gets worse in clean pass or completion (compare_runs.py).
  2. Zero added KiCad DRC errors on every board that was clean before (compare_runs.py).
  3. Time within budget on every board (with --work, the budget is work units; wall time only stops the job).
  4. Routed boards byte-identical unless the change is meant to change results (compare_runs.py --expect-identical; then the differences are recorded).
  5. Quality is judged at equal work, speed at equal wall time. The work budget charges search expansions and flood cells only (the work profile shows what else a run did), so a change that moves work into dearer operations, such as reaching negotiation sooner, takes longer at the same work while routing more in the same time (doc 05 §37). A claim that a change is faster or slower needs runs at equal wall time; compare_runs.py points at the boards.

docs.title: 6. Implementation status (2026-10-02; sets, work budgets and refill 2026-10-08, D81)
docs.text:
• bench/run.py samples PCBench boards per Freerouting tier, routes each with a binary snapshot, judges with kicad-cli pcb drc, and compares with Freerouting's published per-board results (benchmarks.json).
  • Samples: tier A 40 of 453 boards, tier B 40 of 560, tier C 30 of 122, tier D all 22 (seed 1).
  • Added errors compare physical instances involving a track, via or arc (decision A16), plus error-severity thermal/island findings after refill (D106); other new pad-only reports remain diagnostics. Evaluated capped error reports are unknown, not clean.
  • Results go to bench/results/<run>/ and the progress site's benchmark panel.
  • Latest (final8): tier A 100% clean, B 65.0%, C 56.7%, D 50.0% (Freerouting 2.5.0-RC12: 100%, 50.0%, 46.7%, 36.4%); no router-introduced DRC errors on any board.
  • Sets, --work, --refill and compare_runs.py (D81), measured on origin/main a5532a9:
  • --set quick --work 1000000 --route-args "--variants 1" reproduces the earlier quick-tier run (made with TM_ROUTE_ARGS) byte for byte on all 30 boards: 40.0 % clean, 89.2 % completion, about 30 s with --jobs 4.
  • --set mid --work 20000000: 0 of 11 clean, 76.4 % completion, 3 minutes with --jobs 4.
  • --set planes --work 3000000 --refill --route-args=--soft-zones: 86.1 % completion. Without --refill the judge reads the stale fills, and without the copied project files KiCad judged demo outputs on default rules (hundreds of false track_width and clearance errors on RoyalBlue, StickHub and plane_smd).
  • Timing (D86). The summary's seconds used to be the winning variant's own time. With --work every board runs all eight variants, and at one thread per board (the old default) they ran one after another, so a board's job took several times the reported figure (more than eight times when the winner is one of the quicker variants): on the mid set at 20 M, 6–16 s reported against 45–107 s of process time. seconds now covers the whole job, variant_seconds keeps the winner's time and variants lists every variant. A per-variant profile (decelerator4030, LimeSDR, logicbone at 5 M and 20 M) put 81–89 % of the process in the seven losing variants and under 2 % in reading, set-up, clean-up and writing. Times in runs made before D86, including the Freerouting comparisons, are the winner's only.
  • Work profile and route CPU time (D88). The counters change no output (quick 30/30 byte-identical) and cost no measurable time. Two mid runs at 20 M (--jobs 4 --threads 3, the same work), origin/main against D87 (#21): the four byte-identical boards moved +9 % to +14 % in CPU time between the runs (noise of one sequential pair on this 14-core Mac, or a slow-down that left their output alone: one pair cannot tell); only sbc (+41 %) and kitspace_d20 (+24 %) moved beyond it. A 10 % threshold alone would have flagged seven boards. Single CPU-time comparisons of under about 15 % are not evidence here.

docs.title: 7. tscircuit BGA breakouts: sets srj19 and srj20 (D90, measured 2026-10-11)
docs.text:
The dense-package work (M9) had no public reference figure. tscircuit publishes 400 synthetic BGA breakout problems in Simple Route JSON and a dashboard with its own router's results on them, so these two sets give one. The format support is doc 08 §9.

Data. Fetched into bench/data/tscircuit/ at pinned commits by scripts/fetch_fixtures.sh tscircuit, never copied into this repository:

Set Source Commit Licence Problems srj19 github.com/tscircuit/dataset-srj19 (BGA breakouts with passive components on the other side) c1206f3 MIT 200, two layers, 11–87 connections (7,395), 0.15 mm traces, vias 0.3 / 0.2 mm srj20 github.com/tscircuit/dataset-srj20 (BGAs with missing balls) 9384fb8 none stated (no licence file, none in package.json): local benchmarking only 200, two layers, 11–108 connections (8,715), 0.12 mm traces, no via size given

Both use a 0.8 mm ball pitch with 0.36 mm square pads, every connection has two points, and neither states a clearance, a board-edge rule or blind vias.

Conversion. bench/prepare_srj.py (run by the fetch step once the engine is built) converts every problem with tracemaker srj-import --clearance-mm 0.1 --hole-to-hole-mm 0.1 into bench/data/tscircuit/boards/<set>/<sample>/unrouted.kicad_pcb with its project. The two distances are those of tscircuit's published pass criterion (below), so KiCad's judge and theirs test the same thing; the importer's own default (0.15 mm, tscircuit's router fallback, and no hole rule) is reported as a variant. Via size for srj20 is tscircuit's fallback (0.3 / 0.15 mm). The script checks every board by counting: connections in the problem = ratsnest the board implies = connections tracemaker route reports. All 400 convert and all 400 pass. bench/sets/srj19.txt and srj20.txt name the fixture directory in a #fixtures: line, which bench/run.py now reads, so the sets run by name.

Judges. The primary judge is KiCad's DRC with the board's rules; a board is a clean pass when nothing is unconnected, no evaluated error instance was added, and no evaluated error type is capped (D106). The second score is tscircuit's own. bench/srj_score.py exports every routed board with tracemaker srj-export and runs tscircuit's evaluateRelaxedDrc on it: the function behind the "relaxed DRC" column of its dashboard, from tscircuit-autorouter 5bcf774 (lib/testing/) with @tscircuit/checks 0.0.233, called as its benchmark calls it (scripts/benchmark/benchmark-run-task.ts): 0.1 mm between copper of different nets, 0.1 mm between via holes (same net included), traces continuous and inside the board. scripts/fetch_fixtures.sh tscircuit-checker installs it (node, packages pinned to the versions that repository names). A board passes when every connection is routed and the checker reports nothing. The checker was not re-implemented.

tscircuit's dashboard counts boards: "completed" is the share of problems its router solved outright, comparable with fully routed below and not with mean completion; "relaxed DRC pass" is the share solved with no checker error. Its figures, read on 2026-10-10 for its router at 1× effort: srj19 91.5 % completed, 89.5 % passing; srj20 77 % and 77 %. They were not reproduced here: tscircuit's router was not run on this machine, and its run time per problem is not known to us.

Results. python3 bench/run.py --set <set> --work <N> --jobs 12 --threads 1 --route-args "--variants 1 --no-gpu", then python3 bench/srj_score.py <run>. All 200 boards of each set, defaults otherwise.

Set Work Mean completion Fully routed Clean pass (KiCad) Relaxed pass (tscircuit's checker) Median s p95 s srj19 1 M 75.7 % 23.0 % 23.0 % 23.0 % 1.5 2.2 srj19 10 M 92.5 % 60.5 % 60.5 % 60.0 % 9.2 14.1 srj19 50 M 96.7 % 79.5 % 79.5 % 78.5 % 34.2 50.2 srj19, tscircuit's router (its dashboard) 91.5 % 89.5 % srj20 1 M 53.1 % 9.5 % 9.5 % 9.5 % 1.4 1.9 srj20 10 M 81.3 % 33.5 % 33.5 % 33.5 % 9.1 10.9 srj20 50 M 87.6 % 50.0 % 50.0 % 50.0 % 40.9 51.9 srj20, tscircuit's router (its dashboard) 77 % 77 %

10 M is the sets' standard budget (the trend rows show how much the figure depends on it). Seconds are the route's own wall time on one thread with twelve boards running at once on a machine shared with other jobs: indicative only.

  • TraceMaker is behind tscircuit's router on both sets at every budget tried: by 12 points of fully routed boards on srj19 and 27 on srj20 at 50 M.
  • No run added a KiCad DRC error on any board (26 runs, 2,500 board routes): every fully routed board is a clean pass. What is missing is completion.
  • KiCad and tscircuit's checker agree except on 1 board at 10 M and 2 at 50 M (srj19), which KiCad passes and the checker fails with "overlaps … (accidental contact)" between two traces. An independent distance calculation on the exported traces puts the copper of each reported pair at least 0.21 mm apart. The checker (checkEachPcbTraceNonOverlapping) also reports two separate collinear segments of different nets as touching at some spacings (reproduced with two-segment inputs), which a lattice router's output contains. The relaxed column is the checker's verdict as it is.
  • TraceMaker's own count of routed connections is sometimes one lower than KiCad's (it joins tracks at their end points; KiCad 10 also joins copper that overlaps). The harness uses KiCad's count, and the export follows KiCad's rule; the two agreed on every board.

Budget and portfolio, first 50 problems of each set (fully routed = clean pass in every row):

srj19 srj20 1 M, one variant 22 % 8 % 10 M, one variant 66 % 34 % 50 M, one variant 88 % 46 % 200 M, one variant 88 % (median 30 s, p95 172 s) 56 % (median 151 s, p95 195 s) 10 M, default portfolio (8 variants, each with the whole budget) 88 % (median 143 s on one thread) 48 % (median 135 s)

srj19 stops improving between 50 M and 200 M; srj20 is still rising. The default portfolio at 10 M does as well as one variant at 50 M for more total work.

Escape options, 10 M, one variant, first 50 problems:

Option srj19 fully routed (mean completion) srj20 fully routed (mean completion) none 66 % (92.4 %) 34 % (82.4 %) --escape-plan 60 % (93.0 %) 32 % (81.4 %) --escape-flow 60 % (92.2 %) 28 % (79.1 %) --escape-plan --via-in-pad 60 % (93.0 %) 32 % (81.4 %) --via-in-pad byte-identical to none, 50/50 boards byte-identical, 50/50 --blind-vias, --micro-vias byte-identical to none, 50/50 byte-identical, 50/50

None helps. The escape plans route a few more connections on srj19 but finish fewer boards on both sets. The problems allow neither blind nor micro vias, so those two options correctly do nothing. --via-in-pad (which the problems do not allow either: allowViaInPad is absent) changes no board, also not at 0.15 mm clearance where tracemaker escape reports dead balls; why it finds no pad to use was not investigated. The router was not tuned in this work.

Stricter variant: the importer's defaults (bench/prepare_srj.py --clearance-mm default --hole-to-hole-mm default: 0.15 mm clearance, no hole-to-hole rule), 10 M, one variant, all 200 boards.

Set Mean completion Fully routed = clean pass Relaxed pass srj19 81.8 % 14.5 % 10.0 % srj20 78.2 % 29.0 % 29.0 %

At 0.15 mm a 0.15 mm trace does not fit between two balls of srj19 (0.44 mm gap), so inner balls can leave only through vias; srj20's 0.12 mm traces still fit. The 9 srj19 boards that are clean in KiCad and fail the relaxed check have vias of one net closer than 0.1 mm hole to hole, which KiCad does not test without a hole-to-hole rule: the reason the benchmark sets carry that rule.

Limits of the comparison. The judges differ (KiCad's DRC against tscircuit's checker; here they agree to within 1 % of boards). The rules are an interpretation where the files are silent (clearance, hole spacing, via size for srj20; no board-edge clearance, which tscircuit's relaxed check does not apply either). The budgets are not matched to tscircuit's effort setting. The problems are synthetic and two-layer only.

docs.title: 8. M14: srj19/srj20 against tscircuit's current run, and fanout31 (2026-10-11)
docs.text:
tscircuit's dashboard run 38105514608-1 (commit 65522c8): srj19 92.0 % completed / 90.0 % relaxed pass, srj20 78.5 % / 78.5 % (360 s per board, 32 vCPU; median 19–23 s). TraceMaker, one variant, 50 M work, --fast-bends and the new default limits (40 rips, 40 passes): srj19 176/200 = 88.0 %, srj20 117/200 = 58.5 % (section 7: 79.5 % and 50.0 %). With the default eight-variant portfolio on the boards that miss: srj19 +10, srj20 +9 (about 93 % and 63 %). Per-board comparison with the dashboard run, the gap sets (srj19-gap, srj20-gap, srj19-p1fail, srj20-p1fail) and every experiment: doc 16 §10. bench/fanout31_run.py scores the 72 fan-out cases (solved = every connection routed, no unconnected item after the zone refill); results in doc 16 §10.1.

Update, same day (doc 16 §11): with preferred layer directions and the package penalty switched on automatically for breakout boards, one variant at 50 M gives srj19 181/200 (90.5 %) and srj20 124/200 (62 %); the 16-variant portfolio (50 M each, 16 threads, median 164–168 s) closes 7 more on srj19 (188/200 = 94.0 %, tscircuit 92.0 %) and 9 more on srj20 (133/200 = 66.5 %, tscircuit 78.5 %). fanout31: 57 of the 60 cases run solved (tscircuit 48/72); AM3352 is not solved (6–23 connections open at best; tscircuit solves none of its 12 cases either).

docs.title: 9. M15: negotiation as transactions (2026-10-11 evening, doc 16 §12, doc 05 §41)
docs.text:
The breakout profile (D100: transactions, reach-check 2, flood weight 25 %, field prefill and cache) is automatic on breakout boards, so the commands of §8 need no extra options and their results change: one variant at 30 M work gives srj19 178/200 (was 181 at 50 M, 46 → 32 s CPU per board) and srj20 129/200 (was 124 at 50 M, 67 → 59 s). The portfolio is the breakout portfolio with four rounds (D101):

python3 bench/run.py --set srj20 --work 30000000 --route-args "--variants 1 --no-gpu --fast-bends"
python3 bench/run.py --set srj20-m15fail --work 30000000 --jobs 3 --threads 16 --route-args "--variants 16 --no-gpu"        # 71 boards: +19
python3 bench/run.py --set srj20-m15fail3 --work 70000000 --time 330 --jobs 3 --threads 16 --route-args "--variants 16 --no-gpu"   # 24 boards: +8

Sets added: srj20-p2fail (76: the boards P2 leaves open), srj20-e39 (39 of them), srj20-m15fail (71), srj20-m15fail2 (52), srj20-m15fail3 (24 of fewer than 70 connections), srj20-m15fail4 (16), srj19-m15fail (22), srj20-rem67. Results: srj19 191/200 = 95.5 % (178 + 13), srj20 160/200 = 80.0 % (156 within 330 s) (129 + 19 + 8 + 4 with GPUs and 150 M, up to 433 s), tscircuit 184 and 157. These are composites of single-variant and portfolio runs (the wall limit of the last step makes it non-deterministic: 330 s, 16 threads; tscircuit's 360 s, 32 vCPU). quick and mid are byte-identical to the baseline outputs.

Work-budget note: on a breakout board a reachability-flood cell counts a quarter of an expansion against --work, so --work budgets from §7–§8 are not comparable with these (30 M here is about 100–140 s of CPU per hard board; 50 M plain was 67–115 s).

docs.title: 10. Advice (M16, doc 17 §8)
docs.text: bench/advice_eval.py --set SET --name RUN --work W --variants V --advisor CMD [--half even|odd|all] routes each board with route --advisor CMD: a plain portfolio, then, if connections are left, the advisor and a portfolio with its advice (the unadvised variants again plus advised ones); the better result stands. bench/results/RUN/advice.json has one row per board (connections routed by the plain run, by the advised run, whether it was kept, the best advised variant) and a summary; the stuck report and advice of each board are stored beside it, so a result can be reproduced with route --advice FILE. The gate of issue #26 stage 2 is read on the odd half of a set, the even half being where an advisor is tuned.

docs.title: 11. M17: PCBWorld-Bench's real boards and the failing tier B-D boards (2026-10-16, D121, D122)
docs.text: Records: bench/records/m17/ (README with all tables; raw boards.jsonl of every run).

docs.title: 11.1 What PCBWorld-Bench's "679 real boards" are
docs.text:
Doc 18 (A1) took PCBWorld's D3 for an independent second corpus of real boards. Reading the paper (arXiv 2607.05915, the PDF is in the repository clone) and its data tools shows it is not: D3 is derived from PCBench, the corpus this repository already benchmarks. The authors convert PCBench boards to KiCad 9 (design rules kept, then drc_fix_v9.py lowers severities to ignore and a few rule floors to 0), keep the 679 whose converted human layout is fully connected and has no violation, build a "guide board" with one uniform width per net, and split the pool by pad count into D3-A (100 smallest boards), D3-B (287) and D3-C (292). Their evaluation uses fixed test lists (configs/datasets/d3.json): 99 D3-A boards, 10 D3-B, 10 D3-C, and publishes results for D3-A and D3-B only (D3-C is "reserved for future research"). All 119 test boards are PCBench fixtures here by name (bench/sets/pcbworld-d3-test.txt). The PCBWorld repository holds no boards and its conversion needs a KiCad 9 pcbnew built from their engine; that conversion was not reproduced.

What D3 gives, then, is a fixed, published, pad-count-ordered subset with published baselines, not new boards.

docs.title: 11.2 TraceMaker on the 119 test boards
docs.text:
TM_BINARY=build/dist/src/app/tracemaker python3 bench/run.py --set pcbworld-d3-test --time 120 --jobs 3 --threads 8 --name m17-pcbworld-d3 (the release binary, default eight-variant portfolio, KiCad 10.0.6 judge: every connection routed and no error added against the input). bench/pcbworld_d3.py prints the tables.

class boards TraceMaker clean mean routability boards open median s Freerouting 2.5.0-RC12 clean (PCBench nightly) D3-A 99 97 (98.0 %) 0.994 2 1.3 94 (94.9 %) D3-B 10 10 (100 %) 1.000 0 10.0 9 (90.0 %) D3-C 10 9 (90.0 %) 0.996 1 61.4 8 (80.0 %)

The same boards with Freerouting 2.1.0 and the paper's settings (-mp 10, 4 GiB heap, the jar's other defaults; the paper's Table 20), three runs per board from the fixture's DSN, session imported (bench/ses_import.py) and judged by the same judge (bench/pcbworld_fr.py; a run over 600 s counts as a failure: 10 of 357 runs, on four boards):

class Freerouting 2.1.0 clean, mean of 3 runs clean in any of 3 runs mean routability TraceMaker clean, Freerouting not Freerouting clean, TraceMaker not D3-A 0.670 73 (73.7 %) 0.978 24 0 D3-B 0.500 5 (50.0 %) 0.992 5 0 D3-C 0.200 3 (30.0 %) 0.758 6 0

Boards lost. To Freerouting 2.1.0 (this judge): none. To the 2.5.0-RC12 nightly flag: one, D3-A AVR-ISP_pogo-plug_1.27mm_AVR-ISP_pogo-plug_1.27mm, where 3 of 6 connections stay open ("boxed in"; the footprint is a row of 0.4 mm strip pads 0.15 to 0.3 mm apart; its stuck report names fixed copper around the pin; no cause beyond that was found). The other two boards TraceMaker leaves open, D3-A memsarray_mems_modules (9 of 10 routed) and D3-C kitspace_f-91w (80 of 83, the 120 s limit), are not clean in the nightly run either, and Freerouting 2.1.0 hit the 600 s limit on both in all three runs. Against the paper's other methods (KiCadRoutingTools, OrthoRoute, the agents and the RL policies) no per-board result is published, so no board can be named.

What these numbers do not say. The paper's Table 3 (Freerouting 2.1.0 0.80 / 0.78 clean pass on D3-A / D3-B, KiCadRoutingTools 0.74 / 0.20, PPO 0.86 / 0.45, GPT-5.4 0.65 / 0.00; best of five rollouts selected by the paper's potential function) comes from a different judge: KiCad 9, the converted boards with their patched rule files, absolute violations. Freerouting 2.1.0 with the same jar and settings scores 0.670 at one run and 73.7 % over three runs under this repository's judge, against the paper's 0.75 at one run and 0.80 over five, so this judge is not the paper's and the paper's rows for the other methods cannot be set beside TraceMaker's. The only like-for-like comparison here is TraceMaker against Freerouting 2.1.0 under one judge, from one DSN, and it is not the paper's DSN. There is no "better than the paper's methods" claim. D3 test boards are small (median 1.3 s); tier D of this repository is the harder test, and doc 18 §8's expectation that A1 "could look good and teach little" holds.

docs.title: 11.3 --txn and --relax on the failing tier B-D boards (C1)
docs.text:
The 33 boards of tiers B, C and D that the 0.9.0 run left open (bench/sets/pcbench-bd-fail.txt; 16,935 connections; none added an error). Same work for every arm; KiCad-judged.

arm (100 M work per variant) routed boards better / worse than the base clean boards CPU one variant, base 15,289 0 4,858 s one variant, --txn 1 15,320 (+31) 7 / 0 0 3,924 s one variant, --relax (5 rounds of 20 M) 14,206 (-1,083) 3 / 28 0 4,644 s eight variants, base 16,105 0 77,014 s eight variants, --txn 1 16,223 (+118) 15 / 4 (by one connection each) 0 96,039 s eight variants, --relax (5 rounds of 20 M) 15,596 (-509) 11 / 16 2 106,470 s
  • --txn 1 (negotiation as transactions, automatic on breakout boards only) routes more connections on non-breakout boards in both settings: up to +16 on mechkeys_LFK78, never more than one fewer on a board. It completes no board that the base leaves open, so clean pass does not move. It costs more CPU for the same work in the portfolio (+25 %).
  • --relax is a rescue, not a better default: it loses connections on most of these boards (down to -107 on kitspace_d20_tri_r0.3) and finishes kitspace_ardfpga and Hardware_Playground_multisensor_cr2032 with no error added, which nothing else did. Taking the better of base and relax per board gives 16,148 routed (+43) and the two clean boards.
  • Bug found by the experiment: --relax (and --rounds, --round-work, --ramp-from) did nothing with --variants 1; the first relax arm was identical to the base on all 33 boards (bench/records/m17/c1-relax-ignored.md). They now run a portfolio of one (tests/integration/round_options.py).
  • Not concluded: whether --txn 1 as one or two of the eight default variants beats the current default at equal wall time on tiers A to D, which is what changing the default needs; whether a relax pass after a plain run that leaves connections open pays for its time. One seed, one budget, and mini_mass_prog_bench_prog_rig hit the one-hour safety stop in the --txn and --relax arms. Records and caveats: bench/records/m17/README.md.

Quick tier with the release binary: 30 of 30 routed boards byte-identical to main's.

docs.title: Working rules for implementation sessions
docs.text:
1. Read PLAN.md, the docs for the milestone, and CLAUDE.md first.
  2. Every accelerated path (GPU, cache, index) lands with its reference path and an equivalence test.
  3. Every change runs the quick benchmark subset; a regression on any board blocks the change.
  4. Keep the viewer working: new stages emit events from day one.
  5. Update the doc when the design changes, in the same change, and record the decision in 12-decisions.md.

docs.title: 13 — Viewer protocol (v1, JSON over WebSocket)
docs.text:
Part of the TraceMaker plan. Start at ../PLAN.md. v1 uses JSON for speed of development; FlatBuffers (doc 09) replaces it once the message set is stable. Coordinates are integer nanometres.

The engine serves the viewer at http://<host>:<port>/ and streams messages on ws://<host>:<port>/ws. The host is the local machine unless the user asked otherwise; a viewer that other machines can reach requires a token (?token=... once, then a cookie) and every /ws upgrade must come from the server's own origin (docs/09, Security). On connect the server sends the latest board snapshot, then every later message in order. Messages marked transient may be dropped under load; all others are state and must be delivered.

type fields meaning board name, bbox:[x0,y0,x1,y1], layers:[{name,index}] (copper, top first), nets:[name], outline:[[[x,y],…],…], pads:[pad], tracks:[track], vias:[via], zones:[{layer,net,polys:[[[x,y],…]]}], footprints:[{ref,x,y,angle,back,bbox}], optional freeze (false when the engine was started with route --no-freeze: the viewer does not hold the scene on a routing stall) Full scene (sent on connect and after big changes) track_add track A track was committed track_remove id A track was removed (rip-up) via_add / via_remove via / id Same for vias footprint_move ref, x, y, angle Placement change (pads follow; resend board if simpler) ratsnest edges:[[ax,ay,bx,by,net],…] Current unrouted connections frontier (transient) conn, layer, pts:[[x,y],…] Sampled points of an active search frontier path_try (transient) conn, pts:[[x,y,layer],…] A candidate path being evaluated failure conn, net, rung, cause, a:[x,y], b:[x,y], blockers:[track/via/pad ids] (still empty), blocker_nets:[net ids] (nets of the connections the rejected route would have ripped), region:[x0,y0,x1,y1] (the two pads ±1.5 mm, nm). Optional, from issue #8 (a reader that does not know them ignores them; they are present only when the router measured them): reason (boxed_in, no_legal_path, exact_check, rip_limit, rolled_back, ...), width_nm, clearance_nm, min_width_nm (the attempt's track width, the clearance applied, and the narrowest width the rules allow: the board minimum, else 0.1 mm), gap_nm (the widest track that gets through from the closest approach on towards the target with routed copper counted; 0 = not even a hairline), gap_fixed_nm (the same with only fixed copper counted), gap_layer, at:[x,y] (where the way is narrowest, or the closest approach when none gets through), verdict (placement, rule, contested, unknown), rule (where the width and clearance came from, and what would open the way), rejected:[[x,y,layer],...] (the path that was tried, corners only, at most 64; left out when the search never left the source pad) A failed attempt (failure memory) advice.hint kind, text, origin (file or advisor) One hint of an advice file in use (doc 17); stage events named advisor mark a consultation advice.rejected why The advisor failed, was too slow, or its advice was refused; the run goes on unadvised return_path net, name, detour_mm, max_separation_mm, voids, splits, missing_stitches, signal:[{layer, pts:[[x,y],…]}], return:[{layer, pts}] (the return along the trace: over copper its mirror image, across a void the detour; drawn from the end of the trace back to its start), callouts:[{kind, p:[x,y], text}] (signal_pad, ref_pad, signal_via, return_via, missing_stitch, separation, split) One net's reference-return audit (issue #7, doc 05 §42). State, kept per net for late clients; coordinates in nm footprint_check checked, ok, mismatch, unverified, untrusted, errors, warnings, footprints:[{ref, lib_id, status, p:[x,y], datasheet?:{id, brand, part, document, revision?, page?, figure?, url?}, issues:[{severity, kind, pad, text, label, p:[x,y]}]}] (only footprints with an issue) The footprint check against datasheet land patterns (issue #5, doc 05 §43). kind: pad_count, missing_pad, extra_pad, position, size, drill, pad_type, orientation, mirrored, pattern, no_reference, untrusted_source; text is a sentence, label a few words for a mark on the board. State (the latest one is kept for late clients); coordinates in nm critical_nets nets:[{name, tier, why, vias, length_mm, unrouted, void_crossings?, detour_mm?, splits?, warnings:[text]}], totals:{nets, vias, void_crossings, over_via_limit} The critical nets after a route with --critical-* or --si-rules (issue #24, doc 05 §44): tier 1 clocks, crystals and RF, 2 high-speed links, 3 memory and fast buses; vias and length added by the route; where the board has a reference plane, how often the net runs over a void of it. Each net's return_path message follows. State (the latest is kept for late clients) escape_plan corridors:[{id, net, pad:"REF.NUM", via, pts:[[x,y],…]}] Escape corridors reserved for dense-package pins (M9); id is the board pad index. With --escape-flow (doc 05 §14) pts continues past the dog-bone via site along the planned channels, on the layer the via changes to. Sent at the start and after each restart; the viewer draws them (toggle X) escape_release id The pin is connected (or given up): its corridor is gone escape_dead id, net, pad, p:[x,y], why A pin enclosed by fixed copper even for a negotiated, necked-down search: not retried (red cross in the viewer) bus name, nets:[net,…] A bundle of a bus (doc 05 §38): the nets whose connections between two components are routed lane by lane, in lane order. Sent once per bundle when routing starts bus_lane bus, conn, net, state:"leader"|"followed"|"left" A connection of a bundle was routed: it leads, it has its neighbour lane's layers and vias, or it left the bus bus_skew bus, skew, limit Length matching of a group is done: longest minus shortest member and the limit, nm heatmap name, x0, y0, cell, w, h, layer, max, data:[…] (row-major, 0–255), optional scale ("sqrt": byte = round(255·√(v/max)), non-zero cells ≥ 1; absent: linear) Overlays, latest per name replaces the previous one. The router sends expansions (A* expansions per cell, cumulative) and history (largest PathFinder history cost per cell), layer -1 stats stage, iteration, routed, total, unrouted, rips, failures, elapsed_s, extra:{} Progress counters (≤ 10 Hz) stage name, state:"begin"|"end", detail Pipeline stage changes log level, text Human-readable log line

Object shapes: - pad: {id, net, layers:[copper index…], shape:"circle"|"segment"|"polygon", pts:[[x,y],…], r} (same rounded-core model as the DRC: circle = 1 point + r; oval = 2-point segment + r; polygon may have r > 0) - track: {id, a:[x,y], b:[x,y], w, layer, net} - via: {id, p:[x,y], d, drill, net, top, bottom}

Ids are stable for the lifetime of a session (the engine assigns them).

docs.title: Recordings (replay log)
docs.text: tracemaker route --record FILE writes the same messages, one JSON object per line, each with a leading "t" (seconds since the start of the run; portfolio runs keep only the winning variant's events). The first line is the board snapshot of the unrouted board. Transient messages (frontier, path_try) are not recorded; heatmap messages are. If FILE ends in .zst the lines are stored as a sequence of independent zstd frames (decision D45): the snapshot is a frame of its own, later frames close every 1 MiB of text, and frames carry checksums. zstd -dc FILE gives the plain form. tracemaker-view <board> --replay FILE reads either form (detected from the zstd magic number) and republishes the messages at their recorded times.

docs.title: The failure verdict (issue #8, D113)
docs.text:
gap_nm and gap_fixed_nm are the bottleneck of the best way from the closest approach towards the target, measured with the router's own obstacle tests (so clearances, rules, pads, holes and edges are the lattice's own): a widest-path search over a probing grid in a corridor of ±2 mm around the straight line, at most 12 mm long, whose node value is the widest track legal there (a binary search on the width) and whose way value is its smallest node; layer changes need a legal via. The verdict follows from the numbers, W being the net class width and M the narrowest legal width:

Verdict When Next step contested gap_fixed_nm >= W: fixed copper alone leaves room for W, gap_nm < W: routed copper of other nets closes the way negotiation, not a placement edit rule M <= gap_fixed_nm < W (a narrower legal track passes), or the board minimum clearance would pass M change the net class width or the clearance rule placement gap_fixed_nm < M and the board minimum clearance does not help move a part unknown no probe (the search never ran at the net's own width, touched its window's edge, or was a zone connection), the gap takes W (so something else stopped the search), or the diagnostic budget (a deterministic number of obstacle tests per run) is used up none: a failed search alone proves neither

Measuring costs obstacle tests, so it is done at a connection's 1st, 2nd, 4th, 8th ... failure and reused in between (the path is always fresh). Nothing is counted as work and nothing changes in the search: a run with a sink attached routes exactly as one without (tested: same copper, same number of expansions).

docs.title: 14 — Placement test plan
docs.text:
Part of the TraceMaker plan. Start at ../PLAN.md. Design: 04-placement.md. Gates: 11-roadmap.md M7 and M8. Written 2026-10-03.

This plan says how component placement (tracemaker-place) is tested: what is checked, on which boards, against which baselines, and what has to be true before placement is called good. It covers the existing modes (full, refine, auto with --route-check) and the M8 additions (routable, eco).

docs.title: 1. What "good placement" has to mean
docs.text:
A placement is good when, in this order:

  1. It is legal. No new courtyard overlaps, parts inside the board outline, pads keep copper, edge and solder-mask clearances, locked and fixed parts untouched, and the board still opens in KiCad unchanged apart from the moved footprints.
  2. It routes at least as well as the human placement. Measured by TraceMaker and Freerouting, judged by KiCad's DRC, with the same budget for both placements.
  3. It respects design intent that the netlist does not state. Decoupling capacitors stay close to their chip, connectors stay at the edge, crystals stay close to their oscillator pins, mechanical parts stay put.
  4. It is short. Wirelength (HPWL) and airwire crossings go down, with a reported distance from the proven lower bound.
  5. It is reproducible and reasonably fast. The same seed gives the same board at any thread count, and placement time is recorded.

Wirelength comes fourth on purpose: the M7 evaluation showed that shorter wirelength from denser packing can make a board route worse (13 fully routed boards against 15 for the human placement), so wirelength alone never decides that a placement is better.

docs.title: 2. Test levels
docs.text: Level What Where Runs L0 unit Geometry, legality, cost, solvers, determinism src/place/test_place.cpp (Catch2, ctest -L place) Every build L1 property Invariants on random and fixture inputs (below) test_place.cpp, tagged [property] Every build L2 board Place real boards, check legality and the KiCad round trip src/place/eval_place.py --truth Every placement change L3 routability Route human vs placed boards with a fixed budget; KiCad DRC bench/place_auto.py, bench/place_bench.py (to build, §7) Every placement change (quick set); weekly (full set) L4 baselines SA-PCB and other placers on the same boards bench/place_baselines.py (to build) Per milestone L5 human review A designer looks at placed boards in KiCad Checklist (§6) Per milestone

docs.title: 2.1 Unit tests (L0) — existing
docs.text: The 11 tests in test_place.cpp: KiCad rotation convention; convex hull; power-net name detection; translated closer() agreement with the exact geometry predicate; min-cost flow on a small graph; the HPWL lower bound is exact on a chain and bounds random placements; the raster fast path is conservative (raster free implies exactly legal); legalisation removes every overlap; the full pipeline is legal, deterministic and its incremental cost is exact; rotation descent is monotone; problem extraction from a KiCad board.

docs.title: 2.2 Property tests (L1) — to add
docs.text:
Each property is checked on 50 seeded random problems and on 5 fixture boards:

# Property P1 Every output placement is legal under the exact checker (not only the raster). P2 Locked parts, fixed parts (connectors at the edge, mounting holes, parts with Edge.Cuts or keepouts) and parts touching existing routed copper keep their position, rotation and side exactly. P3 The reported HPWL equals an independent recomputation from the written board. P4 Lower bound ≤ HPWL of every placement found (human, full, refine). P5 Same seed ⇒ byte-identical output board for 1, 3 and 16 threads. P6 refine never increases the cost it optimises; LNS and parallel tempering never return a worse best state than their start. P7 --route-check and auto never return a placement with more unrouted connections than the input (same work budget). P8 eco moves at most the configured number of parts and only parts within the configured distance of failed connections. P9 Placing an already optimal toy problem (two parts, one net) returns the analytic optimum.

docs.title: 3. Datasets
docs.text:
Set Boards Purpose Notes Q — quick 10 PCBench tier-A/B boards (fixed list below) Every placement change 2–4 minutes on 16 threads D — development The 23 boards of doc 04 §7.3 Tuning Already used: never quote results from it as final H — held-out 40 PCBench boards never used in placement or routing development (seeded sample, §3.1) Milestone results Frozen binary; no tuning afterwards DAC DAC 2020 benchmarks (bench/data/dac2020_prepared, 10 boards with Specctra files, 11 in total) Placement benchmark built for this purpose Locked parts are marked in the files; the authors' metrics are via count, layers and bounding-box area S — from scratch The H boards with every movable part piled at the board centre (generated) full mode as a schematic-to-board flow; the M8 gate's "schematic-to-board set" Human placement still serves as the reference K — KiCad demos Demo boards with movable parts Rule coverage (net classes, custom rules, zones) Not a quality benchmark

Quick set Q: ChirpHardware_chirp, IGN01A_IGN01A, LadybugLiteBlue_HW_LadybugBlueLite, PiPlay_SDHat, Solare-BQ24210_Solare-BQ24210, beast-phat_beast-phat, domotics_out-board, kitspace_hbridge_driver, scimpy_volumebuffer, uC3Moy_uC3Moy.

docs.title: 3.1 Selecting the held-out set H
docs.text:
Sample with a fixed seed (7) from PCBench boards that:

  • appear in no bench/results/*/boards.jsonl, no quality.jsonl and none of the D boards;
  • have at least 10 movable parts and at most 300 parts;
  • have a courtyard on at least 80% of their parts (otherwise legality is undefined);
  • route completely in their human placement with TraceMaker at a 120 s budget (so routability changes are attributable to placement).

Stratify 20/20 by part count (below and above the median). Record the list in bench/place_sets/H.txt and never change it; a new held-out set gets a new name.

docs.title: 4. Metrics
docs.text:
All metrics are computed from the written .kicad_pcb, never from the placer's internal state.

Group Metric Definition Legality New KiCad DRC errors courtyards_overlap, pth_inside_courtyard, npth_inside_courtyard, copper_edge_clearance, clearance, shorting_items, solder_mask_bridge, hole_clearance errors in the placed board that the human board does not have Legality Round trip kicad_truth.py on the placed board equals tracemaker inspect --json except for moved footprints Legality Fixed parts Count of locked or fixed parts whose position, rotation or side changed (must be 0) Routability Unrouted (TraceMaker) Unrouted connections after tracemaker route --work W --threads 8, W fixed per board size, and at 120 s Routability Unrouted (Freerouting) Same with Freerouting 2.5 and 1.9 via bench/compare.py (independent router: guards against a placement tuned to TraceMaker) Routability Clean pass Fully routed and no router-introduced KiCad DRC errors Routability Route quality Track length, vias, bends (bench/quality.py) of the routed placed board vs the routed human board Intent Decoupling distance For each capacitor whose nets are one power and one ground net shared with an IC, the distance to the nearest such IC's power pin; report median and maximum, human vs placed Intent Connector edge Connectors (reference prefix J/P/CN or footprint library "Connector") within 2 mm of the edge, human vs placed (must not drop) Intent Crystal distance Crystal/oscillator to the IC pins it connects to (median, maximum) Intent Orientation Share of two-pin passives at 0°/90°/180°/270°; mixed 45° rotations count as violations Wirelength HPWL Signal HPWL, weighted HPWL (power nets ×0.1) Wirelength Lower-bound gap Weighted HPWL ÷ the min-cost-flow lower bound (any rotation) Wirelength Crossings Airwire (MST) crossings Wirelength Area Bounding box of all parts (the DAC 2020 metric) Process Time, determinism Placement wall time and moves; output hash for 1 and 16 threads

docs.title: 5. Baselines and comparisons
docs.text: Baseline How Why Human placement The fixture as given The real target: a designer accepted it TraceMaker refine, full, auto, routable, eco tracemaker-place --mode ... Mode-against-mode SA-PCB Build The-OpenROAD-Project/SA-PCB (BSD-3, archived 2026) under build/tools/, adapter from .kicad_pcb The M7 gate: HPWL ≤ SA-PCB Random legal placement full with the annealer off and a random start (seeded) Sanity floor: every metric must beat it Ablations full without rotations, without crossings term, without the routability term Each part of the cost must help or be removed

docs.title: 6. Human review checklist (L5)
docs.text:
For 5 boards per milestone (2 from H, 2 from DAC, 1 from S), a designer opens the human and placed boards side by side in KiCad and scores 1–5:

  1. Would you manufacture this placement without changes?
  2. Decoupling capacitors next to their pins?
  3. Connectors, switches, LEDs and mounting holes where the enclosure expects them?
  4. Silkscreen readable (references not under parts)?
  5. Thermal parts (regulators, power transistors) spread and near copper?
  6. Analogue/digital and high-current/small-signal separation kept?

Record the scores and comments in dev/placement_review.md. A score below 3 on question 1 for any board is a release blocker for that mode, whatever the numbers say.

docs.title: 7. Tooling to build
docs.text: Tool Purpose bench/place_bench.py One command for L3: place (all modes) → route with TraceMaker (work budget and 120 s) and optionally Freerouting → KiCad DRC → metrics of §4 → bench/results/<run>/place_summary.json and report.md; reuses eval_place.py, quality.py, compare.py bench/place_sets/ Frozen board lists Q, D, H, DAC, S bench/make_scratch_set.py Builds set S: movable parts piled at the board centre, everything else unchanged bench/place_intent.py Design-intent metrics (decoupling, connector edge, crystal, orientation) bench/place_baselines.py SA-PCB build, adapter and runs; random-placement floor Dashboard panel Latest placement run: legality, unrouted vs human, HPWL ratio, intent metrics

docs.title: 8. Gates and pass criteria
docs.text:
Gate Criterion Set G1 legality (every change) 0 new KiCad DRC errors of the legality group; 0 moved fixed parts; round trip exact; P1–P9 pass Q (and H at milestones) G2 routability (every change) Unrouted (TraceMaker, fixed work) summed over Q not above the human placement; no board worse by more than 1 connection in auto Q G3 M7 gate HPWL ≤ SA-PCB on ≥ 80% of H boards; G1 on H H G4 M8 gate Clean pass ≥ 90% of S boards with routable/full (TraceMaker, 120 s); eco closes at least half of the H boards that none mode leaves unrouted S, H G5 independence On H, the placed boards' unrouted count with Freerouting 2.5 is not above the human boards' H G6 intent Median decoupling distance and connector-at-edge count not worse than human on H H G7 human review No board scored below 3 on question 1 L5 boards

A change that fails G1 or G2 is not merged. G3–G7 are reported with every milestone result, pass or fail.

docs.title: 9. Procedure
docs.text:
1. ctest --preset release -L place (L0, L1).
  2. bench/place_bench.py --set Q --modes refine auto --work 3000000 (L2, L3) on every placement change.
  3. At a milestone: freeze the binary, run --set H, --set DAC, --set S with all modes, Freerouting comparison on H, baselines (L4), then the human review (L5).
  4. Publish: report/ section and the dashboard panel; record decisions in doc 12.
