docs.text: The issue asks for a check against datasheet footprints with a trusted list of brands. What can be done reliably and offline is to compare with a record someone made from the datasheet and to say whose word that record rests on; an untrusted or missing reference is reported as such, never as "fine" (doc 05 §43)

docs.title: D116 — Viewer binds loopback by default, token elsewhere
Decision
docs.text: The live viewer binds 127.0.0.1 by default; on any other address it requires a random token (page and /ws; URL once, then an HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict cookie), unless --view-insecure. Every /ws upgrade with an Origin must come from the server's own origin; a loopback viewer without a token also checks Host; at most 16 WebSocket viewers and 128 connections; TM_VIEW_HOST sets the host once (issue #4)

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Keeping 0.0.0.0 as the default and documenting it (docs/09 already promised loopback, and the stream carries the whole board); TLS (certificates are a deployment problem, an SSH tunnel with the loopback bind covers the untrusted-network case); a login or accounts; a token only for remote clients with no Origin check (a web page open in the browser reaches a loopback viewer too)

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The issue is right that the code did not do what docs/09 said. The default is what changes behaviour: anyone who watched a route from another machine now adds --view-host 0.0.0.0 (or TM_VIEW_HOST) and opens the printed URL. A token in the URL is weak against someone who can read the network, and the notice says so (docs/09 Security)

docs.title: D117 — JLCPCB routing rules as opt-in options
Decision
docs.text: JLCPCB's three routing rules (issue #24) are options, off by default: critical nets (named, or from the component rules' roles and differential pairs, in three tiers) routed first; a via multiplier for them with a per-net via report and a report threshold; and a cost for their tracks over voids of the adjacent reference plane (a lattice map rasterised from the zone fills; --split-hard closes those cells), reported after the route by the audit of D114. --si-rules turns the three on with x3 and +4 pitches per step

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Turning them on by default (no thresholds come with the advice, and the effect on completion has to be measured first: the numbers are in bench/records/issue24); a hard rule only (a cost leaves the way open when there is none); a via cap enforced in the search (the report threshold is what is built); making them part of --component-rules (the roles are read either way and the rules stay a separate switch)

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The issue asks for the three rules with a cost the benchmark sets must justify and defaults that stay off until they do. A cost finds the clean path where there is one and says so where there is not; a hard rule, which the issue allows, is behind a flag. The first attempt let a critical net hop onto the plane layer to cross a slot, and a smoothing pass undid the detour: both are in the tests (doc 05 §44)

docs.title: D118 — Milestones M17 to M21 follow the owner's answers
Decision
docs.text: The next milestones (M17–M21, docs/11, doc 18) follow the owner's answers of 2026-10-15: hobbyists first with high speed limited to the Kookabus boards; KiCad 11 is supported; pin swap is a proposal file only and never written into a board; the agent interface is built with a pre-agreed stop rule (it must route more than the plain run at the same compute on a held-out half, otherwise it stays a library). Order: install and measure, session server and agent interface, KiCad 11, hobbyist wins, Kookabus high speed

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Signal-integrity features first (the issues #4–#24 line of work); a pin-swap pass that edits nets; building the agent interface without a stop rule; waiting for KiCad 11 before preparing

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The audience decides what is valuable: a release nobody can install, or a layer count that costs money, matters more to a hobbyist than a tuning profile. KiCad 11 is expected about February 2027 and removes the bundled Python the plugin uses; a swap that edits a design needs back-annotation and the owner's review; the passive hint channel measured no gain (D109–D112, doc 17 §8), so the active interface must earn its keep before more is built on it

docs.title: D119 — Agent board session over MCP and JSON lines
Decision
docs.text: An agent drives the engine through a board session (tracemaker session, doc 19): tools over MCP on standard input and output and over JSON lines; copper comes only from the router behind the exact check; each route is a transaction kept only if it adds no DRC error (judged with the zones refilled when the route used soft zones); states can be undone and restored; the log of calls replays by result and state digests; hints are an advice object read by the advice code; save writes only to --out; the work limit is soft and counted from what was spent. The engine has no model, key or network. A scripted baseline agent and bench/agent_eval.py are the first test of D118's stop rule: not met (the tabu agent routes what the plain run routes on all 16 boards; on 16 fresh boards the plain run routes 960, the control 968, the persist agent 967 and a model-driven arm of four agents 968, doc 19 §9.3): an agent matches what four more seeds give and does not exceed it, so nothing more is built for agents until the router can tell one more (which end is fenced, which lanes are free)

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: An HTTP server or a model client in the engine; tools that place copper by coordinates; a hard work cap that changes what work means (a first call must equal the command line, which it does: same routed, tracks, vias and work on srj20 sample054); redaction in the session

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The advisor channel (D109–D112) measured no gain from passive hints; the open question is an active agent with engine feedback (PCBWorld, doc 18), which needs a way to try one without trusting it. Everything an agent can do is a transaction of the existing router, so rules 1, 2, 4 and 6 hold by construction and are tested; the session is also the core of the KiCad assistant (D1 of doc 18)

docs.title: D120 — Per-shape zero edge clearance as in KiCad 10.0.6
Decision
docs.text: The engine's DRC takes a required copper-to-edge clearance of zero as KiCad 10.0.6 does, per shape: a straight track, a via and a circle, oval or round-rect pad violate only once they cross the outline's centre line (touching is allowed, no epsilon: 1 nm of crossing is flagged); a rect or trapezoid pad and an arc track violate already when they touch it; above zero a gap below the clearance minus 0.5 µm violates (measured on a straight track only). Frozen as 71 KiCad results in tests/integration/edge_touch (issue #42)

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: One rule for all shapes (touching flagged: the old behaviour, 3 false errors on four srj20 boards; crossing only: would miss a flush rect pad that KiCad flags); the epsilon at zero clearance (KiCad has none there: 1 nm of crossing is flagged); a tolerance of a few nm; treating zone fills and copper graphics by measurement now (not measured, they keep the touching rule)

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: Issue #42: the router puts tracks on lattice points, so a track edge on the centre line of an outline is common, and a session that verifies with the engine's DRC refused a legal route. KiCad's answer depends on the shape class it tests with (segment and circle strictly, polygon and arc inclusively), so the test is a table of measured counts, not a formula; rule_parity's style (frozen oracle, --rejudge to refresh) keeps it from drifting

docs.title: D121 — Release as Linux tarball and KiCad plugin package
Decision
docs.text: A release is two files built and tested by CI: a Linux x86_64 tarball (the three binaries, the built viewer, an example board, the agent skills) and the KiCad plugin package with the router, the placer and the viewer inside. They come from the dist preset (CPU only, libstdc++, libgcc, SQLite and zstd linked statically; RelWithDebInfo stripped at install so the code is the tested code), need glibc 2.38 and nothing else, and the binaries find the viewer at ../share/tracemaker/viewer or TM_VIEW_DIR. The Release files workflow builds them in the CI container, installs them in a clean Ubuntu 24.04 container with no compiler or Python, routes the example, and on a v* tag attaches them to the release as a draft

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Building on an older glibc to run on Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 12 (needs GCC 15 on an old distribution; recorded as the way to widen the floor); a .deb/AppImage/Flatpak/Docker image; a Python module in the plugin package (it must match KiCad's Python and the plugin falls back to the binary); macOS arm64 (the presets exist, nothing was built or run); a CUDA build (GPU memory is shared and the CPU path is the reference); publishing without a draft

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: Release 0.9.0 has only a video, and GCC 15 is a high bar for hobbyists. A static CPU binary and a zip are the least that gets a person to a routed board in five minutes; checked on Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13 and current Fedora in 5 s, and the unpacked plugin in a live KiCad 10.0.6 (bench/records/m17). The workflow's package and install jobs passed on GitHub in the pull request (PR #44); its tag-triggered publish step (draft release) has not run yet

docs.title: D122 — PCBWorld D3 run as PCBench boards with Freerouting rerun
Decision
docs.text: PCBWorld-Bench's real boards (D3) are PCBench boards, so A1 became: run the 119 published test boards (99 D3-A, 10 D3-B, 10 D3-C) and re-run Freerouting 2.1.0 with the paper's settings under this repository's judge as the only like-for-like baseline; the paper's other rows are quoted, not compared. TraceMaker: 97/99, 10/10, 9/10 clean. --txn 1 helps on non-breakout boards (+118 connections on 33 failing tier B-D boards, eight variants, equal work), --relax is a rescue (two boards completed, 509 connections fewer in all); neither changes a default yet. --relax, --rounds, --round-work and --ramp-from now run a portfolio of one with --variants 1

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Reproducing the paper's board conversion (needs a KiCad 9 pcbnew built from their engine); a "better than" claim against KiCadRoutingTools, OrthoRoute, the agents and the RL policies (different judge and rule files, no per-board results); making --txn 1 the default now (it changes the default portfolio and needs tiers A to D at equal wall time first)

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: Doc 18 assumed D3 was an independent set; reading the paper showed it is a PCBench subset with relaxed rules. The paper's Freerouting 2.1.0 scores 0.75 (one run) here at 0.670, so the judges differ and only same-judge numbers mean anything; the experiment that found --relax ignored with one variant is the reason for the second change

docs.title: D123 — One project brand, the trace logo
Decision
docs.text: The project has one brand (branding/): the trace logo (a red-layer trace, a via and a blue-layer trace between two pads, picked by the owner from 25 options) in a light and a dark form with outlined text, a square icon, PNGs, an .ico and a social preview. It is used in the README (<picture>, dark mode aware), the live viewer (favicon and header), the development site, and the KiCad package (resources/icon.png and the action's toolbar icons)

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Keeping the generated 64x64 board icon of the PCM script; text left as live fonts (the SVG changes with the reader's fonts); a logo with a drawn pen, chip or board (the owner chose the plain trace)

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The viewer already says red is front copper and blue is back copper, so the logo reads as the product; hollow pads and via keep it usable on any background; the PCM script reads the PNG from branding/ and no longer draws its own

docs.title: D124 — Rule relaxation spent on signals, not power nets
Decision
docs.text: A rule relaxation (the rule-escalation ladder of the real-world study) is spent on signals, not on power nets: power and ground nets stay at the board's own clearance and via sizes (class copies) and the router's new option --no-neck-nets stops its neck-down for them (doc 05 §45). A relaxed routing counts as routed only after a safety simulation (reports/realworld/py/safety.py: ngspice crosstalk on the extracted copper of every compromised signal pair, IPC-2221 and DC drop for narrowed nets, via impedance, with stated assumptions) does not FAIL.

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: Owner's rule (2026-10-17): power nets have less margin to play with than signals, and pushing a rule needs proof that it is safe.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Power nets that only route by necking down now stay unrouted (the board is then reported as open, not hidden); the verdict rests on assumed drivers, loads and currents.

docs.title: D125 — Legalisation may subdivide long tracks
Decision
docs.text: Legalisation can cut long tracks into pieces so that they bend where a neighbour is too close (--legalize-subdivide MM, LegalizeOptions::subdivide_mm; off by default, no change without it): the vertices a route has cannot resolve a pinch at the middle of a straight track between fixed ends

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Moving only existing vertices (D104); a new gridless polish engine (doc 16 F6); a local LP window

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: Cutting reuses the Gauss-Seidel projection and keeps the exact check as the safety net; merged back to one segment where the track stayed straight (doc 05 §46); measured: A 10 mm track between fixed pads with a 0.06 mm pinch resolves with a 1 mm cut and not without; real boards: not yet shown to close an open connection (doc 05 §46)

docs.title: D126 — Four opt-in escape features from the EtherCAT review
Decision
docs.text: Four opt-in escape features from the EtherCAT shield review: --escape-length, --escape-persist, --radial-supply, --via-drops (doc 05 §47)

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: One bundle router with planar order and layer assignment (not built); a finer lattice and part moves (the review measured them to do nothing)

docs.title: Reason and results
docs.text: Each is a small change on the existing escape plan, planner or endpoint code and cannot add a violation (every commit is still checked exactly); measured: EtherCAT 177 -> 185 of 207 routed, other boards neutral to slightly negative, so all stay off by default

docs.title: D127 — Soft mask and copper graphics, fine-lattice finish
Decision
docs.text: --soft-mask-graphics (net-less mask openings drawn as footprint graphics stop keeping tracks and vias out) and --soft-copper-graphics (net-less copper drawn as board polygons stops enclosing pins) and, in the real-world closure loop, a fine-lattice finish (each open net alone on the best copper at 10-20 um with its own and its neighbours' rules at the loosest tier)

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Treating the openings as pad apertures; a finer default lattice (memory and time on large boards)

docs.title: Reason and results
docs.text: The first took test-jig's 9 blocked jumper pins out of 'enclosed'; the second closed memsarray's last connection; both only act when nets stay open, the first is opt-in in the router and reported as judgement-class violations (doc 05 §48)

docs.title: D128 — --first-nets-ordered routes first nets in list order
Decision
docs.text: --first-nets-ordered: route the --first-nets in the order of the list (doc 05 §49)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The group was only moved to the front; its inner order ignored the list, which made an order experiment on the EtherCAT shield meaningless

docs.title: Consequences and results
docs.text: Off by default, nothing changes without it; a global ordering by list position would change existing crystal-line uses

docs.title: D129 — --bundle-escape river escapes on dense packages
Decision
docs.text: --bundle-escape: bundle (river) escapes, a block of parallel lanes in pin order from one package side to one side of another part, placed before the search (doc 05 §50)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Review item 1 of the EtherCAT shield: the router cannot build a straight 0.5 mm-pitch comb of 5-19 mm connection by connection, group reroutes in any order ended at 4-15 open, escape corridors and bus lanes do not make the net itself stay straight

docs.title: Consequences and results
docs.text: Off by default, nothing changes without it; every piece passes the exact check; lanes are protected from ripping, which can leave a net that needs the lane's ground unrouted (the closure loop then relaxes it); one layer only

docs.title: D130 — --supply-first routes dense-package supply nets first
Decision
docs.text: --supply-first: nets with 2+ perimeter pins on one dense package and no pour join the --first-nets (doc 05 §51)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The last open connections of the EtherCAT shield were all the core and 3V3 nets: routed late as pin-to-pin edges round the package, they lose to the comb; routed first they cost the others little

docs.title: Consequences and results
docs.text: Off by default; the bundles stay first (after the supply nets they were worse); a supply net that needs the lane's ground stays unrouted and the closure relaxes it

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: --package-tunnels: stub, via and back-layer run between two perimeter pins of one net on a dense package, placed before the lanes (doc 05 §52)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: In every best state of the EtherCAT study the last open connection was the core rail's pin 38, cut off from its trunk under the package; the designer's solution is a tunnel (review item 5)

docs.title: Consequences and results
docs.text: Off by default; every piece passes the exact check and nothing is placed unless the whole tunnel does; costs connections at the loose first-round rules, to be judged in the closure loop

docs.title: D132 — KiCad-measured shapes and net-less arcs in the judge
Decision
docs.text: Whole-tier runs (2026-10-19) found 15 boards with an added error; five shapes KiCad measures were underestimated and are fixed, and the judge no longer counts a net-less arc as routed copper (judge version instance-v3-graphic-arcs): (1) copper text boxes use KiCad's measured stroke-font advances (a table in 1/21 of the height, space 0.76; the old estimate was 10-50 % too narrow), (2) custom-pad primitives gr_poly, gr_rect, gr_line, gr_circle, gr_arc are all read and grown by half their pen width, (3) Margin-layer graphics keep their stroke as the edge clearance obstacle, (4) a pad with a negative local solder_mask_margin widens the solder_mask_bridge reach (0.2 + 0.2 |margin| mm), (5) judge: Arc [<no net>] is a copper graphic, not routed copper

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Treating the 15 as noise; calibrating by trial and error on the routed boards; changing KiCad's rules

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The domotics, DPS-1200FB, OricMouse, VC4000, type5 text cases, flatpack2 (custom pad, 0.1155 vs 0.127 mm), kitspace_firefly, RaspberryPi-PoE, rfidBoard_POE, phone_amp, Hornbill (Margin lines up to 2 mm wide) and free-of-charge_BMS (mask bridge) re-ran with no added error; MySensors and PowerGlove and livolo were judge artefacts (KiCad names a different piece of the same footprint graphic from run to run). The numbers come from kicad-cli pcb export svg plots and DRC runs of small test boards (tests/test_kicad_measured_shapes.cpp). quick is byte-identical before and after. The negative-margin rule is an envelope of two measurements, not KiCad's formula

docs.title: D133 — Viewer framing for named pages (--view-embed)
Decision
docs.text: A viewer can be framed by named pages: route --view-embed "<origins>" replaces X-Frame-Options: DENY with Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors <origins> on the viewer's pages; the default (no option) is unchanged, the token still guards every request, and the value is checked (letters, digits and .:/*-_[] and spaces only) because it goes into a header. The stack-test page (devsite/stack.py, :8771) embeds each running board's viewer this way; bench/viewport.py gives every board its own port (8800-8899) and one shared token (bench/results/.view-token), bench/run.py --view and bench/escalate.py use it

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: A reverse proxy in the devsite (needs a WebSocket relay and an Origin rewrite); dropping the header for everyone; binding the viewers to loopback and tunnelling (the token would stay private, but the page could not reach them)

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: Routing with the viewer is byte-identical to without (one board, 4-variant portfolio, checked); only the first portfolio variant streams. Anyone who can open the stack page can read the token and open the viewers: the same trust as the page itself. Also added to the stack page: a burndown chart (boards not yet clean over the campaign, from the modification times of the result files; bench/ledger.py burndown())

docs.title: D134 — Documentation site: MkDocs, Diátaxis, decision records, Doxygen
Context
docs.text: By release 0.10.0 the project had 19 numbered design docs, 131 decisions in one table in docs/12-decisions.md (about 100 KB, D115 onwards appended under the risk register), milestone records in bench/records/ and reports, but no published site, nothing written for a user who wants to install and route a board, no reference that is guaranteed to match the code, no C++ API reference, and nothing that said which docs describe the code as it is and which are plans. A single decision could not be linked to, and a replaced decision could not be marked as such.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A documentation site built by MkDocs with the Material theme from docs/ (mkdocs.yml), published to GitHub Pages from the gh-pages branch by .github/workflows/docs.yml, versioned with mike: dev from main, X.Y and the latest alias from a tag vX.Y.Z. Pull requests build it with --strict.
  2. Organised by Diátaxis (Procida, Diátaxis, diataxis.fr): tutorials, how-to guides, reference, explanation, plus a project section. The numbered design docs keep their file names and place in docs/, and the navigation sorts them; links to files outside docs/ are pointed at GitHub by scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py.
  3. One Architecture Decision Record per decision (Nygard, "Documenting architecture decisions", 2011) in docs/decisions/DNNN.md with a status (accepted, superseded with superseded_by, proposed, rejected); docs/12-decisions.md keeps the risk register and an index generated by scripts/decisions.py. D1–D131 were converted from the table with their text unchanged and short titles added; D19, D31, D36 and D53 are marked superseded by D121, D52, D58 and D56. D87 is reserved for open PR #21.
  4. A header on every page: status (current, partly-built, plan, historical), code (the paths the page describes) and an optional reviewed date. scripts/docs_check.py fails on a bad header and warns when the code has had more than 25 commits since the page changed or was reviewed. Non-current pages get a banner on the site.
  5. Generated reference pages, committed and checked by CI: the command line from each program's --help (scripts/gen_reference.py cli) and the benchmark results from bench/records/*/summary.json (scripts/gen_reference.py bench).
  6. A C++ API reference by Doxygen (docs/api/Doxyfile), published under api/ of each site version. The headers keep their plain // comments: scripts/doxygen_filter.py reads the block above a declaration (and a trailing member comment) as its documentation. scripts/check_api_docs.py counts undocumented declarations per header against a committed baseline (1385 in 75 headers at the start) and warns in CI when a header's count rises.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Sphinx with Breathe/Exhale: the strongest C++ API integration, but reStructuredText or MyST for prose, a heavier build, and most of these docs are prose.
  • Moving the design docs into docs/explanation/: a tidier tree, but it breaks every "doc 05 §34" and docs/05-routing.md reference in code comments, commits, issues, reports and PDFs.
  • Rewriting every header to /// comments: the style the Doxygen manual expects, but it touches all 82 headers, conflicts with branches in flight, and changes the house comment style for no gain in content.
  • Failing CI on undocumented declarations: 1385 exist today; a ratchet that warns on new ones moves the count the right way without blocking work.
  • A hand-entered "verified in version" field: it would claim reviews nobody made; reviewed is set only by someone who checked, and staleness otherwise comes from git.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Nothing in the engine changes; no routing or placement output can change, so the quick tier was not run.
  • A branch that appends a row to the old decision table must convert it with scripts/decisions.py import before merging (CI's decisions.py check says so).
  • GitHub shows each page's YAML header as a small table at the top of the file.
  • GitHub Pages has to be pointed at the gh-pages branch once, by the owner.
  • The site needs Python packages pinned in docs/requirements.txt; the engine build does not.

docs.title: D135 — macOS 15: floating-point parsing without std::from_chars
docs.text: Contributed by Chris Hemingway (@cHemingway) in pull request #46.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The macOS build supports macOS 15 as well as 26. Floating-point text is read through tmk::parse_double (core/parse_double.hpp): std::from_chars everywhere except Apple platforms, where it is strtod_l in the "C" locale held to from_chars' grammar (no leading space, + or hex; overflow and underflow to zero rejected, subnormals kept). Test scripts run under macOS's bash 3.2 (no mapfile; empty arrays expanded as ${a[@]+"${a[@]}"} under set -u)

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Requiring macOS 26 (Apple's libc++ has floating-point from_chars only from there, and the Metal port was built on 26.4); a deployment target of 26 (the binary would not run on 15); strtod without a locale (reads 0,5 under a comma locale); Boost.Charconv (a new compiled dependency for four call sites); requiring Homebrew's bash for the tests

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: Macs on 15 could not build the engine at all. strtod_l is correctly rounded on both libcs, so the two paths give the same double: a unit test checks that bit for bit on Linux, and 2,000,000 strings through the macOS path against libstdc++'s from_chars gave 0 mismatches after subnormals were allowed (the first version rejected them, as strtod sets ERANGE for them). On macOS 15 the quick tier is byte-identical CPU against Metal (30/30) and matches the last Linux run board for board (25/30 clean, 99.0 %); DRC parity with native kicad-cli 10.0.6 holds (doc 07 §8.2, bench/records/macos15/)

docs.title: D136 — Run report rendered from the route summary alone
Context
docs.text: Candidate D3 of doc 18 (milestone M20): one file a designer can read to audit a run, covering what was routed, what is open and why, which rules were read and which were not, the signal-integrity audit, the DRC comparison, the options and the seed. Its gate asks that every number in it be traceable to a JSON field. The pieces existed as separate outputs (--json, --stuck-report, warnings in the log, tracemaker drc).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• route --report FILE writes the report: HTML, or Markdown when FILE ends in .md. tracemaker report SUMMARY.json -o FILE renders it again from a saved summary. Off by default.
  • The report is a pure function of the summary. report::render (src/report/render.cpp) reads only the JSON and does no arithmetic; every number and name it prints is a field, and the HTML marks each with its JSON pointer (data-src, a hover title and a "show the JSON field" switch). The Markdown gives pointers as footnotes, as a column of key/value tables, and as the row source of other tables. With --report and no --json, the summary is written beside the report as FILE.json.
  • --report adds sections to the summary: rules (files found, minimums, net classes with net counts, custom rules, and not_read: the project reader's, rule engine's and board reader's warnings), stuck (the stuck report of doc 17 §3 for the final result, without its advisor parts), and drc (TraceMaker's DRC of the board the router started from and of the board as written, zones refilled when the board has copper zones, counts by type, routing errors added, and the unconnected items after the route with both ends).
  • Every summary gains open, completion_pct, time_limited and run (version, board, paths, date, seed, work budget, time limit, variants, threads, and the options as given on the command line and in --config).
  • RouteResult::time_limited: set when the wall-clock limit, not the work budget, ended a search (or, in a portfolio, any variant's or the rounds'). The router never reads it. The route logs a warning and the report says the result depends on machine speed.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• A report built from the router's in-memory state: faster to write, but nothing would make its numbers checkable afterwards, and the gate would rest on review alone.
  • Calling kicad-cli for the DRC comparison: it is the judge of the benchmarks, but not installed where hobbyists run the plugin, and slow. The engine's DRC gives KiCad's names and, for routing rules, KiCad's results (doc 03 §6); the report says to sign off with kicad-cli.
  • Instance matching of violations as bench/drc_judge.py does: more exact, but its normalisation is tuned to kicad-cli's text. Counts by type are stated as such.
  • PDF output: a dependency for little gain; the HTML prints.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Reports for seven of the eight plane boards (bench/records/m20-run-report): no routing error added on any. The unconnected count after the refill equals the report's own DRC count on every board, two independent paths agreeing. A unit test parses the HTML and checks every value against its pointer, and that the renderer's own text carries no number.
  • The first runs showed why time_limited matters: under load, the default 120 s limit, not the work, ended runs, and results moved between runs (RoyalBlue54L-Feather 102 and 37 connections). A designer now sees it.
  • Options off: quick tier byte-identical to main (30/30).
  • Open: interf_u spends more than 20 minutes on one core after its portfolio with main's binary too (27 s in the 14 October records), so it has no report; the gate's review by someone who did not write the report; the KiCad plugin and the Python module do not pass --report yet.

docs.title: D137 — Starved thermal reliefs and GPU back-off from the October test campaign
Context
docs.text:
Two findings of the overnight soak (2026-10-25) and the full test campaign after it (2026-10-26), both in bench/records/test-campaign-2026-10/:

  1. With --soft-zones, interf_u gained six KiCad starved_thermal errors on every run: new B.Cu tracks cut a GND pad's spokes off the pour, or left them in an island only that pad reaches. The soft-zone refill (doc 05 §36) counts unconnected items, which do not change, so the router reported nothing and kept the copper.
  2. With both shared GPUs full of other jobs, every cost-to-go field asked the CUDA driver for free memory before falling back to the CPU, and the threads queued on the driver's lock for seconds per field: interf_u took 2,900 s against 20 s with --no-gpu, ErgoDone 1,708 s against 6 s, all boards byte-identical.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• drc::starved_thermals follows DRC_TEST_PROVIDER_ZONE_CONNECTIONS::testZoneLayer of KiCad 10.0 on a board with current fills: spokes counted as crossings of the fill with the pad grown by half its thermal gap; spokes into a fill polygon with a single connection (CN_ZONE_LAYER::HasSingleConnection) count only when the pad has no other; tracks touching the pad that run from inside that outline into the fill count as spokes (on any layer, as KiCad); the minimum is the board setup's min_resolved_spokes (read from the project, default 2), and a severity of ignore turns the check off. tracemaker drc prints the pads it finds; the JSON report does not carry them (its types are the parity-checked ones).
  • Soft zones check the reliefs after the refill repair, name the starved pads in the log and put starved_thermals in the summary's refill object. Pads already starved in the input do not count. A thermal repair then runs one transaction per starved pad: the nets whose new copper crosses the pad's spoke lanes (each spoke grown by the zone's minimum width and the clearance, cut back from other nets' pads) lose their new copper and are routed again alone, with every starved pad's lanes as keep-outs; the result is kept only if fewer reliefs are starved and nothing more is unconnected after a refill (rule 4). --no-refill-repair turns it off with the unconnected repair.
  • The after-route passes (power widening, stitching vias) are judged on starved reliefs too when fills are soft.
  • GPU back-off (gpu/backoff.hpp): a CUDA device that refused (has_free_memory false) is not asked again for 30 s, the delay doubling while it keeps refusing (to 15 min) and resetting when it accepts. Fields computed meanwhile on the CPU are the same fields, so outputs do not change.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Rip every net that crosses any starved pad's spokes at once (tried first): cured all seven reliefs on interf_u but lost seven connections, so the transaction discarded it. Per pad, two of six were repaired with no connection lost.
  • Protect only the two spokes the fewest new nets cross: those were already free; the starvation came from islands further out, so nothing was ripped and nothing improved.
  • Keep spoke lanes out of the first pass for every thermal pad on a soft zone (prevention instead of repair): would change every soft-zone board and block the channels between pins of a plane net on the plane layer; not tried.
  • Stop asking the GPU for the rest of the run after one refusal: simpler, but a run that starts while another job holds the GPU would never use it once freed. The doubling back-off costs a few probes per hour.
  • Make --no-gpu the default (the campaign found the GPU path slower on short runs even when the GPUs are free): a separate decision, left open.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• interf_u at 3 M work, --soft-zones --si-rules: KiCad's starved_thermal 6 → 4, 140/164 routed and 26 unconnected either way, route time 15 → 76 s (six router runs for the repair). The other seven plane boards and the quick tier are byte-identical.
  • The engine's check finds KiCad's pads on every plane board run (and none where KiCad finds none) with one extra pad on interf_u (U9.C4: three islands, which KiCad does not count as single-connection there); erring that way only costs a repair attempt.
  • Not repaired: spokes into islands bounded by copper that does not cross the spokes themselves (three of the four left on interf_u). Not modelled: custom-pad spoke primitives and min_resolved_spokes constraints in custom rules.
  • Docs: doc 05 §36.1, doc 07 §4; records in bench/records/test-campaign-2026-10/.

docs.title: D138 — Generated pours and the layer-count advisor
Context
docs.text: M20's C3 item (doc 18 §4): "Create a ground (or power) pour on a free inner or back layer when a board has none; try 2, 4 and 6 layers and report the least that completes". Gate: on PCBench boards with no zones, the count completed with a generated pour against without, DRC clean; the advisor's answer matches a brute-force run. Doc 05 §18 had called pour creation "a possible feature (not built); it would close a few boards, not most". PCBench boards have no zones and no stackup; most are KiCad 5 files with two copper layers. The records are in bench/records/m20-c3/.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• route --pour auto|NET@LAYER (repeatable; passes::plan_pours). auto applies only to a board without copper zones: the ground net by name (GND, GNDD, VSS, ...; the one with the most pads) on In1.Cu when the board has inner layers, else on B.Cu. The zone covers the outline's box plus 0.5 mm (the refill clips it to the board), clearance the net class clearance but at least 0.3 mm, minimum width 0.25 mm, islands removed, and solid pad connections.
  • A pour turns on soft zones (doc 05 §36): it is filled before routing, other nets route through it, and the refill, refill repair and thermal check after routing decide what it connects. The output holds the zone with the engine's final fill (BoardEditor::add_zone, set_zone_fills); the summary lists it under pours.
  • route --copper-layers N and tracemaker layers BOARD --count N -o OUT (BoardEditor::set_copper_layer_count): inner layers are added after the last inner entry in the file's own numbering (KiCad 9's even ordinals or the older 1..30), or removed from the top inner layer down when nothing names them (tracks, arcs, blind or micro vias, zones, graphics, texts, pads); otherwise the edit is refused and the document is untouched. A stackup block is removed, so KiCad builds its default one for the new count.
  • route --try-layers 2,4,6 (app::run_layer_advisor): the counts are routed fewest first, a count the board cannot take is recorded as not tried, and the advisor stops at the first count the engine judges complete (exit 0: every connection routed and, with zones, nothing unconnected after the refill). It writes that board, or else the count with the fewest open connections (ties to fewer layers); the summary's layers lists every count tried.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Thermal reliefs, KiCad's default for a new zone. The first run (c3-bd-pour) used them: 22 of the 33 boards gained KiCad starved_thermal errors (up to 18 on one board), because routed tracks of other nets cut spokes off the pour. The thermal repair of D137 rerouted pad by pad with the first pass's full budget each, which took Aleste from 28 s to 3,708 s and still left 12. A solid connection only needs the fill to touch the pad. The cost is hand soldering of through-hole ground pins; the designer can switch the zone to reliefs in KiCad and see what starves.
  • A pour on F.Cu or on every free layer. On a two-layer board the back layer carries fewer pads, so it is cut less. More than one generated pour is possible with NET@LAYER entries.
  • The advisor judged by KiCad. It would need kicad-cli in the route; the engine's own count after a refill is the same judge the route summary uses, and the check against KiCad is the brute force of the gate.
  • The advisor trying every count and keeping the best. The question is the cheapest board that completes, so it stops at the first count that does.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Measured in bench/records/m20-c3 (doc 05 §53):

  • The advisor's answer equals the brute force's on 28 of 28 board-and-option pairs (14 two-layer boards, with and without a pour): MicroMaple at 4 layers without a pour (the written board is byte-identical to the brute force's), serial_gw at 4 and MicroMaple at 6 with one; the other boards complete at none of 2, 4, 6.
  • A pour closes no board of the 33 non-clean tier B to D boards; open connections after KiCad's refill 1,368 → 1,290 (18 boards better, 10 worse). On 4 and 6 layers it is 1 against 1 and 2 against 1 boards on the 14.
  • The pour run is about three times slower (1,267 s → 3,905 s for the 33 boards): the first pass checks the soft fills and the refill repair routes against them as fixed copper.
  • Open: two solder_mask_bridge on the Teensy test layout (tracks across a net-less B.Mask opening that the pour now fills; §48's openings are not kept out of the pour); D137's thermal repair still gives each starved pad the first pass's whole budget, which is slow on boards with many starved reliefs in designer zones.
  • Options off, the quick tier is byte-identical (30/30). Docs: 05 §53 (and §18), 18 §10, 11.

docs.title: D139 — Custom rules keep the per-class cache unless it would judge them differently
Context
docs.text:
Doc 05 §27 said: "Disallow masks retain the per-class cache. Physical-hole rules do too when independent of NetName, NetClass and inDiffPair. Other custom rules, including unparseable conditions, require exact checks." Exact mode (use_cache = false) also turns off the cost-to-go fields, which need the cache, so the GPU sits idle.

WholeBoard writes JLCPCB's manufacturing limits into every board's .kicad_dru: track_width, hole_size, via_diameter, annular_width, hole_to_hole, hole_clearance, edge_clearance, silk_clearance, text_height and text_thickness, one hole_to_hole rule with A.Net != B.Net (not readable: Net is unknown), and until now a clearance rule on A.Type != 'Zone' && B.Type != 'Zone'. Any one of them put the router in exact mode. On a 240 x 140 mm four-layer PoE switch (1,194 connections) every variant logged fields 0 GPU + 0 CPU over a 7,200 s run.

The router reads the rule engine per point only for clearance (RuleEngine::clearance, in both the cached and the exact path), disallow and physical_hole_clearance. Hole and edge clearances come from the board minimums in both paths; sizes, silk, text, length and skew are not per-point checks. A rule that is not applied (unreadable condition) is skipped in both paths. So for every rule above, exact mode judged each point as the cache does, only slower.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• needs_exact_ is set only by a valid clearance rule whose condition references NetName or inDiffPair (the cache's stand-in net would be judged for every net of its class), and by a valid physical_hole_clearance rule that references NetName, NetClass or inDiffPair (unchanged). NetClass in a clearance condition keeps the cache: the cache is per class.
  • Cached via codes probe a via (ItemKind::Via) in fixed_code(via_probe = true) and fixed_via_code, as via_state does, so a clearance rule on Type, Width or Position_X/Y gives the same answer cached and exact. Without custom rules the probe kind does not change clearance().
  • Unreadable rules are still warned by name and not applied (rule 6); they no longer change how the rest is checked.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Read A.Net. It makes WholeBoard's hole-to-hole rule valid for the DRC, but leaves every other rule forcing exact mode. Separate change.
  • Fold plain minimums into the cache's values. Not needed: the router does not read them per point at all.
  • Keep exact mode for Type conditions. Would keep WholeBoard boards exact; the via probe makes the cache agree.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Measured on the PoE switch (placed board, 300 s, eight variants, bench/records/d139/): with WholeBoard's rules file and the old engine the variants routed 116, 116, 221, 116, 116, 1079, 116, 92 (no fields). With this change and the file without its clearance rule: 882, 1004, 1057, 994, 899, 1099, 1006, 570 (7,695 GPU fields). With the clearance rule kept, six variants still stall near 116: that rule lowers the clearance of non-zone pairs from the class's 0.15 mm to the 0.127 mm board minimum, and the variants slow down on it (open; WholeBoard no longer writes the rule). Quick tier: 30/30 boards byte-identical, gates pass (PCBench boards have no rules file). Doc 05 §27 changed.

Memory. Boards that were in exact mode now allocate the per-class caches: three board-sized arrays per (net class, track width) in each variant's router, about 120 MB per class on a 240 x 140 mm four-layer board at 0.1 mm. The PoE switch had 83 net classes (WholeBoard wrote one per impedance pair) and the eight variants reached 181 GB of 184 GB within 17 minutes of routing. WholeBoard now merges identical classes; the engine still has no bound on cache memory (open: share caches between classes with the same values, or size them to the routed windows).

docs.title: D140 — Unfilled zones are filled for routing; the router keeps custom hole clearance
Context
docs.text: A 1,194-connection, four-layer WholeBoard board (PoE switch, every part on F.Cu, GND and +54V zones on In1/In2 written without fills, JLCPCB rules) routed 1,184 connections in two hours. The user saw it use too few vias and layers. The routed board showed why: the zones had no fill, so the router routed GND and +54V as tracks (1,773 mm, part of it on the other net's plane layer) instead of dropping vias into the planes, and those wide tracks crowded the fine-pitch escapes where the open connections were. KiCad's DRC of the same board also found 14 hole_clearance errors: the router ignored the custom "Hole to copper" rule (0.254 mm). Doc 05 §54.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Zones without a fill are filled in memory before routing and the run uses soft zones (plane targets, refill after routing). On by default; route --no-fill-planes turns it off. The written zones stay as they were.
  • RuleEngine::router_hole_clearance(): the board minimum raised to every applied custom hole_clearance rule, used by every router check. Rules with a condition or layer are applied everywhere, with a warning.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Ask for --soft-zones. It does not help alone: a zone with no fill has no area, so it is no plane target.
  • Write the fills into the output. KiCad refills on its own; leaving the zones as written keeps rule 8.
  • Per-pair hole clearance in the router. Exact for conditional rules, but every cache and margin in route::Obstacles assumes one value; the floor is exact for unconditional rules, which is the common case (JLCPCB).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Boards without unfilled zones or custom hole-clearance rules route as before (quick tier byte-identical, 30/30).
  • Soft zones bring their costs: the refill and refill repair after routing take time on large boards.
  • The full-board result on the switch board (one hour, same options) was not measured before this was shipped.
  • Open: conditions using A.Net are not evaluated (JLCPCB's "Hole to hole").

docs.title: D141 — Pin swap: the free-assignment oracle gains too little to build the pass
Context
docs.text: M20's C2 item (doc 18 §4): "Pin and gate swap: feasibility experiment first ... measure routed count, vias and layers with and without the freedom. Build the pass only if the gain is large", on at least ten boards; a pass, if built, would only propose swaps (doc 18 §7). Vendors claim fewer crossings and layers, but no independent number was found. PCBench boards do not say which pins are interchangeable. The records are in bench/records/m20-c2/.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The experiment uses an oracle, bench/pin_swap.py: swappable groups by construction (connector signal pins: reference J, P, CN, CON or X, one pad type and size, not a supply, ground or differential-pair net by name, the net's only pad on the connector; resistor arrays RN/RP of 4, 8 or 16 pads, resistors as units either way round), nets assigned to pads by a minimum-cost assignment of the distance to the nearest pad of the net elsewhere (the Hungarian method, Kuhn 1955; a minimum Euclidean bipartite matching has no crossing pairs). The swapped copy permutes the pads' (net ...) nodes and nothing else.
  • Result: no clear gain (the 20 failing tier B-D boards with a group: open connections 982 → 978, 5 boards better and 5 worse, vias −3 %, length −1 %, 0 → 0 clean; the 10 quick boards with a group: 27 → 26 open, 7 → 6 clean). The pin-swap pass is not built, and C2 is closed with this measurement.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Pins from the schematic's library (pin functions, units of multi-unit symbols). The honest eligibility list, and what a pass would need; not needed to bound the gain, which the oracle overestimates.
  • Gate swap of logic parts (74xx units). Needs the symbols' unit structure; the PCBench boards with such parts are few, and a connector group is the larger freedom.
  • Crossing count as the oracle's cost. Distance matching already removes crossings between the group's own connections; the routed result, not a proxy, is what was measured.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The oracle is an upper bound: on these boards the order of connector pins is not what leaves connections open (C5, doc 05 §55, says what does). A swap pass would cost an eligibility list the user must supply and a back-annotation step, for about 3 % of vias.
  • bench/pin_swap.py stays for boards where the eligibility is known (a user's own); the layer count was not measured on the swapped copies.
  • Docs: 05 §56, 18 §11, 11 (M20 row).

docs.title: D142 — KiCad drift job: the newest KiCad image upgrades, re-reads, judges and routes four boards weekly
Context
docs.text: M19 (doc 18 A4): "Scheduled job running DRC parity and round trip against the newest KiCad container and, when one exists, a KiCad 11 release candidate". The project pins KiCad 10.0.6 (scripts/kicad-cli); KiCad 10.0.7 was released on 2026-10-18, and no KiCad 11 tag exists on Docker Hub. kicad/kicad:nightly was the obvious image for the road to KiCad 11, but it is stale: it is 10.0.0-rc1.1-513 built on 2026-02-27. The records are in bench/records/m19-drift/.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• scripts/kicad_drift.py BOARD ... (any kicad-cli, e.g. the image's own or the docker wrapper): the newest kicad-cli upgrades a copy of each board to its own file format (pcb upgrade --force); then tracemaker check-roundtrip must re-write it byte for byte, tracemaker drc and kicad-cli pcb drc must count the same violations of the fifteen routing-relevant types (as scripts/drc_parity.py, capped at KiCad's 199 per type), and a routed copy (route --work 2000000, with the project files beside it) must give kicad-cli no error type the input did not have. Exit 0 only if every check passed.
  • .github/workflows/kicad-drift.yml: weekly (Monday 04:17 UTC) and by hand. A resolve job reads the kicad/kicad tags and picks the newest release X.Y.Z and, when it is newer, the newest release candidate X.Y.Z-rcN; the dist binary is built in the CI container and checked inside each image on plane_smd and three KiCad demos (ecc83, pic_programmer, complex_hierarchy, from KiCad's 10.0 branch). It does not gate pull requests.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• kicad/kicad:nightly. Stale (above); a fixed tag would have reported 10.0.0-rc1 as "the newest" for months.
  • The DRC parity corpus and the fixture sets in CI. The full corpus is 2.4 GB of downloads and hours of kicad-cli; four boards in two formats (KiCad 5 demos upgraded, a KiCad 9 board) catch a format or rule change, and the parity tools run on the full sets by hand.
  • Gating pull requests. A new KiCad release must not block unrelated work; the weekly run is a warning to act on.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Run locally: 4/4 boards pass every check with KiCad 10.0.6 (host wrapper and inside the image, the way CI runs it), 10.0.7 and the stale nightly. The KiCad 11 part of M19 (reader and writer for the 11 formats, the plugin on the IPC API) waits for a KiCad 11 release candidate; the job will start checking one the week its tag appears.
  • Found on the way: route -o OUT wrote only the board, so KiCad opened OUT with its default rules (net classes and custom rules live in the project files): plane_smd's routed copy showed 127 clearance and 139 track_width errors that were not there. route now copies the input's .kicad_pro and .kicad_dru to OUT's name when OUT has none (never over existing ones; test "route -o copies the project files").
  • Docs: 18 §12, 11 (M19 row).

docs.title: D143 — Open connections by cause; half the portfolio searches from the crowded end
Context
docs.text: M20's C5 item (doc 18 §4): "classify the dense-package failures of tiers B–D by cause (pin boxed in, via sites, layer count) and fix the largest class"; its gate is "a table of failures by cause; the fix is chosen from it". The boards are the 33 tier B-D boards the default leaves open (bench/sets/pcbench-bd-fail.txt). The records are in bench/records/m20-c5/, and the design is in doc 05 §55.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• tracemaker causes BOARD [--json FILE] (src/app/causes.{hpp,cpp}) and bench/failure_causes.py. Each open connection of a routed board is routed again alone (2 M work) on copies of the board whose routed copper is locked. Each copy has other nets' copper removed in one region: within 2 mm of an end for nets with no pad on that end's part, then all copper within 2 mm, then all copper farther away, then everything. The cause is the first copy on which the connection routes. Pins that the escape analysis says cannot leave their package, and connections that route on none of the copies, are classes of their own. On the 33 boards, the largest class is copper near the pins: 779 of 1,320 open connections.
  • RouterOptions::crowded_source: a strict search starts from the more crowded end of its connection. Crowding is the copper of other nets routed in this run, plus the pads of other nets of the end's own part, within 1 mm of the pad's box. A boxed-in pin is then proved by the enclosure test at once, instead of after a flood from the open end. route --crowded-source turns it on in every variant.
  • By default it is on in four of the portfolio's eight designed variants: 1, 5, 6 and 7 ("fast bends, shortest first", "cheap vias", "cheap crossings, escape plan", "dear vias"; their names say "crowded source"). The breakout portfolio and the seeded variants beyond eight are unchanged. The hidden --no-crowded-portfolio restores the old portfolio.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• In all eight variants. On the 33 failing boards it was 1,204 open against 1,220, but it lost two of the 59 boards that had been clean (AmpOne and bumps, one connection each). Rule 9 does not allow that.
  • An option only, off. The gain is the largest of any change measured on these boards since M17: 1,383 → 1,220 open, against --txn's +118 connections at 100 M work in M17.
  • Spend the budget differently, by capping strict searches at 100,000 expansions, by stopping the strict pass at 70 % of the budget, or by charging tracks near other parts' pads (a halo). Each was worse on the 33 boards (1,422, 1,536 and 1,394 open); they move work around without proving a boxed-in end sooner.
  • Counting the input board's copper too. The routed-item index holds only this run's copper, and the failing boards start unrouted; a second index was not worth it for boards that are already routed.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Real binary, default portfolio, KiCad judging (doc 05 §55): open connections on the 33 failing boards fell from 1,383 to 1,220, with 18 boards better, 6 worse, and 0 → 1 clean. On the 59 previously clean boards, 69 → 46 with clean 44 → 46. On the mid tier, 1,306 → 1,093 with 7 boards better and 2 worse by one connection each. On the quick tier, 32 → 24 with clean 25 → 26 and no board worse. No board gained an error.
  • The four variants were chosen by scoring every subset from per-variant results of 71 boards (portfolio_subsets.py). The mid tier, the quick tier and 21 of the clean boards were not used, and agree; it is not a precise optimum (on the mid tier alone another subset scores a little better).
  • Found afterwards (2026-10-28), outside the measured sets:
  • On the plane tier with --soft-zones (3 M work, seed 1), multichannel_mixer gains one KiCad starved_thermal, which the route reports (refill.starved_thermals) and its thermal repair (D137) does not fix. Without the crowded variants (--no-crowded-portfolio) it has none. On the same run RoyalBlue routes 125 against 103 connections, and StickHub 127 against 126. The starved_thermal errors on interf_u and the solder_mask_bridge errors on StickHub are there either way.
  • The plane_smd integration test used two variants. Variant 1 alone now leaves one connection open there, so the test uses four variants (assumption A84). The default eight route the board either way.
  • The classification is an upper bound on what each region costs: one connection alone on a locked board is easier than all of them together. Two more inner layers close 124 of the 1,320.
  • Docs: 05 §55, 18 §13, 11 (M20 row).

docs.title: D144 — --si-rules stitches the critical nets' unstitched layer changes and says where the rest are
Context
docs.text: Doc 18 B3 (M21): "Run the return-path stitching pass (--stitch-vias return) inside --si-rules, re-audit, and report unstitched layer changes and remaining detours as warnings with the net and the place". The reference-return audit (doc 05 §42) and the stitching pass (§39.3) existed. The stitching pass took its signal nets only from component rules of kind reference_plane or from --stitch-return, not from the critical nets that --si-rules routes. The critical-net report counted void crossings without saying where they were or whether a layer change was left without a return via. The records are in bench/records/m21-b3/.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• With --si-rules, after routing, the audit runs on the critical nets. A layer change it finds without a closure, with the same reference net on both sides, makes that net a return-path stitching target of that reference net, at 5 mm. That is the audit's own radius, so a change the pass stitches is closed in the audit too; the catalogue's 5.08 mm is larger. The stitching pass then runs as --stitch-vias return does, kept only if no net has more unconnected items with its vias (rule 4). --no-si-stitch turns it off; the other values of --stitch-vias combine with it.
  • The audit runs again on the stitched board. The critical-net report gains missing_stitches per net and in the totals, with missing_stitches_before_stitching. Its warnings name each unstitched layer change: the layers, the place in millimetres, and the reason. The reason is one of: no via of the plane net within 5 mm; two different reference nets with no capacitor between them; no reference copper on one side. They also name each void whose detour is over the audit's 2 mm threshold. At most eight places are listed per net, then a count of the rest.
  • The audit at a layer change: a signal layer whose trace is only a stub from a pad to the via can lie wholly over the via's own antipad, and so had no reference layer by coverage. At the via, such a layer now takes the adjacent layer (N+1, then N-1) with copper within 2 mm.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Stitch every critical via whatever the audit says. The pass already skips a via with a plane via or plated pad within the distance. Driving it from the audit's own findings means the warnings after it and the vias it placed are about the same changes.
  • A capacitor between two different reference nets. That is a placement change, not a via; it stays a warning that says so.
  • Stitching during routing (a via that brings its return via). It would cost every critical search a second via site. The after-route pass is a transaction that can be dropped, and the measured need is small (below).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Plane tier, --si-rules --soft-zones, 3 M work, no knowledge base: the critical nets' layer changes are almost all closed already, by plated GND pads and by stitching the boards carry. One change on StickHub is left; it has no plane copper on one side, which no via can fix, and the warning says so. Over five seeds with KiCad judging (bench/records/m21-a5, arms si and sistitch) it is the same: one change before and after, no via placed, no added KiCad error. Option sets other than --si-rules leave 2 to 7, so the pass matters on boards whose critical nets change layer far from a plane via, which the plane tier does not have. The mechanism is shown on a constructed board (doc 05 §57).
  • With the options off, and with --si-rules --no-si-stitch, routing is as before; with the pass, only the vias it adds differ.
  • Docs: 05 §57, 18 §14.

docs.title: D145 — KiCad 10 tuning profiles: KiCad's width rules, and per-layer widths by narrowing
Context
docs.text: Doc 18 B1 (M21): KiCad 10 projects can give a net class a tuning profile, with a track width and pair gap per signal layer, and KiCad's DRC then requires those widths when the project sets tuning_profile_track_geometries to a severity other than ignore. The engine read none of it, and its router has one width per net (doc 15 §15). The format and KiCad's rule were taken from KiCad 10.0's sources (common/project/tuning_profiles.cpp, pcbnew/drc/drc_engine.cpp) and its QA projects, and checked against kicad-cli 10.0.6. Design: doc 05 §58. Records: bench/records/m21-b1/.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• read_design_rules reads tuning_profiles and each class's tuning_profile (model::TuningProfile, DesignRules::profile_of). It adds KiCad's implicit rules (CustomRule::implicit) in KiCad's place, before the custom rules, carrying the severity of tuning_profile_track_geometries, ignore included:
  • per profiled layer, an exact track_width, with A.inDiffPair('*') added for a differential profile;
  • for pairs, an exact diff_pair_gap.

The rules have KiCad's name ("tuning profile 'NAME'"), so the engine's DRC and KiCad's report the same violation. - Where KiCad 10.0.6's behaviour differs from its source, the engine follows the behaviour (doc 05 §58): - The severity of track_width comes from the last matching rule, so an ignored profile rule hides the board minimum. - hasExactNetclass is evaluated only in implicit rules; in a user's rule KiCad never matches it. - The coupled-pair clearance at the profile's gap applies to the two halves' tracks only (NetClass::tuning_pair_gap), not to a track against the partner's pads. KiCad's AB.isCoupledDiffPair() clearance rule is not added. - Routing, whatever the severity (a profile is the designer's statement of the impedance): - A single-ended profile's nets route at the widest of its widths. After routing, each track is narrowed to its layer's width, judged like the other after-route passes. - A differential profile's pairs route at one layer's width and gap, preferring a layer the class's SMD pads are on, then the geometry most layers share. A disallow track rule keeps them off layers with another width or gap. - Width and pair-gap rules do not switch the router to exact checks (they set no clearance). - --json has tuning_profiles, and the log has a line per profile; a class naming an undefined profile is warned about. - The delays (per layer, per via, time-domain tuning) are read but not used: they are B2's.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Per-layer width inside the router. About twenty call sites of the router take one width per net (clearance disks, via codes, escape stubs, caches keyed by width); changing all of them is a large, risky change for a gain that narrowing gives for single nets.
  • Route at the most common width, and keep other layers clear (also for single-ended nets). Correct, but it gives up layers. On boards whose inner layers are narrower, the nets would lose the inner layers entirely.
  • Narrow pairs too. A pair's centrelines stay where they are, so narrowing widens its gap by the width removed; KiCad's exact gap rule would then fail on those layers.
  • Apply the profile only when KiCad would check it. Then the router's tracks would differ from the designer's stated impedance just because the check is off; the widths are the design either way.
  • Follow KiCad's source rather than its behaviour (evaluate hasExactNetclass everywhere, relax the pads to the profile's gap). The judge is kicad-cli: on RoyalBlue that gave three added clearance errors, and the parity corpus would disagree on two cases.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Classes without a profile, and projects without profiles, are unchanged: the reader adds nothing and the route job does nothing.
  • Pairs with a profile route on fewer layers when the profile's layers disagree.
  • Single-ended nets keep the clearance of their widest layer on every layer. That is conservative on the narrower layers.
  • Measured (bench/records/m21-b1, KiCad 10.0.6 with the check at error): no added KiCad error on two plane-tier boards given profiles. On RoyalBlue, 68 inner tracks are narrowed, and routing with the single-ended profile alone is the same as without profiles (125/147). The USB pair profile costs five connections (120/147).
  • The parity corpus has four new cases, and all 220 match KiCad.
  • No real board with profiles was available; the Kookabus boards are still missing (doc 18 §7).
  • Found afterwards (B2, same night; D147): the fixtures' net settings were at schema 4, which KiCad migrates by giving every class an empty profile, so the "no added KiCad error" above was measured by a KiCad that checked no profile. Rejudged at schema 5, three fixes followed (Default's profile inherited, the pair width from a single-ended profile, no neck-down on profiled nets). Results with those fixes: plane_smd 48/49 with no added error; RoyalBlue 102/147 with the single-ended profile and 104/147 with both. Both have no width error, and the second has 5 diff_pair_gap_out_of_range errors at the USB-C connector. "Narrowing is free" does not hold (doc 05 §58, bench/records/m21-b1/runs/b1-v5).
  • Docs: 05 §58, 18 §15, 11 (M21 row).

docs.title: D146 — --si-rules keeps critical-first: five seeds settle #24's options
Context
docs.text: Doc 18 A5 (M21): issue #24's three routing rules (--critical-first, --critical-via-cost, --split-cost; --si-rules turns on all three) were measured on one seed (bench/records/issue24). That table suggested that the costs without the order (--split-cost 4 --critical-via-cost 3) were better than --si-rules. A5 asks for five seeds on the plane tier before deciding. Records: bench/records/m21-a5.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• --si-rules keeps all three rules, critical first included. No default changes: the options stay off unless asked for.
  • Doc 05 §44 gets the five-seed table's conclusion.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Drop critical-first from --si-rules (the one-seed table's best, split + via). It would leave unrouted the crystal net and the debugger USB pair on RoyalBlue, which critical-first routes in every seed: 23 of 28 critical nets against 27. It would gain 5 connections of the other nets and 9 fewer unconnected by KiCad. A rule set meant for the critical nets should not trade them for the others; the user who wants the costs alone can still ask for them.
  • Turn some of the options on by default. The cost terms' gains on common nets are small (2-4 vias, 3-6 crossings over 23 nets), and critical first costs every board some completion. Defaults stay off.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Measured over five seeds (bench/records/m21-a5): the critical-net measures do not vary with the seed. Each arm's are identical in all five; only the other nets' connections vary, by up to 8 of 882. The arms' differences are therefore systematic, not noise, on this binary.
  • With all three rules, the cost terms' gains on common nets vanish (22 → 22 vias, 74 → 74 crossings). Why is not measured. Tuning the costs together with the order is open.
  • B3's return stitching had nothing to stitch on these boards under --si-rules (one change, with no plane copper on one side).
  • Docs: 05 §44, 18 §16, 11 (M21 row).

docs.title: D147 — Time-domain matching measured as KiCad 10.0.6 measures it, and KiCad's net-class and pair-coupling semantics
Context
docs.text: Doc 18 B2 (M21): length and skew groups in picoseconds, with per-layer and via delays from B1's tuning profiles, tuned to a target delay and checked against KiCad's own rules. The gate is a DDR-style generated fixture and two real boards within tolerance by KiCad's DRC, in delay. The engine read ps as a unit but measured lengths its own way, and its router read time rules as lengths. Checking B2 against KiCad also showed that the B1 fixtures (D145) had been judged by a KiCad that read no profile at all (net settings at schema 4). Design: doc 05 §59 and the note at the end of §58. Records: bench/records/m21-b2 and bench/records/m21-b1/runs/b1-v5.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Measure as KiCad 10.0.6 does, quirks included (drc/length.hpp): its chain merge, which depends on order on branched nets (file order here, pointer order in KiCad); via spans; clipping in vias and pads; and its rounding of lengths and delays. The DRC's length and skew check groups items by rule and compares a ps rule with the delay. A minimum skew fails on the reference net, as in 10.0.6.
  • Tune delays in the router (tune_delays): ps windows first, then ps skew groups or pairs, with meanders weighted by each layer's delay per mm. Time rules are no longer read as lengths.
  • Net classes as 10.0.6 resolves them:
  • Default joins a net's effective class when the matched classes leave a field unset, or when none of them has a profile and Default has one.
  • hasNetclass is evaluated.
  • A class with no profile takes Default's.
  • Net settings older than schema 5 lose their profiles, with a warning.
  • Profiled nets are not necked down, and a single-ended profile sets the pair width too.
  • Port KiCad's diff-pair coupling test into the DRC (drc/coupling.hpp, check_diff_pairs), so that diff_pair_gap and diff_pair_uncoupled rules are checked, the profile's implicit gap rule included. The router does not yet use it.
  • The route summary no longer records --view-embed. Like --view-token, it gave away the machine's addresses.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Follow KiCad master's merge (simple two-end joints only). It is the better rule, but the judge is 10.0.6, and the two agree on every net that does not branch inside a via.
  • Tune the delay by length, converting each window with one delay per mm. That is wrong as soon as a net changes layer or has a via, and a profile gives each layer its own delay.
  • Keep the B1 results with a note. They were measured by a judge that saw no profile; they had to be redone.
  • Make the router avoid coupling-gap errors now. That needs the coupling test inside the commit check for pair nets with a maximum gap, and the pad-to-pad joins of interleaved connectors handled. It is left open and reported.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• KiCad's QA board: the delays match to 0.01 ps, with the same one violation.
  • Length parity: of 329 nets on four demo boards, 325 match to under 1 µm. Four branched power and mesh nets differ by up to 1.58 mm, because of 10.0.6's order dependence.
  • ddr8, interf_u and RoyalBlue end KiCad-clean on their delay rules (20, 7 and 1 errors with the build before B2), interf_u and RoyalBlue at the same routed counts.
  • B1 rejudged: plane_smd 48/49 with no added error. RoyalBlue drops to 102 (single-ended) and 104/147 (both profiles), from 125: KiCad's exact width with no neck-down is the price of a single-ended profile on Default. Five diff_pair_gap_out_of_range errors remain at RoyalBlue's USB-C connector.
  • Open:
  • the router does not avoid coupling-gap errors;
  • fromTo() is not evaluated;
  • the bus tuner ignores ps skew;
  • a net in two classes uses the first one's parameters;
  • KiCad's pair-name suffixes with trailing digits are not paired.
  • Docs: 05 §58 (rejudged) and §59, 18 §17, 11 (M21 row).

docs.title: D148 — The router avoids KiCad's diff-pair coupling-gap errors
Context
docs.text: D147 ported KiCad 10.0.6's diff-pair coupling test into the DRC, but not into the router. B1's RoyalBlue fixture with the USB pair profile (a 0.15 mm gap, so a rule with min = max = 0.15 mm) was left with five diff_pair_gap_out_of_range errors by KiCad. They sit at the USB-C connector, where the interleaved D+/D− pads are joined pad to pad and the halves leave in parallel before the pair forms. Rule 1 says nothing goes on the board without the exact check, and these errors broke it. Design: doc 05 §59. Records: bench/records/m21-b2/runs/couple-b1, couple-b2.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The coupling test is part of Obstacles::segment_state for a net whose partner exists and that has a non-ignored diff_pair_gap rule with a minimum or a maximum on the layer. A new track is coupled with each of the partner's tracks on that layer by drc::couple, with the same epsilon and the same visibility test as the DRC.
  • When the gap is out of range and the partner track was routed, it is rippable.
  • When the partner track is fixed copper, the track is blocked.
  • The search tests each lattice step of such a net as well. With the test only at commit, the router found the same path that the check then refused, and the USB connections failed with "exact check rejected the lattice path" (101 of 147 routed against 104).
  • The bounds are taken per net and layer from the last matching rule for a track of the net, as the DRC does. A rule that depends on the place is taken as it matches anywhere.
  • The visibility test ignores pad holes on layers that have none of the pad's copper. It may call a pair coupled that KiCad would call hidden, so it is stricter than KiCad, never looser.
  • Always on. Boards without such a rule skip the test entirely.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Commit check only: cheaper per step, but it lost three connections on RoyalBlue as described above.
  • A cost on the lattice for the partner's neighbourhood, the way pairs are steered towards their gap: it would not be exact, so the commit check would still be needed, and it would not cover the "nothing between" condition.
  • Route pairs as coupled pairs end to end: the right long-term answer for pairs, but much larger. It also would not cover the pad-to-pad stretches at the connector, where KiCad sees coupling before the pair forms.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• RoyalBlue with the profile still routes 104/147, with no gap errors (353 tracks against 349).
  • The other four B1 fixtures and the three B2 fixtures are identical to the runs before: routed counts, tracks, vias and added errors.
  • A unit test routes a pair whose pads are 2 mm apart under a 0.15–0.25 mm gap rule. With the rule ignored the straight tracks break it, and with the rule in force none do.
  • Cost: one coupling test per partner track on the layer, on each step of a pair net, and only on boards with a bounded gap rule.
  • Still open:
  • diff_pair_uncoupled is checked but not routed for.
  • Pairs are recognised by the last character only, unlike KiCad's MatchDpSuffix.
  • Doc 05 §59 has a new paragraph and a new results line, and its "Not done" item is removed.

docs.title: D149 — Differential pairs named as KiCad's MatchDpSuffix names them
Context
docs.text:
The engine paired nets by their last character only (P/N, +/−). For inDiffPair() it matched the whole name minus that character, or the whole name. KiCad 10.0.6 (DRC_ENGINE::MatchDpSuffix, inDiffPairFunc) does it differently: - It skips trailing digits and underscores before the polarity character, so DQS_P0 pairs with DQS_N0. - It matches inDiffPair against the base before that character, or against the base without a trailing underscore.

Doc 05 §59 listed this as not done. vme-wren's DDR4 strobes are such pairs, and KiCad reports coupling-gap errors on them that the engine could not see.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• drc::match_dp_suffix ports MatchDpSuffix exactly, including counting the polarity character in the suffix. The rule engine pairs every net through it, keeping the partner, the polarity and the base.
  • inDiffPair('x') matches the base, or the base without a trailing underscore, by wildcard as KiCad does.
  • Pair routing, the gap relaxation between pair halves, the DRC's coupling check and the router's coupling test all take polarity and partner from the rule engine. They no longer read the last character themselves.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: • Keep the last-character rule and add a digits special case. Its rules would still differ from KiCad's, and the inDiffPair base would still be wrong for names like D_P. In KiCad that base is D_, so inDiffPair('D') matches it through the underscore rule.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rule parity has two new cases, diff_pair_suffix and diff_pair_suffix_base, judged by KiCad 10.0.6. All 231 match. The build before this change fails diff_pair_suffix.
  • Among 4,143 fixture boards, two pair differently:
  • vme-wren (DQS_P0..3/DQS_N0..3);
  • a freerouting fixture (/N1//P1 and others).

Neither board is in a bench set or a test, so the bench tiers are unchanged. - A net whose name happens to fit the rule and whose complement exists is now a pair, as it is in KiCad. - On vme-wren, our DRC now finds the DQS0 pair's coupling-gap errors at 1.5173 mm, as KiCad does. It still misses the pair at 1.8573 mm and reports DQS1–3 uncoupled lengths that KiCad does not. Both look like the visibility test, which sees via rings that KiCad has removed on unconnected layers (remove_unused_layers, not modelled). The CK and WR_CLK uncoupled differences were there before.

docs.title: D150 — Vias and pads that remove unconnected copper, and tuning patterns left out of pair coupling
Context
docs.text: D149 left vme-wren's pair verdicts different from KiCad's and blamed via rings that KiCad removes on unconnected layers (remove_unused_layers), which the engine did not model. The same gap gave 22,362 clearance and 21 shorting reports on vme-wren where KiCad gives none: the engine judged rings, and filled zones around rings, that are not on the board. Looking further, two more KiCad 10.0.6 rules in the diff-pair coupling test (drc_test_provider_diff_pair_coupling.cpp) were missing: tracks of a tuning pattern are left out, and nearly parallel tracks are coupled because SEG::Intersect in line mode gives up when the crossing point does not fit in 32 bits. Doc 05 §60, records in bench/records/d150-padstacks.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Read the padstack mode of vias and through-hole pads token by token in file order, as KiCad's parser sets it, with zone_layer_connections.
  • Flash as KiCad does (drc::flash_layers): a conditional layer keeps copper where a zone joins it there or where a same-net track, arc, via or pad reaches its hole on that layer (CN_VISITOR), with KiCad's exclusions.
  • Split the copper item: copper on the flashed layers, plus a hole-shaped bare part on the others, checked at copper clearance and left out of connectivity and of the copper-only checks.
  • Refill recomputes the zone connections first, as KiCad's filler does, and knocks a same-net via that no zone joins out of the fill on that layer.
  • Router: stricter than KiCad. A new track keeps clear of a same-net bare part, and a new via keeps clear of a same-net item that may lose copper, instead of relying on KiCad to flash the layer.
  • Tuning patterns: members of a (generated (type tuning_pattern)) group are marked when read and skipped by the DRC's coupling test and length sums and by the router's coupling test.
  • Nearly parallel tracks: drc::couple computes the crossing point as SEG::intersects does (128-bit rescale, wrapping 64-bit addition) and couples the tracks when it falls outside 32 bits.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
• Treat such vias as copper on every layer (as before). Safe for the router, but the DRC reports thousands of errors KiCad does not, and the refill leaves voids KiCad fills.
